## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:62

> **Indeed, the believers, Jews, Christians, and Sabians—whoever ˹truly˺ believes in Allah and the Last Day and does good will have their reward with their Lord. And there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.**

### Expanded Commentary

**A Verse That Widens the Horizon**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings indeed and christians into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. Its first term in 2:62 sets the subject, while the later term shows what that subject demands, permits, or exposes. The order of 2:62 gives the reader a path through the verse: begin with what Allah names, follow the consequence, and resist the temptation to turn a living address into a slogan.

Cf. 5:69. Sabeans renders ṣābiʾ, which some derive from the verb ṣabaʾa insofar as it can be used to mean to go from one religion to another. It also means to rise, as in the case of stars, or to come upon, to emerge, or to arise. Others read it as coming from ṣabā, meaning to incline, as in from one religion to another (al-Ṭabarī). The pagan Arabs used to call the Prophet Muhammad a ṣābiʾ in this sense, in that he had left the religion of his forefathers (al-Rāzī).

**Who Were the Sabeans?**

According to the commentators the ṣābiʿ could be: (1) people who have no recognizable religion; according to some accounts, there were people who declared, There is no god but Allah, but had no rites or books or prophet, and did not accept the Prophet Muhammad; (2) people who worshipped angels and faced the qiblah, reciting the Psalms; (3) a group of the People of the Book who left their religion; (4) people who think they are following the religion of Noah; or (5) monotheists who believe in the effects of the planets, and hence are unbelievers .

In the early centuries of Islamic history, the people of Ḥarrān in Syria who followed a religion deeply influenced by esoteric elements in earlier Greek and Near Eastern religions called themselves Ṣabeans to enjoy the status given to the ṣābiʾūn in the Qur'an. Members of the present-day Mandaean sect in southern Iraq and Iran are also called ṣābiʾ. They are monotheists and consider John the Baptist to be their prophet; their main ritual is baptism, and many believe that they migrated to their present site from the Jordan Valley.

**Al-Ghazālī on the Reach of Divine Mercy**

Christians renders naṣārā (sing. naṣrān or naṣrānī), which most plausibly derives from Jesus hometown of Nazareth (al-Nāṣirah), but several other etymologies are also given. Acts 24:5 describes an accuser who speaks pejoratively of Paul as a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes, which is the only time this term appears in the Bible. This pejorative use continued in the early centuries of Christianity, but later developed, in some quarters, as a way of labeling Jewish Christians as distinct from Pauline Christians, and other terms, such as the Middle Persian tarsāg and of course kristiyān, came into use as labels for the followers of Christ.

The precise origin of naṣārā has, for some, some bearing on whether certain beliefs mentioned in the Qur'an, such as the worship of Mary and Jesus (5:116) or Allahs taking a consort (72:3), stem from a local sect of Christians with beliefs different from mainstream Chalcedonian Christianity. Using etymologies in this way, although often interesting, can be misleading, since the origin of a word often has scant connection with its later use; for further discussion of these issues, see 3:3–4c; 4:171c; 5:17c; 5:73c.

**Reading the Verse Without Abusing It**

Those who are Jews makes use of the verb hāda/yahūdu, which is very likely derived from the noun yahūd, or Jew, and is literally something like those who hād, where hād is a verb. Among the etymologies given are that hād means to be repentant, to incline toward one other, or to move (as when one recites the Torah; Th).

Concerning this verse the commentator al-Qushayrī writes, “The differences in paths, with the oneness of the origin, does not hinder the beauty of acceptance. Whosoever affirms [Allah] the Real in His signs, and believes in the truth and His Qualities of which He informs them—namely, the Truth and His Qualities—then the differences in religious paths [or laws, sharʿ] and the differences in the appellation of names do not impinge on the realization of the good pleasure [of Allah].”

**The horizon beyond the immediate scene**

The theologian and mystic Abū Ḥamid al-Ghazzālī (d. 505/1111), in his famous work Fayṣal al-tafriqah, argues that the “Christians of Byzantium” and the “Turks” (still outside the Islamic world at that time) would come under Allah’s Mercy. Those who know the teachings and virtues of the Prophet and yet still deny him deserve to be called disbelievers, but al-Ghazzālī gives wide latitude in recognizing the obstacles to this knowledge. How could a Turk who had never heard of Muhammad be faulted? Moreover, why should a person who grows up hearing the Prophet Muhammad referred to as “the great liar” investigate his truth claims, since one would not expect the same from a Muslim who hears of someone accused of being a false prophet?

Hearing the name Muhammad means nothing if one learns only of the opposite of his true attributes. One could extend this reasoning to point out that one is unlikely to deem a religion good or desire to learn about it, if the only followers one meets are bad. Such mitigating circumstances, namely, that birthplace, upbringing, and social experience mediate one’s knowledge of religion, provide ample space for Allah’s Mercy to encompass those who believe in Him and in the Hereafter and act righteously.

**A divine name that governs the meaning**

Some argue that the verse refers to certain Jews, Christians, and Sabeans who adhered to these faiths before the Prophet’s mission, but who then acknowledged him when he came—people such as Salmān al-Fārsī, Abū Dharr al-Ghifārī, and the monks Waraqah ibn Nawfal and Baḥīrah (al-Rāzī); others have understood it to include Zoroastrians as well.

Al-Zamakhsharī and some others argue that those who believe refers to the hypocrites, because they affirm belief outwardly, and lump them together with Jews, Christians, and Sabeans to form a first group, which is then juxtaposed with those mentioned in the second part of the verse, the true believers in the Prophet and Islam. If this interpretation is accepted, this would be the only instance in the Qur'an when those who believe was used ironically or with the implication of referring to the hypocrites. Al-Rāzī mentions the double usage of believe in 4:136, O you who believe! Believe in Allah and His Messenger, as an example where one can be called a believer in two senses, necessitating the command to believe, though this is not the interpretation given to that particular verse when it is discussed on its own. Indeed, in 4:136, al-Rāzī seems to approve of the opinion that the use of muʾmin (believer) without any qualifier is reserved solely for Muslims.

**Mercy and warning held together**

Some argue that these other groups are believers simply insofar as they affirm the truth of the Prophet Muhammad (al-Ṭabarī). However, Christians who affirm the message of Muhammad would no longer be Christian at all, just as those who practice idolatry would no longer be idolaters if they accept Muhammad. Still, it is not uncommon for commentators to insert the phrase and follows Muhammad and acts according to his Law as a gloss on whosoever believes in Allah (Aj) Al-Qurṭubī mentions an opinion, attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, that 3:85 (Whosoever seeks a religion other than submission, it shall not be accepted of him, and in the Hereafter he shall be among the losers) abrogates this verse. But a widely accepted principle of abrogation is that only legal rulings or commands can be abrogated, not descriptive statements, especially as regards ones status in the Hereafter.

For the commentator al-Bayḍāwī, this verse refers to those who fulfilled their obligations before their religions were abrogated by Islam, or it means that these various kinds of disbelievers are saved when they believe sincerely (since he interprets the first reference to be to hypocrites).

**The deed before its final account**

Many commentators on this verse disallow those who deny Islam and the Prophet to be included among those who are saved from eternal fear and grief, but as al-Ghazzālīs position makes clear, such denial is hard to verify, especially since ones rejection of Islam in later times might simply be a verdict pronounced upon Muslims and not upon the Prophet himself. Moreover, the plain sense of the verse cannot be denied without introducing inconsistencies: in no other instance is a believer used as a name for a hypocrite, and in no sense does a Jew or Christian following the religion of Muhammad continue to be called a Jew or Christian. Moreover, the affirmation of the belief of Jews and Christians is reinforced elsewhere in the Qur'an, including 3:110; 5:48; 22:67–69; for a fuller discussion, see the essay The Qur'anic View of Sacred History and Other Religions. Also see commentary on 3:110–15 for similar issues relating to religious communities.

**Why the promise or threat is just**

No fear shall come upon them, nor shall they grieve is a description of ones life after death, the equivalent of what might be called salvation. It describes the reward of those who follow Allahs Guidance (v. 38), those who submit with faith (2:112), whoever believes and is righteous (6:48), the friend of Allah (10:62), and those who say, Our Lord is Allah (46:13).

The verse's reference to indeed widens the scene beyond the immediate reward or pain. A deed in 2:62 may appear small when measured by public attention, yet its meaning changes when it is known by Allah and carried into the final account. Warning and mercy belong together in 2:62: accountability is serious because the human being is not abandoned to meaninglessness.

A useful way to test the verse is to ask what would change if indeed were taken seriously when no audience was present. The answer cannot be only a feeling, because 2:62 connects inward recognition with a discernible choice. Nor can it be only an outward display, because the choice in 2:62 loses its Qur'anic meaning when it is made for reputation rather than for Allah. The passage holds intention and action together in 2:62.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:63

> **And ˹remember˺ when We took a covenant from you and raised the mountain above you ˹saying˺, “Hold firmly to that ˹Scripture˺ which We have given you and observe its teachings so perhaps you will become mindful ˹of Allah˺.”**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Mountain Over Their Heads**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between took and mountain. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:63. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:63. Cf. v. 93; 4:154. Mount renders ṭūr, which commentators point out is a word of Syriac origin for mountain (jabal; Ṭ), but is nevertheless an Arabic word. There is general agreement among the interpreters that this verse literally means that a mountain, either Sinai or a mountain from Palestine, was uprooted and made to physically move and float over the Israelites, in order to frighten them . However, it seems just as likely that the phrasing here, raised the Mount over you, parallels the English construction the mountain loomed above them.

**"Take Hold with Strength" — The Terms of Take**

Exodus 19 mentions a thick cloud on the mountain and that Mount Sinai was wrapped in smoke, because the Lord had descended upon it in a fire; the smoke went up like the smoke of a kiln, while the whole mountain shook violently (vv. 16, 18). Before this, the Israelites were commanded, Be careful not to go up the mountain or to touch the edge of it. Any who touch the mountain shall be put to death (v. 12). Since the Qur'an does not describe the mountain as floating, but only as rising above the Israelites, one can understand that it loomed over them in a terrifying and meaningful way, an interpretation that is all the more plausible in light of the descriptions from Exodus 19.

**Raised Hands and a Raised Mountain**

To take hold . . . with strength is understood to mean doing so earnestly and obediently and resolving to act upon it . In it means in the Torah given to Moses (Ibn Kathīr).

The verse describes took not as a private opinion but as a direction that changes perception and conduct. In 2:63, guidance is recognized by what it makes a person do with knowledge, power, and desire. For 2:63, inward assent is linked to an observable response: the heart's claim is tested by the path it chooses when the claim becomes costly.

In 2:63, the distinction between public appearance and inward truth is especially relevant. A person may use the language of took while arranging the act around another purpose. Here the reader should let the sentence do that work.

**Certainty, doubt, and moral action**

The exegetical tradition approaches took from more than one angle, but its differences are more useful when their shared question is made visible. The commentators ask what the wording of 2:63 includes, what it excludes, and how it fits with the other passages of the Qur'an. A responsible reading can preserve those alternatives in 2:63 without pretending that every possibility has equal strength.

There is also a distinction between understanding took and using it as a label for other people. The first task belongs to learning; the second requires evidence, fairness, and awareness of one's own motives in 2:63. The verse 2:63 addresses the reader before it supplies material for judging a neighbour. Its warning becomes safer and more productive when self-examination comes first.

The theology and practical instruction of 2:63 therefore support one another. If Allah knows or commands mountain, that knowledge or command changes how a person handles time, power, money, speech, and private desire. A doctrine that never reaches those choices has not yet been read at the level demanded by 2:63.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:65

> **You are already aware of those of you who broke the Sabbath. We said to them, “Be disgraced apes!”**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Sabbath and the Trick**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between already and sabbath. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:65. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:65. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:65.

**What the Transformation Means**

Outcast can also mean lowly (al-Rāzī). This is understood by some to refer to the people described in 7:163, who were tried by Allah when fish would come to them only on the Sabbath. Others interpret it to mean that all previous prophets taught that Friday was the most excellent day, that the Day of Judgment would come to pass on a Friday, and that it is celebrated by the angels in Heaven. The Jews preferred Saturday as the day of Allahs rest, and because of their disobedience they were punished by Allah by being prohibited from engaging in their normal activities on that day. The Christians preferred Sunday, noting its excellence as the first day (al-Ṭabarī).

**The Sin of Hīlah — Outsmarting the Law**

Other instances in which human beings are likened to animals include the following: The parable of those [who were] made to bear the Torah, then did not bear it, is that of an ass bearing books (62:5); And be moderate in thy pace and lower thy voice. Truly the vilest of voices are those of asses (31:19); The parable of those who take protectors apart from Allah is that of the spider that makes a house (29:41); Thus his parable is that of a dog: if you attack him, he lolls out his tongue, and if you leave him alone, he lolls out his tongue (7:176). Also, many aḥādīth speak of people resurrected in the form of various animals, according to their inner nature.

**The verse in its immediate setting**

Al-Qurṭubī interprets it as being akin to the command of 17:50, which literally reads Be you of stone, or of iron, making it rhetorical. One can read this as, As you wish then, be apes, as you have chosen to be. Mujāhid says, Their hearts were transformed, but they did not transform into apes, comparing it to the ass carrying books of 62:5 (Ibn Kathīr).

The passage at 2:65 moves between belief, action, and consequence, so a sound reading must preserve all three rather than allowing one attractive phrase to swallow the rest.

The standard in 2:65 remains practical because it can be applied before a dispute reaches a court or a crisis reaches its worst point. ## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:67

> **And ˹remember˺ when Moses said to his people, “Allah commands you to sacrifice a cow.” They replied, “Are you mocking us?” Moses responded, “I seek refuge in Allah from acting foolishly!”**

### Expanded Commentary

**A Command Without a Reason Stated**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between moses and replied. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:67. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:67. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:67.

**Moses' Refuge: Not Among the Ignorant**

These verses contain an account of an encounter between Moses and the Jews that is rather detailed in comparison to other Qur'anic accounts. First the Israelites balk at Allahs Command, then interrogate Moses on its particulars, and finally obey it. Cf. Numbers 19, where a ceremony involving a red cow is mentioned. The instructions given the Israelites there, similar to those given in 2:71, are that it is to be a cow without defect, in which there is no blemish and on which no yoke has been laid (19:2). The seemingly impertinent questioning of the Israelites is not part of the Biblical account.

**The Background the Verse Withholds**

One account of the background story is that a rich man was secretly murdered by his heir. Moses, as the prophet of Allah, was asked to learn the identity of the killer. After the debate over the cow, the people finally slaughtered it, took a limb from it, and struck the corpse, which then quickened and identified the killer. This would continue the story of the cow up to v. 73. To be ignorant (jāhil) in the Qur'an is more than to have a lack of knowledge; it is a disposition against it, a kind of pathological adherence to ones own way and ones ignorance.

**"Slaughter a Cow" and the Ordinary Height of Tests**

The term could also be rendered ignoramus. Unlike the case of the blind man seeking knowledge from the Prophet (see 80:1–4), the ignoramus is deliberately ignorant and in the dark. Similar instances in the Qur'an show the enmity or vice inherent in the Qur'anic concept of ignorance: Had Allah willed, He would have gathered them all to guidance—so be not among the ignorant (6:35); I exhort thee, lest thou be among the ignorant (11:46); If Thou dost not turn their scheming away from me, I shall incline toward them and be among the ignorant (12:33).

It is also related to the concept of the pre-Islamic Days of Ignorance, called the jāhiliyyah.

**History as a present warning**

Now you have brought the truth means “now you have made it clear to us” (al-Ṭabarī). That they almost did not was because the cow was so costly (according to the story recounted by al-Ṭabarī, there was only one such cow, and it was owned by an old woman who was asking a very high price for it); or because they did not want the identity of the killer to come to light because of the potential scandal . The Prophet said, “Had they taken the nearest cow and sacrificed it, it would have been enough for them.”

**The covenant behind the event**

In Ibn ʿAjībah’s esoteric commentary on this verse, the egotistical soul must be killed in order for the spiritual soul to live. The best time for a soul to inflict the knife of asceticism and poverty upon itself is when it is neither too old, when its habits are ingrained and change becomes more difficult, nor too young (v. 68), when it feels immortal and sees no need to change. It is a soul that does not desire the world (not broken to plow the earth) and is pure of the blemishes that bind it to the world (v. 71). The soul is beautiful if it is good (v. 69). It is only when the soul has been purified and made beautiful and severed its inner attachment to the world that it is worthy to be sacrificed to Allah.

**Memory turned into responsibility**

The reference to moses turns memory into a demand. A community can recount a rescue, a miracle, or a failure and still repeat the same error if it treats history as the property of ancestors. In this passage the earlier event becomes evidence addressed to the present: blessing creates a duty, and a broken promise leaves a recognizable pattern.

The standard in 2:67 remains practical because it can be applied before a dispute reaches a court or a crisis reaches its worst point. One can notice the first small departure from moses: an excuse, a concealed obligation, an unexamined desire, or a promise treated as optional. Returning at that point is easier than defending a settled habit. The warning is therefore also an opening for repair.

**The people and the command**

In 2:67, the verse also sits within the Qur'an's larger refusal to separate worship from truthfulness. Prayer, remembrance, generosity, patience, and justice are different acts in 2:67, but they are trained by the same capacity to stand before Allah without constructing a false account. The statement in 2:67 strengthens that capacity by making one particular choice visible.

A reader who finds the command in 2:67 difficult should distinguish difficulty from impossibility. For 2:67, difficulty may be the place where desire, habit, or social pressure is being corrected; impossibility is a separate legal and moral question. The passage does not praise needless hardship, but it does not permit comfort to redefine moses until the demand disappears.

The final emphasis of 2:67 returns to responsibility. No explanation of moses is complete if it leaves the reader with information about earlier communities but no question about present conduct. The verse 2:67 asks what can be repaired now: a promise kept, a right restored, a motive purified, or a harmful practice abandoned. That is where knowledge becomes guidance.

**What the exegetes disputed**

The choice of the word moses in 2:67 also matters. It leaves room for the full context of 2:67 instead of allowing one translation gloss to carry every shade of meaning. Classical Arabic often places a broad word inside a narrow scene; in 2:67, the surrounding clauses determine whether the emphasis falls on an act, an intention, a condition, or a consequence. Here the reader should let the sentence do that work.

The exegetical tradition approaches moses from more than one angle, but its differences are more useful when their shared question is made visible. A responsible reading can preserve those alternatives in 2:67 without pretending that every possibility has equal strength.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:69

> **They said, “Call upon your Lord to specify for us its colour.” He replied, “Allah says, ‘It should be a bright yellow cow—pleasant to see.’”**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Second Question: The Interrogation Continues**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between call and colour. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:69. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:69. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:69.

**The Yellow Cow: Beauty Specified**

These verses contain an account of an encounter between Moses and the Jews that is rather detailed in comparison to other Qur'anic accounts. First the Israelites balk at Allahs Command, then interrogate Moses on its particulars, and finally obey it. Cf. Numbers 19, where a ceremony involving a red cow is mentioned. The instructions given the Israelites there, similar to those given in 2:71, are that it is to be a cow without defect, in which there is no blemish and on which no yoke has been laid (19:2). The seemingly impertinent questioning of the Israelites is not part of the Biblical account.

**Ibn ʿAjībah: The Beauty of the Purified Soul**

One account of the background story is that a rich man was secretly murdered by his heir. Moses, as the prophet of Allah, was asked to learn the identity of the killer. After the debate over the cow, the people finally slaughtered it, took a limb from it, and struck the corpse, which then quickened and identified the killer. This would continue the story of the cow up to v. 73. To be ignorant (jāhil) in the Qur'an is more than to have a lack of knowledge; it is a disposition against it, a kind of pathological adherence to ones own way and ones ignorance.

**The horizon beyond the immediate scene**

The term could also be rendered ignoramus. Unlike the case of the blind man seeking knowledge from the Prophet (see 80:1–4), the ignoramus is deliberately ignorant and in the dark. Similar instances in the Qur'an show the enmity or vice inherent in the Qur'anic concept of ignorance: Had Allah willed, He would have gathered them all to guidance—so be not among the ignorant (6:35); I exhort thee, lest thou be among the ignorant (11:46); If Thou dost not turn their scheming away from me, I shall incline toward them and be among the ignorant (12:33).

It is also related to the concept of the pre-Islamic Days of Ignorance, called the jāhiliyyah.

**A divine name that governs the meaning**

Now you have brought the truth means “now you have made it clear to us” (al-Ṭabarī). That they almost did not was because the cow was so costly (according to the story recounted by al-Ṭabarī, there was only one such cow, and it was owned by an old woman who was asking a very high price for it); or because they did not want the identity of the killer to come to light because of the potential scandal. The Prophet said, “Had they taken the nearest cow and sacrificed it, it would have been enough for them.”

**Mercy and warning held together**

In Ibn ʿAjībah’s esoteric commentary on this verse, the egotistical soul must be killed in order for the spiritual soul to live. The best time for a soul to inflict the knife of asceticism and poverty upon itself is when it is neither too old, when its habits are ingrained and change becomes more difficult, nor too young (v. 68), when it feels immortal and sees no need to change. It is a soul that does not desire the world (not broken to plow the earth) and is pure of the blemishes that bind it to the world (v. 71). The soul is beautiful if it is good (v. 69). It is only when the soul has been purified and made beautiful and severed its inner attachment to the world that it is worthy to be sacrificed to Allah.

**The deed before its final account**

The verse's reference to call widens the scene beyond the immediate reward or pain. A deed in 2:69 may appear small when measured by public attention, yet its meaning changes when it is known by Allah and carried into the final account. Warning and mercy belong together in 2:69: accountability is serious because the human being is not abandoned to meaninglessness.

The standard in 2:69 remains practical because it can be applied before a dispute reaches a court or a crisis reaches its worst point. One can notice the first small departure from call: an excuse, a concealed obligation, an unexamined desire, or a promise treated as optional. Returning at that point is easier than defending a settled habit. The warning is therefore also an opening for repair.

**Why the promise or threat is just**

The final emphasis of 2:69 returns to responsibility. No explanation of call is complete if it leaves the reader with information about earlier communities but no question about present conduct. The verse 2:69 asks what can be repaired now: a promise kept, a right restored, a motive purified, or a harmful practice abandoned. That is where knowledge becomes guidance.

The choice of the word call in 2:69 also matters. It leaves room for the full context of 2:69 instead of allowing one translation gloss to carry every shade of meaning. Classical Arabic often places a broad word inside a narrow scene; in 2:69, the surrounding clauses determine whether the emphasis falls on an act, an intention, a condition, or a consequence. Here the reader should let the sentence do that work.

**The Hereafter in the argument**

The exegetical tradition approaches call from more than one angle, but its differences are more useful when their shared question is made visible. The commentators ask what the wording of 2:69 includes, what it excludes, and how it fits with the other passages of the Qur'an. A responsible reading can preserve those alternatives in 2:69 without pretending that every possibility has equal strength.

There is also a distinction between understanding call and using it as a label for other people. The first task belongs to learning; the second requires evidence, fairness, and awareness of one's own motives in 2:69. The verse 2:69 addresses the reader before it supplies material for judging a neighbour. Its warning becomes safer and more productive when self-examination comes first.

The theology and practical instruction of 2:69 therefore support one another. If Allah knows or commands colour, that knowledge or command changes how a person handles time, power, money, speech, and private desire. A doctrine that never reaches those choices has not yet been read at the level demanded by 2:69.

An ordinary example makes the moral structure of 2:69 visible without replacing the revelation. Two people may perform an outwardly similar act involving call; one may be protecting a right, while the other is seeking praise, escaping a duty, or taking advantage of confusion. The act's surface does not settle its value. Intention, circumstance, and the rights of others complete the judgment.

The surrounding verses keep the reader from isolating call from the rest of life. In 2:69, revelation corrects the mind but also trains habits: how a person speaks when challenged, gives when unseen, waits when angry, and returns after error. Those habits are where this verse becomes more than information about call. They are the place in which assent to 2:69 is either confirmed or quietly withdrawn.

The most balanced response to 2:69 is neither to make the passage vague nor to claim more than it says. Its boundaries are part of its guidance. Within them, the verse can illuminate a new situation because its underlying moral relation remains stable: call is joined to colour, and the person is responsible for how that relation is honoured.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:72

> **˹This is˺ when a man was killed and you disputed who the killer was, but Allah revealed what you concealed.**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Crime Finally Named**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings killed and revealed into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. Its first term in 2:72 sets the subject, while the later term shows what that subject demands, permits, or exposes. The order of 2:72 gives the reader a path through the verse: begin with what Allah names, follow the consequence, and resist the temptation to turn a living address into a slogan.

**"Allah Is the Discloser of What You Were Concealing"**

On the murder, also see 2:67–71c. With some variations, the commentators relate the story that the Israelites, after searching for a long time, find the cow described by Moses, purchase it for a high price, and sacrifice it. Then they take a part of the cows body and strike the corpse of the murder victim, which is then briefly animated, long enough to answer the question of who the killer was, after which the body reverts to its previous state (Ibn Kathīr). Thus, most commentators understand the command in v. 73 to mean, Strike him [the corpse] with part of it [the slaughtered cow].

**The Cool Logic of the Solvable Cold Case**

Assuming this is the correct interpretation, it would not be the only instance of reanimation in the Qur'an; others include Abraham and the birds (2:260); Jesus and the clay bird (3:49); the unnamed man thought by some to be Ezra, who died and was revived after a hundred years (2:259); and an allusion to this is when dust touched by a messenger (usually thought to be Gabriel) is used to animate the golden calf (20:96).

**The permission is not a blank cheque**

In a related ḥadīth, a man asked, “O Messenger of Allah, how does Allah revive the dead?” “Have you ever passed by a barren valley, and then passed by it again and it was verdant?” “Yes.” “Even so is the Resurrection.” In another version he replied, “Even so does Allah revive the dead.” Sufi commentators have seen in this passage a message that one whose heart has been “slain” by worldliness must sacrifice the egotistical soul in order to give life to the heart through the remembrance of Allah (Ni, Su, Qu). Al-Qushayrī states, “Whoever desires that his heart be given life must sacrifice his soul. So whoever sacrifices his soul with effort gives life to his heart and the lights of vision.”

**The difference between defence and aggression**

In Deuteronomy 21:1–9 the Israelites are commanded to sacrifice a cow in the event that a person is found slain and the murderer remains unknown, after which the elders of the town nearest to the victim wash their hands over the cow and disavow any guilt for the crime. But the two accounts are different; one is the narration of an event, and the other, the prescription of a general law, even though there are similarities between them.

The mention of killed must be read with the restraints carried by the same revelation. Permission to resist wrongdoing does not erase the prohibition of wrongdoing. The verse therefore asks the community to hold two truths together: injustice may have to be confronted, and the means used in confronting it remain subject to Allah's judgment.

**The human cost carried by the wording**

A useful way to test the verse is to ask what would change if killed were taken seriously when no audience was present. The answer cannot be only a feeling, because 2:72 connects inward recognition with a discernible choice. Nor can it be only an outward display, because the choice in 2:72 loses its Qur'anic meaning when it is made for reputation rather than for Allah. The passage holds intention and action together in 2:72.

**Limits that remain binding in conflict**

The relation between killed and revealed also protects the verse from two opposite misreadings. It should not be expanded into a claim the wording of 2:72 does not make, but neither should its brevity be used to make it weightless. Short Qur'anic statements such as 2:72 often function as hinges: they close one movement, open another, and give the next command its moral setting. The careful reader of 2:72 therefore asks what has just been established, what response is now being required, and what kind of character could respond without evasion. Those questions keep 2:72 specific while allowing its guidance to reach a new circumstance.

There is also a distinction between understanding killed and using it as a label for other people. The first task belongs to learning; the second requires evidence, fairness, and awareness of one's own motives in 2:72. The verse 2:72 addresses the reader before it supplies material for judging a neighbour. Its warning becomes safer and more productive when self-examination comes first.

**How the early community understood it**

The theology and practical instruction of 2:72 therefore support one another. If Allah knows or commands revealed, that knowledge or command changes how a person handles time, power, money, speech, and private desire. A doctrine that never reaches those choices has not yet been read at the level demanded by 2:72.

**Power restrained by accountability**

In 2:72, the distinction between public appearance and inward truth is especially relevant. A person may use the language of killed while arranging the act around another purpose. Allah's judgment in 2:72 is not limited to the visible outline, yet the inner intention is not an excuse for ignoring the rights and forms that the revelation establishes. Sincerity completes obedience; it does not cancel it.

In a related ḥadīth, a man asked, “O Messenger of Allah, how does Allah revive the dead?” “Have you ever passed by a barren valley, and then passed by it again and it was verdant?” “Yes.” “Even so is the Resurrection.” In another version he replied, “Even so does Allah revive the dead.” Sufi commentators have seen in this passage a message that one whose heart has been “slain” by worldliness must sacrifice the egotistical soul in order to give life to the heart through the remembrance of Allah (Ni, Su, Qu). Al-Qushayrī states, “Whoever desires that his heart be given life must sacrifice his soul. So whoever sacrifices his soul with effort gives life to his heart and the lights of vision.”

**A divine name that governs the meaning**

In Deuteronomy 21:1–9 the Israelites are commanded to sacrifice a cow in the event that a person is found slain and the murderer remains unknown, after which the elders of the town nearest to the victim wash their hands over the cow and disavow any guilt for the crime. But the two accounts are different; one is the narration of an event, and the other, the prescription of a general law, even though there are similarities between them.

The verse's reference to instructed widens the scene beyond the immediate reward or pain. A deed in 2:73 may appear small when measured by public attention, yet its meaning changes when it is known by Allah and carried into the final account. Warning and mercy belong together in 2:73: accountability is serious because the human being is not abandoned to meaninglessness.

**Mercy and warning held together**

The standard in 2:73 remains practical because it can be applied before a dispute reaches a court or a crisis reaches its worst point. One can notice the first small departure from instructed: an excuse, a concealed obligation, an unexamined desire, or a promise treated as optional. Returning at that point is easier than defending a settled habit. The warning is therefore also an opening for repair.

**The deed before its final account**

The relation between instructed and body also protects the verse from two opposite misreadings. It should not be expanded into a claim the wording of 2:73 does not make, but neither should its brevity be used to make it weightless. Short Qur'anic statements such as 2:73 often function as hinges: they close one movement, open another, and give the next command its moral setting. The careful reader of 2:73 therefore asks what has just been established, what response is now being required, and what kind of character could respond without evasion. Those questions keep 2:73 specific while allowing its guidance to reach a new circumstance.

The theology and practical instruction of 2:73 therefore support one another. If Allah knows or commands body, that knowledge or command changes how a person handles time, power, money, speech, and private desire. A doctrine that never reaches those choices has not yet been read at the level demanded by 2:73.

**Why the promise or threat is just**

An ordinary example makes the moral structure of 2:73 visible without replacing the revelation. Two people may perform an outwardly similar act involving instructed; one may be protecting a right, while the other is seeking praise, escaping a duty, or taking advantage of confusion. The act's surface does not settle its value. Intention, circumstance, and the rights of others complete the judgment.

The surrounding verses keep the reader from isolating instructed from the rest of life. In 2:73, revelation corrects the mind but also trains habits: how a person speaks when challenged, gives when unseen, waits when angry, and returns after error. Those habits are where this verse becomes more than information about instructed. They are the place in which assent to 2:73 is either confirmed or quietly withdrawn.

**The Hereafter in the argument**

The most balanced response to 2:73 is neither to make the passage vague nor to claim more than it says. Its boundaries are part of its guidance. Within them, the verse can illuminate a new situation because its underlying moral relation remains stable: instructed is joined to body, and the person is responsible for how that relation is honoured.

The wording of 2:73 gives the reader a useful order of questions about instructed. What does the term instructed mean in ordinary Arabic, what does the surrounding sentence restrict it to, and what consequence follows when the command is obeyed or refused in 2:73? These questions prevent a commentary on 2:73 from becoming a list of slogans. They make the act of interpretation answerable to grammar, context, and the moral end of this passage at 2:73.

The commentators sometimes preserve more than one report about the setting of 2:73. Such reports should be weighed rather than treated as interchangeable decoration. An occasion can explain why a question arose, but the wording of 2:73 determines how far the guidance travels. The verse speaks first to the situation that occasioned it and then to every reader who meets the same relation between instructed and body.

In 2:73, the distinction between public appearance and inward truth is especially relevant. A person may use the language of instructed while arranging the act around another purpose. Allah's judgment in 2:73 is not limited to the visible outline, yet the inner intention is not an excuse for ignoring the rights and forms that the revelation establishes. Sincerity completes obedience; it does not cancel it.

One can see the social wisdom of 2:73 in a small everyday case. When people share responsibility for instructed, uncertainty about the duty tends to fall on the person with less power or less information. A clear moral rule changes that balance. In 2:73, it tells the stronger party what must not be taken, and gives the weaker party language with which to name the wrong.

In 2:73, the verse also sits within the Qur'an's larger refusal to separate worship from truthfulness. Prayer, remembrance, generosity, patience, and justice are different acts in 2:73, but they are trained by the same capacity to stand before Allah without constructing a false account. The statement in 2:73 strengthens that capacity by making one particular choice visible.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:74

> **Even then your hearts became hardened like a rock or even harder, for some rocks gush rivers; others split, spilling water; while others are humbled in awe of Allah. And Allah is never unaware of what you do.**

### Expanded Commentary

**"Then Your Hearts Hardened" — After All That?**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings even and hardened into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. Its first term in 2:74 sets the subject, while the later term shows what that subject demands, permits, or exposes. The order of 2:74 gives the reader a path through the verse: begin with what Allah names, follow the consequence, and resist the temptation to turn a living address into a slogan.

**Like Stones — Or Harder**

This verse can be understood to describe those present at the incident of the cow or the Jewish contemporaries of the Prophet insofar as they were members of the same group by affiliation and descent (al-Rāzī). In the first case they are rebuked for being unmoved by so obvious a sign as the raising of the dead, and in the latter case for turning away from the Qur'anic teaching about this incident. Even rock can be worn down and split open by the force of water. For the symbolism of water, also see 2:60. Water is a symbol of life and that by which life is made possible, whether it comes from the sky (22:63) or comes from beneath the ground (39:21) or is figured in our creation (21:30); here the image of the rock from which water comes forth is powerfully contrasted to the lifelessness of the hardened heart.

**"Allah Is Not Heedless of What You Do"**

Stones crashing down from the fear of Allah is connected by some commentators with the incident of Allahs disclosing Himself to the mountain in the presence of Moses, on the occasion of which the mountain crumbled (7:143), and with 59:21: Had We made this Qur'an descend upon a mountain, thou wouldst have seen it humbled, rent asunder by the fear of Allah. Some commentators think that all the types of rock in this verse behave as they do because of the fear of Allah (al-Ṭabarī). The living consciousness of Allah by all creation is also mentioned in 17:44: And there is no thing, save that it hymns His praise, though you do not understand their praise; and 34:10: O you mountains! Echo Allahs praises with him, likewise you birds!

**The horizon beyond the immediate scene**

Some aḥādīth mentioned in connection with this verse describe the Prophet as saying, “I know a stone in Makkah that used to greet me before I was made a prophet, and I know it even now.” Regarding Mt. Uḥud, he said, “This is a mountain that loves us, and we love it.” In another related ḥadīth that describes the behavior of apparently insensate objects, the Companions made a pulpit for the Prophet, but when he ascended it, the palm-tree stump beside which he used to deliver his sermons began to cry, at which the Prophet descended, embraced it, and said, “It weeps for the remembrance it used to hear.” In one interpretation, the three kind of stones refer, respectively, to those human beings who weep much, those who weep little, and those who weep in their hearts without showing it outwardly (Ibn Kathīr).

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:75

> **Do you ˹believers still˺ expect them to be true to you, though a group of them would hear the word of Allah then knowingly corrupt it after understanding it?**

### Expanded Commentary

**A Consolation Wrapped as a Question**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between belief and true. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:75. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:75. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:75.

**What Is Taḥrīf? Text or Meaning?**

This verse is addressed, using the plural you, to the Muslim community; they refers to the Children of Israel. It is one of a handful of verses that mention the distortion (taḥrīf) of scriptures by the People of the Book (see also 2:59; 3:78; 4:46; 5:13, 41). According to one interpretation, the party mentioned here are the seventy chosen Israelites (see 2:55c) who were said to have joined Moses on the Mount and directly heard the Word of Allah. When they returned, Moses said, Allah commands thus and thus, but this group would say, No, Allah commands thus and thus, misrepresenting what they had just heard (Ibn Kathīr), or they said, If you are able to do these things, then do them, and if you wish, then do not; there is no harm in it .

**Hope Realigned, Not Abolished**

One argument for this interpretation is that they heard the Word of Allah along with Moses, which is to say they did not read it, but the Qur'an speaks of those who hear Allahs Word indirectly, as in 9:6 (Ibn Kathīr). Other commentators believe that this verse describes the Jewish contemporaries of the Prophet.

**The horizon beyond the immediate scene**

Although lexically taḥrīf seems to be related to “letter” (ḥarf), its meaning is to “slant,” “be oblique,” “twist,” or “deviate” and is often connected by the commentators with the etymologically related inḥirāf, usually understood as “deviation.” Whether the Jews and Christians actually altered their transmitted books or instead skewed their interpretations while retaining a faithful text is a subject of debate in the Islamic intellectual tradition. Although later Islamic commentators and theologians often held a view that the Jews and Christians actually changed the text of the Bible, as epitomized in the work of the fifth-/eleventh-century scholar Ibn Ḥazm, the earlier commentators were not as eager to dispute the text of the Bible and preferred to view the “distortion” as an act of faulty and even malicious interpretation.

**A divine name that governs the meaning**

In his remarks on 3:78 al-Rāzī, for example, doubts that the prophecies pertaining to the Prophet Muhammad (see 7:157) were physically removed, since that would have required collusion on a grand scale with a well-known text. (In his commentary on 2:75, however, he states that with a less widely distributed text such an alteration would not be impossible.) He prefers to think that the prophecies required careful thinking and contemplation in the heart and that those texts, over time, took on a normative interpretation that drifted away from the original intent. This required a certain amount of speculation and assumption on al-Rāzīs part regarding how widespread such texts were, since it is doubtful that he had detailed knowledge of the recording and transmission of the Bible.

**Mercy and warning held together**

Often mentioned in this connection with this verse is the thesis that the scholars and jurists of the Children of Israel would make lawful what was forbidden and forbid what was lawful, in accord with their own desires . After they had understood it also supports the idea that the meaning was distorted, not the text (al-Ṭabarī).

**The deed before its final account**

Other instances in which the Prophet is admonished not to hope too much that his contemporaries will believe in him include 35:8: Truly Allah leads astray whomsoever He will and guides whomsoever He will; so let not thy soul be expended in regrets over them; and 18:6: Yet perhaps thou wouldst torment thyself with grief for their sake, should they believe not in this account. This can be read on a spiritual level as a rebuke to those who, after having experienced visions and openings of spiritual truth, revert to formality and lore and forget the subtle knowledge they once had; or to those who act hypocritically and with bad manners with the sages and the saints and stop keeping company with companions of a spiritual nature (Aj).

**Why the promise or threat is just**

The verse's reference to belief widens the scene beyond the immediate reward or pain. A deed in 2:75 may appear small when measured by public attention, yet its meaning changes when it is known by Allah and carried into the final account. Warning and mercy belong together in 2:75: accountability is serious because the human being is not abandoned to meaninglessness.

The standard in 2:75 remains practical because it can be applied before a dispute reaches a court or a crisis reaches its worst point. One can notice the first small departure from belief: an excuse, a concealed obligation, an unexamined desire, or a promise treated as optional. Returning at that point is easier than defending a settled habit. The warning is therefore also an opening for repair.

**The Hereafter in the argument**

The surrounding verses keep the reader from isolating belief from the rest of life. In 2:75, revelation corrects the mind but also trains habits: how a person speaks when challenged, gives when unseen, waits when angry, and returns after error. Those habits are where this verse becomes more than information about belief. They are the place in which assent to 2:75 is either confirmed or quietly withdrawn.

The most balanced response to 2:75 is neither to make the passage vague nor to claim more than it says. Its boundaries are part of its guidance. Within them, the verse can illuminate a new situation because its underlying moral relation remains stable: belief is joined to true, and the person is responsible for how that relation is honoured.

The wording of 2:75 gives the reader a useful order of questions about belief. What does the term belief mean in ordinary Arabic, what does the surrounding sentence restrict it to, and what consequence follows when the command is obeyed or refused in 2:75? These questions prevent a commentary on 2:75 from becoming a list of slogans. They make the act of interpretation answerable to grammar, context, and the moral end of this passage at 2:75.

The commentators sometimes preserve more than one report about the setting of 2:75. Such reports should be weighed rather than treated as interchangeable decoration. An occasion can explain why a question arose, but the wording of 2:75 determines how far the guidance travels. The verse speaks first to the situation that occasioned it and then to every reader who meets the same relation between belief and true.

In 2:75, the distinction between public appearance and inward truth is especially relevant. A person may use the language of belief while arranging the act around another purpose. Allah's judgment in 2:75 is not limited to the visible outline, yet the inner intention is not an excuse for ignoring the rights and forms that the revelation establishes. ## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:76

> **When they meet the believers they say, “We believe.” But in private they say ˹to each other˺, “Will you disclose to the believers the knowledge Allah has revealed to you, so that they may use it against you before your Lord? Do you not understand?”**

### Expanded Commentary

**Two Faces, Two Speeches**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings meet and disclose into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. Its first term in 2:76 sets the subject, while the later term shows what that subject demands, permits, or exposes. The order of 2:76 gives the reader a path through the verse: begin with what Allah names, follow the consequence, and resist the temptation to turn a living address into a slogan.

**"What Allah Has Unveiled to You" — The Threshold They Knew They Stood At**

This verse refers to a group of Jewish hypocrites (see Sūrah 63) in Madinah . They said We believe, but according to some commentators they really meant only that they acknowledged that Muhammad was a prophet, but not a prophet to the Jews (al-Ṭabarī). What Allah has unveiled to you can mean “what Allah has commanded you” or “what Allah has decided for you” (al-Ṭabarī) or “what knowledge Allah has given you or made easy for you to obtain” (al-Rāzī). Another opinion is that the phrase refers to the prophecies foretelling the coming of the Prophet, so that the first question in this verse would mean, “Do you affirm that he is a prophet, which he can then use to argue against you?” (al-Ṭabarī).

**The Exposure of Double Speech as Ongoing Good News**

Before your Lord (ʿinda rabbikum) is understood to mean that on the Day of Judgment there will be a mutual questioning or interrogation before Allah. According to some exegetes it can also be read, concerning or with regard to your Lord. Others see a similarity in usage between in the sight of your Lord (which is another possible translation of ʿinda rabbikum) and in the Book of Allah. It is argued that these two phrases are often used equivalently, the way Allah commands us and Allah commands us in the Qur'an are . Other exegetes mention that a group of Jews were believers, but then became hypocrites, and this verse describes how their leaders rebuked them for telling the Muslims about the punishments they had endured, because then the Muslims would revile them and say that they were more noble than the Jews in the Sight of Allah . For a similar exposure of secret behavior among the Prophets antagonists, see 2:14; 3:119.

**The first movement of a guided life**

The verse describes meet not as a private opinion but as a direction that changes perception and conduct. In 2:76, guidance is recognized by what it makes a person do with knowledge, power, and desire. For 2:76, inward assent is linked to an observable response: the heart's claim is tested by the path it chooses when the claim becomes costly.

A useful way to test the verse is to ask what would change if meet were taken seriously when no audience was present. The answer cannot be only a feeling, because 2:76 connects inward recognition with a discernible choice. Nor can it be only an outward display, because the choice in 2:76 loses its Qur'anic meaning when it is made for reputation rather than for Allah. The passage holds intention and action together in 2:76.

**Belief made visible in conduct**

The relation between meet and disclose also protects the verse from two opposite misreadings. It should not be expanded into a claim the wording of 2:76 does not make, but neither should its brevity be used to make it weightless. Short Qur'anic statements such as 2:76 often function as hinges: they close one movement, open another, and give the next command its moral setting. The careful reader of 2:76 therefore asks what has just been established, what response is now being required, and what kind of character could respond without evasion. Those questions keep 2:76 specific while allowing its guidance to reach a new circumstance.

The most balanced response to 2:76 is neither to make the passage vague nor to claim more than it says. Its boundaries are part of its guidance. Within them, the verse can illuminate a new situation because its underlying moral relation remains stable: meet is joined to disclose, and the person is responsible for how that relation is honoured.

**The choice hidden inside the command**

The wording of 2:76 gives the reader a useful order of questions about meet. What does the term meet mean in ordinary Arabic, what does the surrounding sentence restrict it to, and what consequence follows when the command is obeyed or refused in 2:76? These questions prevent a commentary on 2:76 from becoming a list of slogans. They make the act of interpretation answerable to grammar, context, and the moral end of this passage at 2:76.

The commentators sometimes preserve more than one report about the setting of 2:76. Such reports should be weighed rather than treated as interchangeable decoration. An occasion can explain why a question arose, but the wording of 2:76 determines how far the guidance travels. The verse speaks first to the situation that occasioned it and then to every reader who meets the same relation between meet and disclose.

**How guidance becomes discernment**

In 2:76, the distinction between public appearance and inward truth is especially relevant. A person may use the language of meet while arranging the act around another purpose. Allah's judgment in 2:76 is not limited to the visible outline, yet the inner intention is not an excuse for ignoring the rights and forms that the revelation establishes. Sincerity completes obedience; it does not cancel it.

One can see the social wisdom of 2:76 in a small everyday case. When people share responsibility for meet, uncertainty about the duty tends to fall on the person with less power or less information. A clear moral rule changes that balance. In 2:76, it tells the stronger party what must not be taken, and gives the weaker party language with which to name the wrong.

**The contrast drawn by the verse**

In 2:76, the verse also sits within the Qur'an's larger refusal to separate worship from truthfulness. Prayer, remembrance, generosity, patience, and justice are different acts in 2:76, but they are trained by the same capacity to stand before Allah without constructing a false account. The statement in 2:76 strengthens that capacity by making one particular choice visible.

A reader who finds the command in 2:76 difficult should distinguish difficulty from impossibility. For 2:76, difficulty may be the place where desire, habit, or social pressure is being corrected; impossibility is a separate legal and moral question. The passage does not praise needless hardship, but it does not permit comfort to redefine meet until the demand disappears.

The final emphasis of 2:76 returns to responsibility. No explanation of meet is complete if it leaves the reader with information about earlier communities but no question about present conduct. The verse 2:76 asks what can be repaired now: a promise kept, a right restored, a motive purified, or a harmful practice abandoned. That is where knowledge becomes guidance.

**Certainty, doubt, and moral action**

The choice of the word meet in 2:76 also matters. It leaves room for the full context of 2:76 instead of allowing one translation gloss to carry every shade of meaning. Classical Arabic often places a broad word inside a narrow scene; in 2:76, the surrounding clauses determine whether the emphasis falls on an act, an intention, a condition, or a consequence. Here the reader should let the sentence do that work.

The exegetical tradition approaches meet from more than one angle, but its differences are more useful when their shared question is made visible. The commentators ask what the wording of 2:76 includes, what it excludes, and how it fits with the other passages of the Qur'an. A responsible reading can preserve those alternatives in 2:76 without pretending that every possibility has equal strength.

There is also a distinction between understanding meet and using it as a label for other people. The first task belongs to learning; the second requires evidence, fairness, and awareness of one's own motives in 2:76. The verse 2:76 addresses the reader before it supplies material for judging a neighbour. Its warning becomes safer and more productive when self-examination comes first.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:78

> **And among them are the illiterate who know nothing about the Scripture except lies, and ˹so˺ they ˹wishfully˺ speculate.**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Masses Behind the Scribes**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings among and nothing into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. Its first term in 2:78 sets the subject, while the later term shows what that subject demands, permits, or exposes. The order of 2:78 gives the reader a path through the verse: begin with what Allah names, follow the consequence, and resist the temptation to turn a living address into a slogan.

**"Nothing but Hearsay": The Religion of Amānī**

The illiterate (ummiyyūn) are those Jews who could not read and write (al-Ṭabarī). In an opinion attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, however, they are a people who accept no prophet or revealed book and who write a book themselves and say that it is from Allah; they were called ummiyyūn because of their opposition to the Books of Allah (al-Ṭabarī). But most do not consider this opinion to be correct, since among the Arabs ummī means someone who cannot write or write well (al-Ṭabarī). The commentators often mention here the ḥadīth, We are an ummī people; we do not write and we do not calculate the months.

**The Ummī Prophet and the Recited Book**

This would support the interpretation that ummī means one who cannot read and write well , since neither the Jews nor the Arabs of Arabia were wholly illiterate; some could read and write well, while some could do so in only a very rudimentary fashion. That the Arabs were not entirely illiterate is clear from the Islamic traditions proven assertion that the Qur'an was written down during the lifetime of the Prophet, though the literate could have been a relatively small number in relation to the whole. For further discussion of the concept of ummī, or unlettered, see 7:157–58c; 62:2c.

**The Book as an address**

Hearsay (amānī) means that they know only what their scholars tell them ; or it means things they invented, such as that the Fire will not touch them except for a certain number of days (see v. 80) or that none will enter Paradise who is not a Jew (2:111). Amānī can also be rendered hope or desire (see also 2:111; 4:123; 22:52; 57:14). They only conjecture is usually glossed as they lie [about Allah] or they think/deem false things [about Allah] (Ibn Kathīr).

The wording around among assumes that revelation is meant to be heard with intelligence and humility together. Understanding is not an invitation to place the reader above the text; neither is obedience a reason to stop thinking. The classical tradition preserved both tasks: clarify the language, then ask what kind of person the clarified command is meant to form.

The answer cannot be only a feeling, because 2:78 connects inward recognition with a discernible choice. Nor can it be only an outward display, because the choice in 2:78 loses its Qur'anic meaning when it is made for reputation rather than for Allah. The passage holds intention and action together in 2:78.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:80

> **˹Some of˺ the Jews claim, “The Fire will not touch us except for a number of days.” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Have you taken a pledge from Allah— for Allah never breaks His word—or are you ˹just˺ saying about Allah what you do not know?”**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Comforting Calculation**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings jews and touch into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. Its first term in 2:80 sets the subject, while the later term shows what that subject demands, permits, or exposes. The order of 2:80 gives the reader a path through the verse: begin with what Allah names, follow the consequence, and resist the temptation to turn a living address into a slogan.

**"Have You Taken a Covenant from Allah?"**

This verse should be read together with the subsequent two verses. This claim of limited punishment is repeated in 3:24. Some commentators mention that the Jews claimed that they would suffer torment for only forty nights, corresponding to the time spent worshipping the calf, after which they would be succeeded by another people (according to some, they claimed that these inheritors of punishment would be the followers of Muhammad); others say it would be forty years; still others, only seven days, one day for each thousand years of the worlds existence (Ibn Kathīr). A covenant is often mentioned in connection with the Israelites (e.g., 2:40, 100) and more generally elsewhere between Allah and humanity (3:77, 81; 7:172; 13:25; 33:7; 36:60). Here it is invoked against the claims that Hell would be experienced by the Jews only for a specific number of days, which the commentators point out are claims made without any warrant from scripture.

**The Doctrine the Verse Guards**

The question of a limited sojourn in Hell is extremely significant, as the main body of Islamic theology accepts the possibility of believers being removed from Hell (see 4:40c; 78:23c), a position adduced from passages such as 6:128; 11:107; and 78:23, but also from aḥādīth that describe intercession on behalf of the denizens of Hell that would allow them to leave it after a period of time (see 2:255c; 57:13c).

Al-Rāzī makes an argument regarding limited punishment in Hell based on three main points: First, he argues that v. 80 is not necessarily a denial that souls might reside in Hell only temporarily, but may be seen as a rebuke against the claim of such an exceedingly small number of days coupled with the impudent confidence in that figure in the absence of an explicit promise from Allah. Second, one cannot assume such forgiveness for all, but this does not prevent the possibility that an individual person may be forgiven after a time in Hell.

**Writing trust into a transaction**

Third, there is a difference between saying that Allah will not remove a believer from Hell and saying that Allah never promised (or made a Covenant) to remove a believer from Hell, since Allah can do something without having explicitly promised to do so. The absence of such a promise does not prevent Allah from in fact removing a person from Hell after a period of time. For more on the question of the perpetuity or eternity of Hell, see 11:106–8c; 78:23c; and the essay Death, Dying, and the Afterlife in the Qur'an.

The language of jews places memory and responsibility alongside material exchange. People forget, die, disagree, and understand conversations differently; a careful record does not accuse every party of dishonesty, but protects the honest party from the consequences of uncertainty. The verse therefore treats clarity as a form of mercy, not as a sign that trust has disappeared.

The passage holds intention and action together in 2:80.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:81

> **But no! Those who commit evil and are engrossed in sin will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever.**

### Expanded Commentary

**"Balā" — The Refutation Word**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between commit and residents. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:81. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:81. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:81.

**Earning Evil; Being Encircled by Sin**

Evil here is most commonly understood by commentators to mean idolatry, the setting up of partners to Allah (or the setting up of other things as equals to Allah) as objects of worship (see also 4:48c). To be surrounded by his sins means to be a persistent sinner, to be one who dies in sin before repenting of it, or to commit major sins as opposed to minor ones and die in that state unrepentant (al-Ṭabarī). The distinction between major and minor sin (corresponding roughly, but not exactly, to mortal sin and venial sin in the Christian tradition) is universal in Islam, although historically there have been many different lists of major and minor sins.

**The Ruin of Decisiveness and the Windows Left Open**

Some are based on certain aḥādīth of the Prophet listing grave sins, while others identify major sins as those connected to ḥadd punishments (e.g., murder and adultery) in the Qur'an or those specifically mentioned in connection with Hell or the curse of Allah. Major and minor sins are not strictly divided: one can repent and be forgiven for major sins, but even a minor sin can become major through obstinacy and repetition (also see 4:31c). Surrounded renders aḥāṭa, which can mean to encircle, enclose, or comprehend. In one respect, ones sin overwhelms ones good actions, as one object encircles another (al-Rāzī), so that the decisive character of the soul is evil rather than good and the heart is what is encircled and overwhelmed (Ibn Kathīr).

**The horizon beyond the immediate scene**

In a way, only idolatry deserves eternity in Hell, as it manifests a decisive orientation of the heart (Ṭs). When Allah says He forgives all sins except shirk, idolatry (4:48; 4:116), this means that He forgives gratuitously all sins other than shirk, not that shirk is unforgivable, since Allah forgives all sins (39:53; R). On the question of forgiveness for shirk, see 4:48c. See also 4:123, which says of the Hereafter, It will not be in accordance with your desires nor the desires of the People of the Book.

Whosoever does evil shall be requited for it. The commentators connect these verses to the Jewish claim of limited days of punishment, indicating that Allah does not punish or withhold punishment on the basis of ones membership in a particular religious community, but on the basis of individual right or wrong actions.

**A divine name that governs the meaning**

The identification of major sin and its consequences became entangled politically in early Islamic history, which is why many of the creeds of the classical period discuss the status of the Companions alongside questions of Allah’s Attributes and eschatology. The internal conflicts of the early period made the Prophet’s Companions subjects in the theology of sin and error, in light of the civil wars involving major Companions and even wives of the Prophet on opposing sides, culminating in the assassination of the two Caliphs ʿUthmān and ʿAlī by extremist elements who labeled them as grave sinners, hence, according to their belief, no longer believers and therefore illegitimate. The status of individual Companions (especially the early Caliphs) became a charged issue in intercommunity politics, in which sin became both a theological and political question pertaining to both religious and temporal authority.

**Mercy and warning held together**

The verse's reference to commit widens the scene beyond the immediate reward or pain. A deed in 2:81 may appear small when measured by public attention, yet its meaning changes when it is known by Allah and carried into the final account. Warning and mercy belong together in 2:81: accountability is serious because the human being is not abandoned to meaninglessness.

The standard in 2:81 remains practical because it can be applied before a dispute reaches a court or a crisis reaches its worst point. One can notice the first small departure from commit: an excuse, a concealed obligation, an unexamined desire, or a promise treated as optional. The first task belongs to learning; the second requires evidence, fairness, and awareness of one's own motives in 2:81. The verse 2:81 addresses the reader before it supplies material for judging a neighbour. Its warning becomes safer and more productive when self-examination comes first.

The theology and practical instruction of 2:81 therefore support one another. If Allah knows or commands residents, that knowledge or command changes how a person handles time, power, money, speech, and private desire. A doctrine that never reaches those choices has not yet been read at the level demanded by 2:81.

An ordinary example makes the moral structure of 2:81 visible without replacing the revelation. Two people may perform an outwardly similar act involving commit; one may be protecting a right, while the other is seeking praise, escaping a duty, or taking advantage of confusion. The act's surface does not settle its value. Intention, circumstance, and the rights of others complete the judgment.

The surrounding verses keep the reader from isolating commit from the rest of life. In 2:81, revelation corrects the mind but also trains habits: how a person speaks when challenged, gives when unseen, waits when angry, and returns after error. Those habits are where this verse becomes more than information about commit. They are the place in which assent to 2:81 is either confirmed or quietly withdrawn.
