## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:106

> **If We ever abrogate a verse or cause it to be forgotten, We replace it with a better or similar one. Do you not know that Allah is Most Capable of everything?**

### Expanded Commentary

**Abrogation: Allah's Prerogative over His Own Speech**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings ever and cause into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. Its first term in 2:106 sets the subject, while the later term shows what that subject demands, permits, or exposes. The order of 2:106 gives the reader a path through the verse: begin with what Allah names, follow the consequence, and resist the temptation to turn a living address into a slogan.

Naskh, usually translated abrogation, has the meaning of conveyance or copying from an original, which could extend to the notion that the entire Qur'an is a naskh, or copy in relation to its origin in the Preserved Tablet (85:22; Th), or something as simple as a written copy of a text. The more relevant sense in this context is to erase or to obliterate, often described as the action that the sun performs on a shadow, the wind upon dust, or even old age upon youth. The root n-s-kh appears four times in the Qur'an: in this verse; in 7:154, referring to the inscription of the tablets of Moses; in 22:52, where Allah effaces the work of Satan; and in 45:29, in regard to the recording of human actions.

**The Rules of the Science**

Naskh (abrogation) as a technical term is a key concept in the fully developed form of Islamic jurisprudence, theology, and Qur'anic commentary, and is a major conceptual tool for understanding the relationship between different commands and prohibitions in the Qur'an and the Sunnah. It is a crucial concept for understanding how the Qur'an is actually used as a source of Islamic Law and practice, and thus many of the classical commentators devote considerable attention to this particular verse. Other verses often mentioned in this connection are Allah effaces what He will and establishes, and with Him is the Mother of the Book (13:39); And when We replace one sign with another (16:101); and And if We willed, We could take away that which We revealed unto thee (17:86).

**"Cause to Be Forgotten": Mercy within Loss**

In its mainstream interpretation, naskh refers to the replacement of one legal ruling (ḥukm) by another one that is instituted or revealed later in time, in which case the original text remains in the Qur'an, but is no longer binding as a matter of law or practice. As widely understood in the Islamic religious sciences, naskh can occur only in matters of commands and prohibitions, not in descriptive passages relating to metaphysics, ethics, history, the nature of Allah, or the Hereafter; a ruling (ḥukm) is a determination of legal status, not doctrine.

Thus there can be no abrogation of a passage such as Allah has power over all things (2:259) or Whosoever believes in Allah and the Last Day and works righteousness shall have their reward with their Lord. No fear shall come upon them, nor shall they grieve (2:62); or accounts of previous prophets found throughout the Qur'an. Naskh would not apply to commandments so universal as to be irrevocable, such as the prohibitions against murder, theft, and adultery and the command to be kind to ones parents.

**The horizon beyond the immediate scene**

Other kinds of naskh have also been posited by some, such as the naskh of both text and ruling. A report attributed to the Prophets wife ʿĀʾishah, for example, states that there were commands in the Qur'an relating to suckling that are now neither acted upon nor part of the Qur'an (see 4:23c). Another type is naskh of the text despite a continuation of its ruling, and the example most often cited here is the punishment of adultery by stoning. In a report attributed to ʿUmar, a verse commanding stoning was part of the Qur'an, but now is not, even though the command of stoning for adultery remains in effect (according to many, if not most, jurists; IK, R, Ṭ). On the question of the stoning verse, see 24:2c.

**A divine name that governs the meaning**

Although it is generally agreed that one Qur'anic ruling may abrogate another Qur'anic ruling revealed earlier in time, there has been considerable difference of opinion about other kinds of naskh, for example, whether Prophetic practice (Sunnah) can abrogate the Qur'an or vice versa, and whether the consensus of the learned community (ijmāʿ) can abrogate a ruling from the Qur'an or a ḥadīth. Moreover, although there has been near universal agreement among the majority of jurists that naskh exists, there has been considerable variation on which verses of the Qur'an and aspects of Sunnah are abrogated.

Scholars such as the famous Islamic thinker and reformer Shāh Walī Allāh of Delhi (d. 1176/1762) placed the number of abrogated verses at 5; the commentator Ibn al-Jawzī named no less than 247; many other lists exist in between, such as Jalāl al-Dīn al-Suyūṭī’s list of 21 instances. A minority of scholars, such as Abū Muslim al-Iṣfahānī (d. 934/1527), have gone so far as to say that abrogation, as a technical concept defined by the mainstream legal tradition, does not actually exist and that the apparently conflicting rulings can be reconciled.

**Mercy and warning held together**

Even among the mainstream upholders of naskh, abrogation must be distinguished from (1) specification, where a verse does not contradict but provides specification regarding the general ruling of another verse; (2) the simple accumulation of law, which may or may not amount to an abrogation; and (3) the disappearance of the circumstances or causes behind the ruling, its sabab or ʿillah (“effective legal cause”). In all cases the question of naskh comes into play as a practical matter only when the verses are considered to be irreconcilable as legal rulings.

**The deed before its final account**

A small minority of scholars, such as Abū Muslim al-Iṣfahānī, reject altogether the mainstream definition of naskh and employ the same passages to make their case either that naskh takes place between religions (e.g., Islam in relation to Judaism and Christianity), meaning that Allah replaces one religion with another, or that sign (āyah) in this verse means miracle. In the Qur'an many things are called a sign: the she-camel of the Thamūd (17:59); the day and the night (17:12); the Companions of the Cave (18:9); Zachariahs lack of speech for three days (19:10); Jesus (19:21); the white hand of Moses (20:22); Mary and Jesus (21:91); the destruction of Noahs people (25:37); the growth of vegetation (26:8); the drowning of the Egyptians (26:67); the destruction of the people of Lot (26:174); the miracles of Moses (28:36); the creation of the heavens and the earth (29:44); the request by the disbelievers for a miracle (29:50); our creation from dust (30:20); a series of items in 30:21–25, none of which refer to the verses of the Qur'an, thus bearing significantly on the nature of the abrogation mentioned in the present verse.

**Why the promise or threat is just**

Cause to be forgotten (nunsīhā) can also be understood in the sense of abandoning, as in 9:67, They forgot Allah; so He forgot them, where it means to forsake or spurn, since Allah could not actually fail to remember something. With different voweling (nansaʾahā), this verb can mean literally defer/delay, in which case the phrase would denote those signs or verses (āyāt) that were abrogated and those that were left unchanged. Ibn Kathīr and others mention a ḥadīth about two men who used to recite a sūrah that the Prophet had taught them. Then one day they tried to recite it, but they could not manage even a letter. They asked the Prophet about this inability, to which he replied, It is one of those that has been abrogated and forgotten, so leave it. This would support a reading of forgetting over deferment.

**The Hereafter in the argument**

In trying to make sense of how one verse of the Word of Allah could be better than another, some interpret better than it as an alleviation when it comes to matters of this world and an intensification when it comes to matters of the next world (al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī). For example, when the night prayer was no longer an imperative of the community (73:1, abrogated by 73:20), that was a change toward ease in this world, but when the fast of Ramadan was imposed (2:185, abrogating 2:184, according to this interpretation), it afforded a greater opportunity for reward in the Hereafter.

Thus, for some commentators the verse must mean No [ruling from a] sign do We abrogate . . . , so that it is the ruling, not the sign, that is called better. Al-Ṭabarī, for example, compares this implied phrase to the missing phrase the love of in the verse they were made to drink [the love of] the calf into their hearts (v. 93), since they did not literally drink the calf. Others mention an interpretation that better than it means a good from it or a good on account of it, since the Arabic word for better (khayr) can also mean a good, depending on the context (al-Qurṭubī).

The verse's reference to ever widens the scene beyond the immediate reward or pain. A deed in 2:106 may appear small when measured by public attention, yet its meaning changes when it is known by Allah and carried into the final account. Warning and mercy belong together in 2:106: accountability is serious because the human being is not abandoned to meaninglessness.

A useful way to test the verse is to ask what would change if ever were taken seriously when no audience was present. The answer cannot be only a feeling, because 2:106 connects inward recognition with a discernible choice. Nor can it be only an outward display, because the choice in 2:106 loses its Qur'anic meaning when it is made for reputation rather than for Allah. The passage holds intention and action together in 2:106.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:108

> **Or do you ˹believers˺ intend to ask of your Messenger as Moses was asked before? But whoever trades belief for disbelief has truly strayed from the Right Way.**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Question-Genealogy That Destroys**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings belief and moses into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. Its first term in 2:108 sets the subject, while the later term shows what that subject demands, permits, or exposes. The order of 2:108 gives the reader a path through the verse: begin with what Allah names, follow the consequence, and resist the temptation to turn a living address into a slogan.

The questioning of Moses and related issues are discussed also in 4:153. The Quraysh would challenge the Prophet to bring a Book with the power to create flowing rivers or demand that he turn Ṣafā (a hill outside Makkah) into gold (al-Ṭabarī) or give them a tree upon which to hang ritual items (al-Rāzī). This last is compared with the Israelites demand to Moses: Make for us a god as they have gods (7:138).

**Exchanging Belief for Disbelief: the Terrible Commerce**

Another pitfall related to questioning prophets is mentioned in 5:101: O you who believe! Ask not about things which, if they were disclosed to you, would trouble you. The Prophet said, That Muslim commits the greatest crime who asks about a thing that is not forbidden, and which then becomes forbidden because of his asking. In another ḥadīth he said, Those who came before you were ruined only through the multiplication of their questions and their differences with their prophets. So if I bid you do a thing, do what you can of it. And if I forbid you a thing, avoid it. Alternatively, one finds praise for the Companions in the commentaries for asking the right kinds of questions, about matters such as orphans and charitable giving (e.g., 2:219–20; IK), and indeed many verses are said to have come down after questions posed by the Companions to the Prophet (e.g., 4:127; 33:35; 58:1–4).

**The Law of Salamah — Safe Passage for the Believers**

The right way renders sawāʾ al-sabīl; sawāʾ can also mean middle, level, or straight (see also 3:64c for other uses of sawāʾ).

The verse describes belief not as a private opinion but as a direction that changes perception and conduct. In 2:108, guidance is recognized by what it makes a person do with knowledge, power, and desire. For 2:108, inward assent is linked to an observable response: the heart's claim is tested by the path it chooses when the claim becomes costly.

A useful way to test the verse is to ask what would change if belief were taken seriously when no audience was present. The answer cannot be only a feeling, because 2:108 connects inward recognition with a discernible choice. Nor can it be only an outward display, because the choice in 2:108 loses its Qur'anic meaning when it is made for reputation rather than for Allah. The passage holds intention and action together in 2:108.

**The first movement of a guided life**

The relation between belief and moses also protects the verse from two opposite misreadings. It should not be expanded into a claim the wording of 2:108 does not make, but neither should its brevity be used to make it weightless. Short Qur'anic statements such as 2:108 often function as hinges: they close one movement, open another, and give the next command its moral setting. The careful reader of 2:108 therefore asks what has just been established, what response is now being required, and what kind of character could respond without evasion. Those questions keep 2:108 specific while allowing its guidance to reach a new circumstance.

One can see the social wisdom of 2:108 in a small everyday case. When people share responsibility for belief, uncertainty about the duty tends to fall on the person with less power or less information. A clear moral rule changes that balance. In 2:108, it tells the stronger party what must not be taken, and gives the weaker party language with which to name the wrong.

Prayer, remembrance, generosity, patience, and justice are different acts in 2:108, but they are trained by the same capacity to stand before Allah without constructing a false account. The statement in 2:108 strengthens that capacity by making one particular choice visible.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:109

> **Many among the People of the Book wish they could turn you ˹believers˺ back to disbelief because of their envy, after the truth has been made clear to them. Pardon and bear with them until Allah delivers His decision. Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything.**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Wish Driven by Envy**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between many and turn. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:109. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:109. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:109.

Some connect this verse with formerly Jewish Companions who, after the Battle of Uḥud, were taunted by their former coreligionists about their condition, which turned them away from Islam and back to Judaism . Cf. 3:186: You will surely be tried in your wealth and your souls, and you shall hear much hurt from those who were given the Book before you, and from those who are idolaters. But if you are patient and reverent, then that is indeed a course worthy of resolve.

**"Pardon and Forbear" — the Command to Bear**

On the question of envy, in a ḥadīth the Prophet said, Let there be no envy except in two things: a man who has been given wealth by Allah and then spends it in the way of Allah, and a man who has been given knowledge by Allah and acts in accord with it and imparts it to people. The notion of envy after exposure to the truth is discussed in 3:19; envy is also mentioned in 2:213; 4:54; 10:90; 42:14; 45:17. The great sin of Satan is often understood to be envy, as shown in 38:76, where Iblīs says of Adam, I am better than him. Some understand the truth that was clear to them to be the fact that Muhammad was a true prophet , although in 3:19 the truth that causes dissension among the People of the Book is understood as revelation considered more broadly.

**"Allah Is Powerful over All Things" — the Promise underneath**

In legal terms, it is thought that this verses command to pardon and forbear was abrogated by 9:29, which addresses the question of jizyah, or indemnity paid by the People of the Book: Fight those who believe not in Allah and in the Last Day, and who do not forbid what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden, and who follow not the Religion of Truth among those who were given the Book, till they pay the jizyah with a willing hand, being humbled . However, as al-Rāzī argues, if this verse is interpreted as a command to perform a certain kind of virtuous behavior, then it is not subject to abrogation, as it is not a legal ruling (ḥukm).

**The Book as an address**

Some argue that the first verse to permit fighting (and by implication to abrogate 2:109) was 22:39: Permission is granted to those who are fought, because they have been wronged. Others believe 9:5 first allowed fighting. The range of opinion on abrogation is perhaps no more relevant than in the matter of war. An expansive view of legal abrogation allows for the many verses dealing with peace and forbearance to be abrogated by those authorizing fighting, which leads to dozens of verses being summarily abrogated. However, as al-Rāzī points out, at least in this particular case, the question of abrogation need not arise; this verse commanding forbearance and tolerance does not contradict the kind of just-war commands related to fighting elsewhere, since even in fighting Muslims are commanded to practice similar virtues, as vv. 190–94 demonstrate. For a fuller discussion of such matters, see commentary on 9:1–5; and the essays The Qur'anic View of Sacred History and Other Religions and Conquest and Conversion, War and Peace in the Qur'an.

**The word that carries the argument**

Until Allah comes with His Command could also be rendered until Allah brings His Command. The Command could indicate the military defeat of either the Quraysh or those Jews who opposed the Prophet or refer to the legal status afforded the People of the Book in 9:29, mentioned above .

The wording around many assumes that revelation is meant to be heard with intelligence and humility together. Understanding is not an invitation to place the reader above the text; neither is obedience a reason to stop thinking. The classical tradition preserved both tasks: clarify the language, then ask what kind of person the clarified command is meant to form.

**Knowledge joined to obedience**

The standard in 2:109 remains practical because it can be applied before a dispute reaches a court or a crisis reaches its worst point. One can notice the first small departure from many: an excuse, a concealed obligation, an unexamined desire, or a promise treated as optional. Returning at that point is easier than defending a settled habit. The warning is therefore also an opening for repair.

The statement in 2:109 strengthens that capacity by making one particular choice visible.

Sincerity completes obedience; it does not cancel it.

One can see the social wisdom of 2:111 in a small everyday case. When people share responsibility for jews, uncertainty about the duty tends to fall on the person with less power or less information. A clear moral rule changes that balance. In 2:111, it tells the stronger party what must not be taken, and gives the weaker party language with which to name the wrong.

**Certainty, doubt, and moral action**

In 2:111, the verse also sits within the Qur'an's larger refusal to separate worship from truthfulness. Prayer, remembrance, generosity, patience, and justice are different acts in 2:111, but they are trained by the same capacity to stand before Allah without constructing a false account. The statement in 2:111 strengthens that capacity by making one particular choice visible.

A reader who finds the command in 2:111 difficult should distinguish difficulty from impossibility. For 2:111, difficulty may be the place where desire, habit, or social pressure is being corrected; impossibility is a separate legal and moral question. The passage does not praise needless hardship, but it does not permit comfort to redefine jews until the demand disappears.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:112

> **But no! Whoever submits themselves to Allah and does good will have their reward with their Lord. And there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Door's Actual Dimensions**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings whoever and good into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. Its first term in 2:112 sets the subject, while the later term shows what that subject demands, permits, or exposes. The order of 2:112 gives the reader a path through the verse: begin with what Allah names, follow the consequence, and resist the temptation to turn a living address into a slogan.

**Reward with the Lord, and the Double Exemption**

For submits his face, see also 4:125; 31:22. Here to submit means to be sincere, and the metaphor is powerful because the face is the noblest part of ones body (al-Ṭabarī), and In one respect the most profound action in the prayer is the prostration, where ones face (the forehead and the nose) touches the ground (al-Rāzī). See also 3:20 and commentary. Although some commentators, such as al-Ṭabarī, understand this to mean submitting ones body and actions, which is how they understand the use of face, others, such as Ibn Kathīr, add to this and say that the twin conditions of ones actions being acceptable to Allah are sincerity and conformity to the Sharīʿah (Islamic Law).

**The Tradition's Two Wings of Acceptance**

This latter view would exclude hypocrites because of their lack of sincerity, but would also rule out Christian monks for their lack of conformity to the Sharīʿah. Al-Rāzī, in the same way, leaves out Hindus, who, whatever their intentions, display in his view repugnant actions. The condition of physical conformity allows the exclusion of other religions, although the plain sense of the passage and those like it does not necessitate such exclusion as asserted by other authorities.

The verse's reference to whoever widens the scene beyond the immediate reward or pain. A deed in 2:112 may appear small when measured by public attention, yet its meaning changes when it is known by Allah and carried into the final account. Warning and mercy belong together in 2:112: accountability is serious because the human being is not abandoned to meaninglessness.

**The horizon beyond the immediate scene**

A useful way to test the verse is to ask what would change if whoever were taken seriously when no audience was present. The answer cannot be only a feeling, because 2:112 connects inward recognition with a discernible choice. Nor can it be only an outward display, because the choice in 2:112 loses its Qur'anic meaning when it is made for reputation rather than for Allah. The passage holds intention and action together in 2:112.

**A divine name that governs the meaning**

The relation between whoever and good also protects the verse from two opposite misreadings. It should not be expanded into a claim the wording of 2:112 does not make, but neither should its brevity be used to make it weightless. Short Qur'anic statements such as 2:112 often function as hinges: they close one movement, open another, and give the next command its moral setting. The careful reader of 2:112 therefore asks what has just been established, what response is now being required, and what kind of character could respond without evasion. Those questions keep 2:112 specific while allowing its guidance to reach a new circumstance.

**Mercy and warning held together**

The choice of the word whoever in 2:112 also matters. It leaves room for the full context of 2:112 instead of allowing one translation gloss to carry every shade of meaning. Classical Arabic often places a broad word inside a narrow scene; in 2:112, the surrounding clauses determine whether the emphasis falls on an act, an intention, a condition, or a consequence. Here the reader should let the sentence do that work.

The exegetical tradition approaches whoever from more than one angle, but its differences are more useful when their shared question is made visible. The commentators ask what the wording of 2:112 includes, what it excludes, and how it fits with the other passages of the Qur'an. A responsible reading can preserve those alternatives in 2:112 without pretending that every possibility has equal strength.

**The deed before its final account**

There is also a distinction between understanding whoever and using it as a label for other people. The first task belongs to learning; the second requires evidence, fairness, and awareness of one's own motives in 2:112. The verse 2:112 addresses the reader before it supplies material for judging a neighbour. Its warning becomes safer and more productive when self-examination comes first.

The theology and practical instruction of 2:112 therefore support one another. If Allah knows or commands good, that knowledge or command changes how a person handles time, power, money, speech, and private desire. A doctrine that never reaches those choices has not yet been read at the level demanded by 2:112.

**Why the promise or threat is just**

An ordinary example makes the moral structure of 2:112 visible without replacing the revelation. Two people may perform an outwardly similar act involving whoever; one may be protecting a right, while the other is seeking praise, escaping a duty, or taking advantage of confusion. The act's surface does not settle its value. Intention, circumstance, and the rights of others complete the judgment.

The surrounding verses keep the reader from isolating whoever from the rest of life. In 2:112, revelation corrects the mind but also trains habits: how a person speaks when challenged, gives when unseen, waits when angry, and returns after error. Those habits are where this verse becomes more than information about whoever. They are the place in which assent to 2:112 is either confirmed or quietly withdrawn.

**The Hereafter in the argument**

The most balanced response to 2:112 is neither to make the passage vague nor to claim more than it says. Its boundaries are part of its guidance. Within them, the verse can illuminate a new situation because its underlying moral relation remains stable: whoever is joined to good, and the person is responsible for how that relation is honoured.

The wording of 2:112 gives the reader a useful order of questions about whoever. What does the term whoever mean in ordinary Arabic, what does the surrounding sentence restrict it to, and what consequence follows when the command is obeyed or refused in 2:112? These questions prevent a commentary on 2:112 from becoming a list of slogans. They make the act of interpretation answerable to grammar, context, and the moral end of this passage at 2:112.

The commentators sometimes preserve more than one report about the setting of 2:112. Such reports should be weighed rather than treated as interchangeable decoration. An occasion can explain why a question arose, but the wording of 2:112 determines how far the guidance travels. The verse speaks first to the situation that occasioned it and then to every reader who meets the same relation between whoever and good.

In 2:112, the distinction between public appearance and inward truth is especially relevant. A person may use the language of whoever while arranging the act around another purpose. Allah's judgment in 2:112 is not limited to the visible outline, yet the inner intention is not an excuse for ignoring the rights and forms that the revelation establishes. Sincerity completes obedience; it does not cancel it.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:113

> **The Jews say, “The Christians have nothing to stand on” and the Christians say, “The Jews have nothing to stand on,” although both recite the Scriptures. And those ˹pagans˺ who have no knowledge say the same ˹about people of faith˺. Surely Allah will judge between them on the Day of Judgment regarding their dispute.**

### Expanded Commentary

**Mutual Annulment Between Reciters of One Book**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between jews and stand. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:113. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:113. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:113.

**Allah Will Judge Between Them**

This verse may have been revealed after a group of Jews argued with the Christian delegation from Najrān (see the introduction to Sūrah 3; IK, Ṭ), though other commentators think that it can apply to Jews and Christians generally and does not require them to be present before each other or even to be contemporaries of the Prophet. Stand on nothing could also be rendered “follow nothing,” and in this sense some commentators suggest that in the beginning of their respective religious histories the Jews and Christians did indeed “follow something” true, but then differed and altered their religion (al-Ṭabarī).

**The Mirror of Negatives**

But, as others point out, this would negate the obvious intent of censure in the verse, which indicates that the Jews and Christians are wrong to make this accusation against each other (Ibn Kathīr). They make these claims even though they recite the Book, which means that in what they espouse they should affirm rather than deny the truths in the other religion; in the case of the Jews, the Torah speaks to the truth of Jesus, and in the case of the Christians, the Gospel affirms Moses and the Torah (al-Ṭabarī).

The people who spoke words like theirs are understood to be peoples before the Jews and Christians (Ibn Kathīr) or possibly the idolaters who opposed Islam (al-Rāzī). The commentator al-Kāshānī notes that the Christians are veiled from the outward by their attachment to the inward, while the Jews are veiled from the inward by their attachment to the outward, and that similar problems beset certain schools of thought in Islam (K).

**The first movement of a guided life**

The suspension of a final verdict regarding religious differences is a consistent theme in the Qur'an. Allahs Judgment or disclosure of the truth in matters of religious disagreement on the Day of Judgment is also mentioned in 3:55; 5:48; 6:164; 10:93; 16:92; 16:124; 22:69; 32:25; 39:3, 46. The Qur'an states that at one time mankind was but one community (10:19), and that even if all were made one community again, they did not cease to differ (11:118). In other instances, the prophets are given the mission of making clear these differences (16:64, in the case of Muhammad; 43:63, in the case of Jesus).

The verse describes jews not as a private opinion but as a direction that changes perception and conduct. In 2:113, guidance is recognized by what it makes a person do with knowledge, power, and desire. ### Expanded Commentary

**The Worst Wrong: Blocking the Houses of Allah**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings more and allahs into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. The order of 2:114 gives the reader a path through the verse: begin with what Allah names, follow the consequence, and resist the temptation to turn a living address into a slogan.

**Entering in Dread; Disgrace Below, Punishment Above**

Mosques translates masājid (sing. masjid), which is derived from the verb to prostrate (sajada). Many commentators attempt to specify the mosques mentioned here. Some point to the Temple in Jerusalem (the Farthest Mosque mentioned in 17:1) and the Kaʿbah in Makkah, since they are named mosque (masjid) in the Qur'an. They also give differing accounts of the destruction of the Temple, which according to some took place with the connivance of Christians. Some say this verse refers to when at Ḥudaybiyah the Makkans stopped the Prophet from entering Makkah to pray at the Kaʿbah in 6/628 and the Muslim pilgrims agreed to go back to Madinah and return the following year (see the introduction to Sūrah 48).

**The Mosque of the Heart**

For al-Ṭabarī, since even the idolaters never tried to destroy the Kaʿbah, it must refer to the Temple. Others see it more generally, saying that it applies to anyone who prevents people from entering any house of worship (al-Qurṭubī). A broader interpretation of ruin (kharāb) holds that in filling the Kaʿbah with idols and the practice of idolatry, the idolaters were seeking its ruin, because it was no longer a mosque of the One Allah but a temple of idols . Some also mention that Abū Bakr had a small mosque in Makkah before the Muslims migrated to Madinah, a mosque the Makkans later destroyed (al-Rāzī).

**The horizon beyond the immediate scene**

Some try to identify specific ways in which disgrace or fear is evidenced by Christians, such as the payment of the jizyah, or indemnity (see 9:29c; Ṭ). But others point out that the notion of disgrace can be quite broad, and that the Prophet would often pray that disgrace not be visited upon him and his community in this world (Ibn Kathīr). Some Sufis discern another level of meaning, saying that the heart is the house of love and knowledge of Allah (the Kaʿbah is the House of Allah), and one does wrong in destroying it through false desires (Aj, Qu).

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:115

> **To Allah belong the east and the west, so wherever you turn you are facing ˹towards˺ Allah. Surely Allah is AllEncompassing, All-Knowing.**

### Expanded Commentary

**East and West in One Hand**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between belong and wherever. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:115. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:115. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:115.

**"There Is the Face of Allah" — the Heart of the Clause**

Allah is elsewhere called the Lord of the East and the West (73:9); Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests (55:17); and Lord of the easts and the wests (70:40). The famous Light Verse (24:35) speaks of a blessed olive tree, neither of the East nor of the West. See also 2:142c. Regarding the remainder of the verse, the commentators converge on two main points: the practical question of the qiblah (the direction of the canonical prayer) and the doctrinal matter of understanding what it means that there is the Face of Allah wherever one turns.

**All-Encompassing, Knowing — and the Mosqueless Prayer**

Most commentators connect this verse to the change in the qiblah, which was at first oriented toward Jerusalem, but which, after the revelation of 2:144, became oriented toward the Kaʿbah in Makkah. Indeed, as a practical matter some thought that this verse gave permission to pray in any direction, but that this was abrogated by 2:144. For some, the present verse was revealed to the Prophet as a reassurance for some Muslims who told him that the previous night they could not discern the proper direction of prayer and later realized they had prayed facing in the wrong direction .

Others connect it to the permission to pray in the direction one is facing while mounted (Āl); this permission pertains to nonrequired prayers.

**The horizon beyond the immediate scene**

Still others prefer to link it to the death of the Negus, the king of Abyssinia who had sheltered many Muslims as refugees during the worst days of the persecution in Makkah. The Prophet said, Your brother the Negus has died; so pray for him. When those present objected that he was not a Muslim, it is said that 3:199 was revealed: And truly among the People of the Book are those who believe in Allah and that which has been sent down unto you, and that which has been sent down unto them. Then when they objected that the Negus did not face the qiblah, this verse was revealed . In another account—regarding 40:60, Call upon Me, and I shall respond to you—some asked the Prophet, In which direction? at which this verse as revealed. In verses such as these where several occasions of revelation are given, commentators often adopt a neutral attitude and acknowledge that the occasion is not decisive in light of the doctrinal content, which in this verse is profound and universal.

**A divine name that governs the meaning**

There is the Face of Allah is understood by some to simply mean, There is Allah, There is the qiblah of Allah (al-Ṭabarī), or There is Allahs Contentment (al-Rāzī). In connection with this verse many mention 28:88: All things perish, save His Face; 55:26–7: All upon it passes away. And there remains the Face of thy Lord, Possessed of Majesty and Bounty; 57:4: He is with you wheresoever you are; and 58:7: He is with them wheresoever they are. Some argue that the very fact that it says wheresoever is the strongest proof against anthropomorphizing Allah, since any body could be in only one place and not more than one place simultaneously (al-Rāzī).

**Mercy and warning held together**

All-Encompassing (wāsiʿ) can also mean unstinting or generous (al-Qurṭubī). Related passages include 53:32: Truly your Lord is of vast forgiveness; and 7:156: My Mercy encompasses all things. Al-Rāzī mentions that, in connection with the ruin of mosques mentioned in the previous verse, one can understand this phrase to mean that, despite destruction of mosques, Allahs remembrance cannot be hindered since He is wherever one turns.

This verse can also be taken as an allusion to the Omnipresence of Allah, who is the First, and the Last, and the Outward, and the Inward (57:3), manifest in all things, though naught is like unto Him (42:11). This verse is understood to mean that Allah is present everywhere and is one of the scriptural foundations for the Sufi doctrine of the oneness of being, or waḥdat al-wujūd.

**The deed before its final account**

The verse's reference to belong widens the scene beyond the immediate reward or pain. A deed in 2:115 may appear small when measured by public attention, yet its meaning changes when it is known by Allah and carried into the final account. Warning and mercy belong together in 2:115: accountability is serious because the human being is not abandoned to meaninglessness.

The standard in 2:115 remains practical because it can be applied before a dispute reaches a court or a crisis reaches its worst point. One can notice the first small departure from belong: an excuse, a concealed obligation, an unexamined desire, or a promise treated as optional. Returning at that point is easier than defending a settled habit. The warning is therefore also an opening for repair.

**Why the promise or threat is just**

The theology and practical instruction of 2:115 therefore support one another. If Allah knows or commands wherever, that knowledge or command changes how a person handles time, power, money, speech, and private desire. A doctrine that never reaches those choices has not yet been read at the level demanded by 2:115.

An ordinary example makes the moral structure of 2:115 visible without replacing the revelation. Two people may perform an outwardly similar act involving belong; one may be protecting a right, while the other is seeking praise, escaping a duty, or taking advantage of confusion. The act's surface does not settle its value. Intention, circumstance, and the rights of others complete the judgment.

**The Hereafter in the argument**

The surrounding verses keep the reader from isolating belong from the rest of life. In 2:115, revelation corrects the mind but also trains habits: how a person speaks when challenged, gives when unseen, waits when angry, and returns after error. Those habits are where this verse becomes more than information about belong. They are the place in which assent to 2:115 is either confirmed or quietly withdrawn.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:116

> **They say, “Allah has offspring.” Glory be to Him! In fact, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth—all are subject to His Will.**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Claim Surveyed and the Immediate Tasbīḥ**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings offspring and belongs into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. Its first term in 2:116 sets the subject, while the later term shows what that subject demands, permits, or exposes. The order of 2:116 gives the reader a path through the verse: begin with what Allah names, follow the consequence, and resist the temptation to turn a living address into a slogan.

**His Absolute Ownership and the Servanthood of All**

Commentators do not restrict this verse to Christian theology; it can also refer to the Arab pagan belief that the angels were the daughters of Allah (16:57; 37:149; 43:16; 52:39); similar disavowals of Divine sonship in connection with Jesus are found in 5:17, 72; 9:30; 19:35. The Islamic arguments against Allahs having a child stem directly from the fundamental Islamic conception of Divine Oneness, Transcendence, Absoluteness, and Uniqueness (tawḥīd) and are based on the principle that Allah is unlike anything in creation, Allah is beyond need of all things, and His Perfection can never be implicated in the limitations inherent in having a son. Since Islam emphasizes Allah as the Absolute, it denies all possibility of relativizing Him through a relationship such as fatherhood.

**The Kalām Core: Why No Sonship Is Possible for Allah**

Although a theologian such as al-Rāzī accepts a purely metaphorical understanding of Allah as “father”—in the sense that a father is prior, is responsible for or is the human cause of a person’s being—he would utterly reject that this in any way reflects the actual filial relationship between Allah and any being. His arguments are representative of much mainstream thought on the question: (1) those beings who are called Allah’s offspring are contingent beings, hence are created, and offsprings are begotten; (2) the offspring is either eternal or not; in the first case there is nothing to make one father and the other son, and in the second case the offspring would be a created being who is begotten; (3) the offspring is of the same species as the progenitor, being similar in some ways, but different in others; this would require that each be made up of parts, which cannot be said of Allah; (4) one has offspring as a result of certain needs such as happiness, care in one’s old age, pride, and so on, none of which are attributable to Allah.

**Devout Obedience as the Believer's Posture**

The term most often translated glory be to (subḥāna) also carries the sense of disassociation, so that Glory be to Him! can also mean Allah is far beyond such a thing! which is a sense brought out often in connection with this verse (al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī). For the general meaning of glorifying Allah, see 57:1c.

**The horizon beyond the immediate scene**

Devoutly obedient renders qānit, whose range of meaning includes compliance, humility, standing, and silence, all of which are emphasized by the commentators on this verse . Since the opposite qualities are all attributes of human beings in this world, some say that this refers to their state on the Day of Resurrection, when everyone will be forced to obey, stand, and be silent before Allah (al-Qurṭubī). Others understand the message of All are devoutly obedient to Him to be similar to that of 13:15: And unto Allah prostrates whosoever is in the heavens and on the earth, willingly or unwillingly (Ibn Kathīr). The context also suggests that the phrase be understood as All [of them] are devoutly obedient to Him, referring to Jesus, Ezra, and the angels who, far from being connected with this incorrect belief, are themselves sincere in their worship of Allah: The Messiah would never disdain to be a servant of Allah; nor would the angels brought nigh (4:172). On devout obedience, also see 3:17c; 4:34c.

**A divine name that governs the meaning**

The verse's reference to offspring widens the scene beyond the immediate reward or pain. A deed in 2:116 may appear small when measured by public attention, yet its meaning changes when it is known by Allah and carried into the final account. Warning and mercy belong together in 2:116: accountability is serious because the human being is not abandoned to meaninglessness.

A useful way to test the verse is to ask what would change if offspring were taken seriously when no audience was present. The answer cannot be only a feeling, because 2:116 connects inward recognition with a discernible choice. Nor can it be only an outward display, because the choice in 2:116 loses its Qur'anic meaning when it is made for reputation rather than for Allah. The passage holds intention and action together in 2:116.

**Mercy and warning held together**

An ordinary example makes the moral structure of 2:116 visible without replacing the revelation. Two people may perform an outwardly similar act involving offspring; one may be protecting a right, while the other is seeking praise, escaping a duty, or taking advantage of confusion. The act's surface does not settle its value. Intention, circumstance, and the rights of others complete the judgment.

The surrounding verses keep the reader from isolating offspring from the rest of life. In 2:116, revelation corrects the mind but also trains habits: how a person speaks when challenged, gives when unseen, waits when angry, and returns after error. Those habits are where this verse becomes more than information about offspring. They are the place in which assent to 2:116 is either confirmed or quietly withdrawn.

**The deed before its final account**

The most balanced response to 2:116 is neither to make the passage vague nor to claim more than it says. Its boundaries are part of its guidance. Within them, the verse can illuminate a new situation because its underlying moral relation remains stable: offspring is joined to belongs, and the person is responsible for how that relation is honoured.

The wording of 2:116 gives the reader a useful order of questions about offspring. What does the term offspring mean in ordinary Arabic, what does the surrounding sentence restrict it to, and what consequence follows when the command is obeyed or refused in 2:116? These questions prevent a commentary on 2:116 from becoming a list of slogans. They make the act of interpretation answerable to grammar, context, and the moral end of this passage at 2:116.

**Why the promise or threat is just**

The commentators sometimes preserve more than one report about the setting of 2:116. Such reports should be weighed rather than treated as interchangeable decoration. An occasion can explain why a question arose, but the wording of 2:116 determines how far the guidance travels. The verse speaks first to the situation that occasioned it and then to every reader who meets the same relation between offspring and belongs.

In 2:116, the distinction between public appearance and inward truth is especially relevant. A person may use the language of offspring while arranging the act around another purpose. Allah's judgment in 2:116 is not limited to the visible outline, yet the inner intention is not an excuse for ignoring the rights and forms that the revelation establishes. Sincerity completes obedience; it does not cancel it.

One can see the social wisdom of 2:116 in a small everyday case. When people share responsibility for offspring, uncertainty about the duty tends to fall on the person with less power or less information. A clear moral rule changes that balance. In 2:116, it tells the stronger party what must not be taken, and gives the weaker party language with which to name the wrong.

In 2:116, the verse also sits within the Qur'an's larger refusal to separate worship from truthfulness. Prayer, remembrance, generosity, patience, and justice are different acts in 2:116, but they are trained by the same capacity to stand before Allah without constructing a false account. The statement in 2:116 strengthens that capacity by making one particular choice visible.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:117

> **˹He is˺ the Originator of the heavens and the earth! When He decrees a matter, He simply tells it, “Be!” And it is!**

### Expanded Commentary

**Badīʿ: Maker Without a Model**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between originator and decrees. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:117. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:117. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:117.

**Kun Fayakūn: the Sovereign Word of Creation**

Decrees translates qaḍā, which can also mean to accomplish, to complete, or to judge. The creative command Be! is also found in 6:73; 16:40; 36:82; 40:68. In each case, all that is necessary to bring a thing into being is for Allah to say Be! In connection with the previous verse, similar language can also be found with regard to Jesus creation in 3:59: Truly the likeness of Jesus in the Sight of Allah is that of Adam; He created him from dust, then said to him, Be! and he was; and 19:35: It is not for Allah to beget a child.

**The Answer to the Months of Waiting**

Glory be to Him! When He decrees a thing, He only says to it, Be! and it is. For some commentators such as al-Rāzī, the command Be! is meant to convey the ease and power by which Allah creates, requiring no preparation, practice, or effort. This view rejects the idea of a sequence of (1) a things nonexistence, (2) Allahs saying Be! and (3) its existence, since one cannot address nothing, and if something exists, it does not need the Be! in order to exist. Others say Be! neither precedes nor follows the creation of a thing, but is coterminous with it (al-Qurṭubī).

This verse is also understood as confirming that Allah knows things prior to their creation, and hence before their existence (al-Qurṭubī).

**The verse in its immediate setting**

This latter idea is expanded upon by Ibn ʿArabī and many members of his school, who explain that Allah says Be! to the forms (or immutable essences, al-aʿyān al-thābitah) in His Knowledge, meaning His Knowledge of His own Qualities and Attributes. More precisely, Allah knows what He will create and brings His Will and Power to bear upon that object of knowledge in order to create it by saying Be! Being within Allahs Knowledge, it is not nothing, but neither is it yet created, nor does it possess existence. Ultimately, these views converge on the unity of Allahs Knowledge, Will, and Power as His inseparable Attributes and on Allahs complete self-sufficiency in relation to what He creates. Be! (kun) also corresponds to the Biblical fiat lux (Let there be light, Genesis 1:3) and serves to emphasize the fact that the existence of everything comes from Allah and His Will and that human beings do not have the power to bring anything into being out of nothing.

**The central term and its range**

The mention of originator gives the verse a definite centre. Its meaning in 2:117 is not a general meditation on religion but an explanation of what this word requires in the situation named here. The passage at 2:117 moves between belief, action, and consequence, so a sound reading must preserve all three rather than allowing one attractive phrase to swallow the rest.

The standard in 2:117 remains practical because it can be applied before a dispute reaches a court or a crisis reaches its worst point. One can notice the first small departure from originator: an excuse, a concealed obligation, an unexamined desire, or a promise treated as optional. Returning at that point is easier than defending a settled habit. The warning is therefore also an opening for repair.

**What the early commentators preserve**

The relation between originator and decrees also protects the verse from two opposite misreadings. It should not be expanded into a claim the wording of 2:117 does not make, but neither should its brevity be used to make it weightless. Short Qur'anic statements such as 2:117 often function as hinges: they close one movement, open another, and give the next command its moral setting. The careful reader of 2:117 therefore asks what has just been established, what response is now being required, and what kind of character could respond without evasion. Those questions keep 2:117 specific while allowing its guidance to reach a new circumstance.

Those habits are where this verse becomes more than information about originator. They are the place in which assent to 2:117 is either confirmed or quietly withdrawn.

The wording of 2:117 gives the reader a useful order of questions about originator. What does the term originator mean in ordinary Arabic, what does the surrounding sentence restrict it to, and what consequence follows when the command is obeyed or refused in 2:117? These questions prevent a commentary on 2:117 from becoming a list of slogans. They make the act of interpretation answerable to grammar, context, and the moral end of this passage at 2:117.

An occasion can explain why a question arose, but the wording of 2:117 determines how far the guidance travels. The verse speaks first to the situation that occasioned it and then to every reader who meets the same relation between originator and decrees.

**The surrounding passage as a guide**

In 2:117, the distinction between public appearance and inward truth is especially relevant. A person may use the language of originator while arranging the act around another purpose. Allah's judgment in 2:117 is not limited to the visible outline, yet the inner intention is not an excuse for ignoring the rights and forms that the revelation establishes. Sincerity completes obedience; it does not cancel it.

One can see the social wisdom of 2:117 in a small everyday case. When people share responsibility for originator, uncertainty about the duty tends to fall on the person with less power or less information. A clear moral rule changes that balance. In 2:117, it tells the stronger party what must not be taken, and gives the weaker party language with which to name the wrong.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:118

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:120

> **Never will the Jews or Christians be pleased with you, until you follow their faith. Say, “Allah’s guidance is the only ˹true˺ guidance.” And if you were to follow their desires after ˹all˺ the knowledge that has come to you, there would be none to protect or help you against Allah.**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Impossibility of Contentment**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings never and pleased into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. Its first term in 2:120 sets the subject, while the later term shows what that subject demands, permits, or exposes. The order of 2:120 gives the reader a path through the verse: begin with what Allah names, follow the consequence, and resist the temptation to turn a living address into a slogan.

**"The Guidance of Allah Is THE Guidance"**

For some commentators this verse is a confirmation that the question in v. 118 is not sincere, but a taunt (al-Qurṭubī). Creed renders millah, a word that also can mean community, but that can furthermore be used to refer to the religious law (sharīʿah) or way that defines a particular religious community (al-Qurṭubī) and is used this way elsewhere (2:130, 135; 3:95; 4:125; 6:161; 7:88; 12:37; 14:13; 16:123; 18:20; 22:78; 38:7). See v. 145 for a similar message about the following of others caprices, meaning their egocentric whims rather than the truth. Some commentators report that when the qiblah was changed to the Kaʿbah away from Jerusalem, this created resentment among the Jews and Christians, who wanted to use a truce as a delaying tactic while trying to turn the Prophet away from the new religion .

**Caprice vs. Knowledge — and the Ummah's Own Warning**

The verse describes never not as a private opinion but as a direction that changes perception and conduct. In 2:120, guidance is recognized by what it makes a person do with knowledge, power, and desire. For 2:120, inward assent is linked to an observable response: the heart's claim is tested by the path it chooses when the claim becomes costly.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:124

> **˹Remember˺ when Abraham was tested by his Lord with ˹certain˺ commandments, which he fulfilled. Allah said, “I will certainly make you into a role model for the people.” Abraham asked, “What about my offspring?” Allah replied, “My covenant is not extended to the wrongdoers.”**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Trial by Words**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings abraham and commandments into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. Its first term in 2:124 sets the subject, while the later term shows what that subject demands, permits, or exposes. The order of 2:124 gives the reader a path through the verse: begin with what Allah names, follow the consequence, and resist the temptation to turn a living address into a slogan.

Abraham was tried or tested, but no specifics about this test are given in this particular passage. The commentators have differed widely over the question. Some believe these words were commands given to Abraham to institute various kinds of bodily cleanliness, grooming, and ritual purification . Others believe they were the rituals and prayers he was to perform, specifically the central rites of the ḥajj, which Muslims consider to have originated with Abraham, including the circumambulation of the Kaʿbah, the running between Ṣafā and Marwah, and the pelting of the pillar representing Satan.

**The Imamate of Mankind**

Others see them as trials of suffering, such as circumcision, the sacrifice of his son (37:102), and the fire into which he was cast by his people, but which Allah made to be cool (21:68–69; Ṭ). Although Abraham is praised throughout the Qur'an, in this verse the commentators highlight his obedience and fulfillment of what was asked of him, mentioning it along with 53:37: And Abraham, who fulfilled. Some mention that this refers to his embodiment of the virtuous human qualities listed in the Qur'an in verses such as 9:112 and 33:35.

Some also say that the word Abraham fulfilled was his selection as an imām. Imām means most generally leader, including a religious or political leader or the person who leads the canonical prayer. In Shiism it also has the particular meaning of one in whom the Muhammadan Light is present and who is designated the spiritual leader of the community by Divine Decree (naṣṣ).

**"My Covenant Does Not Include the Wrongdoers"**

The response to Abrahams prayer means that a wrongdoer or tyrant would not deserve a covenant with Allah and could not rightly be an imām; or it means that such a person could be an imām, but an imām who does wrong would not receive the promise of the Hereafter; or it can simply be read as meaning that not all of Abrahams descendants would be virtuous, as in 37:113: And We blessed him and Isaac. And among their progeny are the virtuous and those who clearly wrong themselves (al-Ṭabarī). In Shiism, the fifth and sixth Imams have cited this verse to indicate that Allah does not set up or allow an unjust imam (Ṭū). Elements similar to those in this verse are found in 25:74: Our Lord! Grant us comfort in our spouses and our progeny, and make us imāms for the reverent.

**The horizon beyond the immediate scene**

The verse's reference to abraham widens the scene beyond the immediate reward or pain. A deed in 2:124 may appear small when measured by public attention, yet its meaning changes when it is known by Allah and carried into the final account. Warning and mercy belong together in 2:124: accountability is serious because the human being is not abandoned to meaninglessness.

A useful way to test the verse is to ask what would change if abraham were taken seriously when no audience was present. The answer cannot be only a feeling, because 2:124 connects inward recognition with a discernible choice. Nor can it be only an outward display, because the choice in 2:124 loses its Qur'anic meaning when it is made for reputation rather than for Allah. The passage holds intention and action together in 2:124.

**A divine name that governs the meaning**

The relation between abraham and commandments also protects the verse from two opposite misreadings. It should not be expanded into a claim the wording of 2:124 does not make, but neither should its brevity be used to make it weightless. Short Qur'anic statements such as 2:124 often function as hinges: they close one movement, open another, and give the next command its moral setting. The careful reader of 2:124 therefore asks what has just been established, what response is now being required, and what kind of character could respond without evasion. Those questions keep 2:124 specific while allowing its guidance to reach a new circumstance.

A reader who finds the command in 2:124 difficult should distinguish difficulty from impossibility. For 2:124, difficulty may be the place where desire, habit, or social pressure is being corrected; impossibility is a separate legal and moral question. The passage does not praise needless hardship, but it does not permit comfort to redefine abraham until the demand disappears.

**Mercy and warning held together**

The final emphasis of 2:124 returns to responsibility. No explanation of abraham is complete if it leaves the reader with information about earlier communities but no question about present conduct. The verse 2:124 asks what can be repaired now: a promise kept, a right restored, a motive purified, or a harmful practice abandoned. That is where knowledge becomes guidance.

The choice of the word abraham in 2:124 also matters. It leaves room for the full context of 2:124 instead of allowing one translation gloss to carry every shade of meaning. Classical Arabic often places a broad word inside a narrow scene; in 2:124, the surrounding clauses determine whether the emphasis falls on an act, an intention, a condition, or a consequence. Here the reader should let the sentence do that work.

**The deed before its final account**

The exegetical tradition approaches abraham from more than one angle, but its differences are more useful when their shared question is made visible. The commentators ask what the wording of 2:124 includes, what it excludes, and how it fits with the other passages of the Qur'an. A responsible reading can preserve those alternatives in 2:124 without pretending that every possibility has equal strength.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:125

> **And ˹remember˺ when We made the Sacred House a centre and a sanctuary for the people ˹saying˺, “˹You may˺ take the standing-place of Abraham as a site of prayer.” And We entrusted Abraham and Ishmael to purify My House for those who circle it, who meditate in it, and who bow and prostrate themselves ˹in prayer˺.**

### Expanded Commentary

**The House: Rendezvous and Sanctuary**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between sacred and sanctuary. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:125. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:125. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:125.

This verse refers to the Kaʿbah, also called the House of Allah or the Sacred Mosque, which was built by Abraham and Ishmael (see v. 127). In pre-Islamic times, the Kaʿbah and the precinct surrounding it was a sanctuary, in that a murderer, for example, would be safe within it (al-Ṭabarī), which would have been seen as a continuation in some sense of its original status as established by Abraham. Some read the verb take to mean “they took,” referring to past people who took the station as a place of prayer (al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī).

**"Take the Station of Abraham as a Place of Prayer"**

The station of Abraham is a place in the close vicinity of the Kaʿbah marked by a stone that is said to have borne the footprint of Abraham. However, some consider the station of Abraham to refer to the ḥajj rites as a whole. Others consider it to be another location important in the ḥajj, ʿArafah, Minā, or Muzdalifah (al-Ṭabarī). Circumambulation is the practice of walking around the Kaʿbah and is one of the major ritual actions of the ḥajj, while bowing and prostration are movements in the canonical prayer.

**"Purify My House" — Abraham and Ishmael at Work Together**

According to a ḥadīth the Prophet took ʿUmar by the hand and said, “This is the station of Abraham,” upon which ʿUmar said, “Shall we take it as a place of prayer?” The Prophet said he was not commanded to do so, and some commentators say that before sunset of that day this verse was revealed. Abraham was to purify it, that is, cleanse it from idolatry and doubt (al-Ṭabarī), which in Abraham’s case would mean to maintain it in that state, a state to which the Prophet Muhammad would return it later.

**The act and the intention beneath it**

Those who make retreat means those who stay there without moving away; it derives from the root ʿ-k-f, which depending on context can mean “devoted to” or “resident in.” The supererogatory Islamic practice of iʿtikāf (from the same root), which consists of spending a period of time, usually a number of days, within the mosque in prayer and remembrance, is based upon the Prophet’s practice of doing so during the last ten days of Ramadan. The practice of seclusion (khalwah), or “spiritual retreat,” in Sufism is also based ultimately upon iʿtikāf.

The subject of sacred joins an act directed to Allah with a consequence visible among people. In 2:125, that union guards against two reductions: worship cannot become a private performance with no social fruit, and social generosity cannot become a substitute for worship. The verse 2:125 asks for an outward practice whose inward intention remains answerable to Allah.

**A visible duty with an inward root**

The standard in 2:125 remains practical because it can be applied before a dispute reaches a court or a crisis reaches its worst point. One can notice the first small departure from sacred: an excuse, a concealed obligation, an unexamined desire, or a promise treated as optional. Returning at that point is easier than defending a settled habit. The warning is therefore also an opening for repair.

The relation between sacred and sanctuary also protects the verse from two opposite misreadings. It should not be expanded into a claim the wording of 2:125 does not make, but neither should its brevity be used to make it weightless. Short Qur'anic statements such as 2:125 often function as hinges: they close one movement, open another, and give the next command its moral setting. The careful reader of 2:125 therefore asks what has just been established, what response is now being required, and what kind of character could respond without evasion. Those questions keep 2:125 specific while allowing its guidance to reach a new circumstance.

The final emphasis of 2:125 returns to responsibility. No explanation of sacred is complete if it leaves the reader with information about earlier communities but no question about present conduct. The verse 2:125 asks what can be repaired now: a promise kept, a right restored, a motive purified, or a harmful practice abandoned. That is where knowledge becomes guidance.

The choice of the word sacred in 2:125 also matters. It leaves room for the full context of 2:125 instead of allowing one translation gloss to carry every shade of meaning. Classical Arabic often places a broad word inside a narrow scene; in 2:125, the surrounding clauses determine whether the emphasis falls on an act, an intention, a condition, or a consequence. Here the reader should let the sentence do that work.

**The measure of sincere giving**

The exegetical tradition approaches sacred from more than one angle, but its differences are more useful when their shared question is made visible. The commentators ask what the wording of 2:125 includes, what it excludes, and how it fits with the other passages of the Qur'an. A responsible reading can preserve those alternatives in 2:125 without pretending that every possibility has equal strength.

The act's surface does not settle its value. Intention, circumstance, and the rights of others complete the judgment.

**A community shaped by obedience**

The surrounding verses keep the reader from isolating sacred from the rest of life. Those habits are where this verse becomes more than information about sacred. They are the place in which assent to 2:125 is either confirmed or quietly withdrawn.

The wording of 2:125 gives the reader a useful order of questions about sacred. What does the term sacred mean in ordinary Arabic, what does the surrounding sentence restrict it to, and what consequence follows when the command is obeyed or refused in 2:125? These questions prevent a commentary on 2:125 from becoming a list of slogans. They make the act of interpretation answerable to grammar, context, and the moral end of this passage at 2:125.

What an evil destination!”**

### Expanded Commentary

The word secure (āmin) is related by root to the word sanctuary (amn) in v. 125. ## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:128

> **Our Lord! Make us both ˹fully˺ submit to You and from our descendants a nation that will submit to you. Show us our rituals, and turn to us in grace. You are truly the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful.**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Builders' Prayer for Submission**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings both and descendants into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. **Muslim as Universal, Not Tribal**

Submit and submitting render muslim, the participle of a transitive verb (lit. submitter to Allah in this context), which is tied to the submission (islām) mentioned in v. 132, both of which are among those verses that testify to the universal meaning of islām, which existed before the revelation of the Qur'an. The rites (manāsik) are often taken to be the rituals of the ḥajj (rites also mentioned in connection with the ḥajj in v. 200), or sacrifice, or simply worship in general (al-Ṭabarī); this general meaning is found in passages such as For every community We have appointed a rite (22:34, 67), referring to their respective rituals and practices.

It is connected with the prayer for a messenger to be sent in v. 129 (al-Ṭabarī).

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:129

> **Our Lord! Raise from among them a messenger who will recite to them Your revelations, teach them the Book and wisdom, and purify them. Indeed, You ˹alone˺ are the Almighty, AllWise.”**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Prayer That Waited Two Thousand Years for Its Answer**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between raise and recite. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:129. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:129. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:129.

**From Among Them: the Wisdom of a Home-Grown Messenger**

The response to this prayer for a messenger is realized in v. 151, where the Prophet is described in terms identical to those in this verse. The Book is most often taken to be the Qur'an, while the Wisdom is understood to be the Sunnah (the exemplary sayings and doings of the Prophet) or more generally knowledge and understanding of the religion (al-Ṭabarī), although the pairing of the Book and Wisdom has more universal import in the Qur'an and is also used in connection with Jesus (3:48; 5:110), the Children of Israel (45:16), and the House of Abraham (4:54).

The wording around raise assumes that revelation is meant to be heard with intelligence and humility together. Understanding is not an invitation to place the reader above the text; neither is obedience a reason to stop thinking. The classical tradition preserved both tasks: clarify the language, then ask what kind of person the clarified command is meant to form.

**Mighty and Wise: the Seal of the Prayer**

The standard in 2:129 remains practical because it can be applied before a dispute reaches a court or a crisis reaches its worst point. One can notice the first small departure from raise: an excuse, a concealed obligation, an unexamined desire, or a promise treated as optional. Returning at that point is easier than defending a settled habit. The warning is therefore also an opening for repair.

The relation between raise and recite also protects the verse from two opposite misreadings. It should not be expanded into a claim the wording of 2:129 does not make, but neither should its brevity be used to make it weightless. Those questions keep 2:129 specific while allowing its guidance to reach a new circumstance.

The theology and practical instruction of 2:129 therefore support one another. If Allah knows or commands recite, that knowledge or command changes how a person handles time, power, money, speech, and private desire. A doctrine that never reaches those choices has not yet been read at the level demanded by 2:129.

An ordinary example makes the moral structure of 2:129 visible without replacing the revelation. Two people may perform an outwardly similar act involving raise; one may be protecting a right, while the other is seeking praise, escaping a duty, or taking advantage of confusion. The act's surface does not settle its value. Intention, circumstance, and the rights of others complete the judgment.

The surrounding verses keep the reader from isolating raise from the rest of life. Those habits are where this verse becomes more than information about raise. They are the place in which assent to 2:129 is either confirmed or quietly withdrawn.
