## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:165

> **Still there are some who take others as Allah’s equal—they love them as they should love Allah—but the ˹true˺ believers love Allah even more. If only the wrongdoers could see the ˹horrible˺ punishment ˹awaiting them˺, they would certainly realize that all power belongs to Allah and that Allah is indeed severe in punishment.**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Rivals in the Love-Market**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between still and allahs. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:165. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:165. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:165.

**"Those Who Believe Love Allah More"**

Equals has the sense of competitors (al-Rāzī), as in v. 22. An alternate reading of the last sentence is, “If thou sawest those who do wrong when they see the Punishment of Allah, [thou wouldst see] that power belongs wholly to Allah.” Loving them like loving Allah means they love their idols as the believers love Allah or that they obey their leaders as they should obey Allah (al-Ṭabarī). It may also mean that they love these equals as they themselves love Allah (thus dividing their love between Allah and the idols), or that they love them as they ought to love Allah, or that they glorify and obey their idols or their own human leaders or other human agencies as they should Allah (al-Rāzī).

**The Sight on the Day It Burned**

These interpretations are all possible because of the wording of the verse, which can be literally rendered, “They love them like unto the love of Allah.” The believers’ love is more ardent because it is directed undividedly at the one true object of love, unlike that of the idolaters, who direct love toward idols during ordinary times but then toward Allah in times of need, as when they call out when on a ship buffeted by waves (al-Rāzī).

The idea of the love (ḥubb) for Allah by human beings appears in this verse and in 3:31: Say, If you love Allah, follow me; 5:54: Allah will bring a people whom He loves and who love Him; and 9:24: Say, If your (family and possessions) are more beloved to you than Allah, . . . then wait till Allah comes with His Command. According to a ḥadīth, a man asked the Prophet, When will the Hour come to pass, O Messenger of Allah? The Prophet said, What have you prepared for it?

**The horizon beyond the immediate scene**

The man said, I have not prepared for it much by way of prayers or fasting or alms, but I love Allah and His Messenger. The Prophet said, You will be with those whom you love. More often, however, dozens of times in fact, the word love (ḥubb) is used in the Qur'an to describe what Allah loves or does not love in human beings. For example, throughout the Qur'an Allah is said to love the virtuous, those who repent, the reverent, the patient, those who trust, the just, those who fight in His way, and those who purify themselves, but He does not love disbelievers, transgressors, sinful ingrates, wrongdoers, the vainglorious, workers of corruption, prodigals, the treacherous, or the exultant.

**A divine name that governs the meaning**

Many commentators use this verse as an occasion to discuss the nature of ḥubb (and the related term maḥabbah), which is the word here rendered as love. The English word love has a broader range of meaning than the Arabic ḥubb, and several Arabic concepts correspond to love depending on its usage. These include raḥmah (most often translated mercy or compassion) and mawaddah, as in a verse describing the sentiments between spouses: He established affection (mawaddah) and mercy (raḥmah) between you (30:21). The Qur'an, the Sunnah, and the mainstream exoteric exegetical tradition do not treat love as a technical or esoteric concept (although the Islamic intellectual, spiritual, and poetical tradition is replete with discussions of the reality and experience of love).

**Mercy and warning held together**

Rather, they accept it as a self-evident reality whose basic meaning is known, while acknowledging the difficulty of explaining how love, and indeed any concept ordinarily used for created objects, can correctly be applied to Allah. The asymmetry between Allahs Love for human beings and human beings love for Allah is reflected in the Qurans almost exclusive discussion of that love as originating with Allah. Because Allah is unlike anything in the world, love for Him is hard to encapsulate in a technical definition, and the exegetes often prefer to describe it by speaking in terms of the fruits of loving Allah.

For example, when we love someone, we long to meet them, miss them and yearn for them when they are not there, do everything we do for their sake, seek to do what makes them happy, and love what they love (Aj). These are all symptoms, as it were, of love.

**The deed before its final account**

In the Islamic spiritual tradition, love is usually spoken of in light of knowledge, which is to say that one loves Allah to the degree that one knows Him, and vice versa. Al-Rāzī says, for example, that when we see the face of the beloved, we want to see the hair, which in theological terms means that even a slight familiarity with Allah will arouse a virtuous desire to know Him even more, and this desire is itself a sign of love. In human life, the lover seeks to banish from the heart all but the beloved and sees all else as a kind of distraction; and among the spiritual wayfarers of Islam this is manifested in a discipline whose method and goal are the constant remembrance of Allah (dhikr Allāh); also see the essay “The Qur'an and Sufism.”

**Why the promise or threat is just**

It is typical for commentators to discuss two kinds of love: One is called “desirous love” or ḥubb al-hawā, which is when we love a thing because of what it does for us. The other kind is love for the sake of the beloved, which arises for no other reason than that the beloved’s beauty, goodness, and perfection kindle love within the lover. More precisely, human beings love, or should love, Allah, but this love should not be seen as a means to something else (al-Rāzī). The first kind of love is said to be incumbent upon all believers in that one can see glorification, acts of obedience, and righteous behavior as means to the peace and happiness that Allah will provide as a reward for them. Lovers in the higher sense love Allah for Allah alone and, because of this love, want to perform those acts that Allah loves, not because of what they will gain; for them diverting oneself from what the beloved loves is more difficult than working for one’s selfish ends.

**The Hereafter in the argument**

At the lower level, we love what is good to us, and Allah’s Goodness to us is everywhere. At the higher level, we love the beauty and goodness of what we know, and Allah’s Beauty and Goodness are the object of our love to the degree that we come to know them; and in the case of Allah the perfections and beauties are endless, and so love for Him is potentially limitless. Sufis have written much about the distinction between what they call “metaphorical,” or majāzī, love and “true,” or ḥaqīqī, love; the former refers to such things as romantic love and love for the things of the world, and the latter refers to love of Allah alone and by extension the love of other beings through the love of Allah.

An idea closely related to love of Allah is love “in” or “through” Allah (al-ḥubb fī’Llāh), typically rendered “love for the sake of Allah”; a similar concept is “loving in Allah’s Glory” (bi-jalāl Allāh). A ḥadīth describes Allah saying, “Those who loved each other in My Glory shall have pulpits (minbars) of light, and the prophets and saints will envy them.” In another ḥadīth He said, “Where are those who loved one another for My Glory? Today I shall shade them in My shade, on the Day when there is no shade but Mine.” The Prophet also said, “Allah says, ‘My Love is realized for those who love one another for My sake, who are honest with one another for My sake, who give charity to one another for My sake, and who visit one another for My sake.’”

The verse's reference to still widens the scene beyond the immediate reward or pain. A deed in 2:165 may appear small when measured by public attention, yet its meaning changes when it is known by Allah and carried into the final account. Warning and mercy belong together in 2:165: accountability is serious because the human being is not abandoned to meaninglessness.

The standard in 2:165 remains practical because it can be applied before a dispute reaches a court or a crisis reaches its worst point. One can notice the first small departure from still: an excuse, a concealed obligation, an unexamined desire, or a promise treated as optional. Returning at that point is easier than defending a settled habit. The warning is therefore also an opening for repair.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:166

> **˹Consider the Day˺ when those who misled others will disown their followers—when they face the torment—and the bonds that united them will be cut off.**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Scene of Disavowal**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings consider and disown into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. **The Ropes Cut**

Those who were followed refers to the leaders of idolatry, while those who followed refers to their minions and adherents; or the two phrases may refer, respectively, to the satans and the human beings who followed them. This may also refer generally to all those who led and followed in the ways of error in the life of the world (al-Ṭabarī). Recourse renders asbāb (sing. sabab), which can mean a rope, a means by which to obtain something, or a cause. Here it is understood to refer to the bonds, the love, or the friendships and blood ties they shared in the world, all of which will be severed from them as a means of help in the Hereafter.

**The Punishment, Seen**

According to another interpretation, the recourse consists of their deeds in this life, which remain sound in the Hereafter if they are righteous deeds, but these means are cut off when they are evil (al-Ṭabarī). It can also point to the fact that they have no way of staving off the punishment or escaping the consequences of their evil actions (al-Rāzī).

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:167

> **The ˹misled˺ followers will cry, “If only we could have a second chance, we would disown them as they disowned us.” And so Allah will make them remorseful of their misdeeds. And they will never ˹be able to˺ leave the Fire.**

### Expanded Commentary

**"If We Had Another Turn"**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between misled and chance. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:167. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:167. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:167.

**Regret Shown, Not Felt Only**

The turn here is the chance to return to the world. The wrongdoers regret is about having done sinful deeds or having failed to perform righteous ones; they are seeing what they would have had in the Hereafter if they had acted righteously and are tormented on account of it. According to another interpretation, they will see the houses of the Garden and wish for them, while the inhabitants of the Garden will see them and wish for Allah to bless them (al-Ṭabarī). Elsewhere it is said, Then on the Day of Resurrection you will disown one another, and you will curse one another (29:25).

**Remedy for the Living**

The conversations that take place between the denizens of Hell are also described in 7:38–39, and Satan tells them on the Day of Judgment, Verily Allah made you the Promise of truth; and I made you a promise, but I failed you (14:22). Al-Ṭabarī understands the last part of the verse to mean that their regret and desire for another chance at life will not remove them from the Fire, and for him this is evidence that the disbelievers will be in the Fire everlastingly.

The verse's reference to misled widens the scene beyond the immediate reward or pain. Warning and mercy belong together in 2:167: accountability is serious because the human being is not abandoned to meaninglessness.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:168

> **O humanity! Eat from what is lawful and good on the earth and do not follow Satan’s footsteps. He is truly your sworn enemy.**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Universal Table Spread**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings humanity and earth into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. Its first term in 2:168 sets the subject, while the later term shows what that subject demands, permits, or exposes. The order of 2:168 gives the reader a path through the verse: begin with what Allah names, follow the consequence, and resist the temptation to turn a living address into a slogan.

It is reported that this verse was revealed in connection with the tribes of Thaqīf, Khuzāʿah, and Banū Mudlij, who had decided that the eating of certain kinds of animals was forbidden, although the plain sense of the verse shows that it is of universal import (al-Qurṭubī). Good (ṭayyib) also has the sense of being pleasant, agreeable, and delicious. Lawful (ḥalāl) is what in Islamic Law is deemed permissible and derives from a root with a range of meanings including “untie,” “set free,” and “unbind.” In the categorization of actions in Islamic Law, it is the opposite of ḥarām, or “forbidden.”

**Occasion and Universal Rollout**

The image of following in the footsteps of Satan is mentioned elsewhere (2:208; 6:142; 24:21) and is often described by commentators as an idiomatic way of saying that a person submits to temptation and commits evil. Satan is often called a manifest enemy in the Qur'an (7:22; 12:5; 17:53; 28:15; 36:60; 43:62).

Some relate this verse to the practice of taking oaths that one will refrain from something or other, but oaths cannot be taken in a state of anger. When they are taken in such a state, one can pay an expiation. On carelessness in oaths, see 2:225. Ibn Kathīr mentions several incidents where some people made oaths that they would do thus and so, but were reprimanded by other Companions for following in the footsteps of Satan. A ḥadīth states, Allah said, I created My servants as ḥanīfs. Then the satans came to them, and diverted them from their religion, and forbade for them what I had made lawful.

**Food and the Answering of Prayer**

A Companion asked the Prophet how he could become someone whose supplications were accepted. The Prophet said, “Make wholesome what you eat, and your supplications will be accepted by Him in Whose Hand is the soul of Muhammad. Let a man put a forbidden morsel in his mouth and [his supplications] will not be accepted for forty days. Any man who raises his meat from ill-gotten gains is most deserving of the Fire.”

The mention of humanity must be read with the restraints carried by the same revelation. Permission to resist wrongdoing does not erase the prohibition of wrongdoing. The verse therefore asks the community to hold two truths together: injustice may have to be confronted, and the means used in confronting it remain subject to Allah's judgment.

**The permission is not a blank cheque**

A useful way to test the verse is to ask what would change if humanity were taken seriously when no audience was present. The answer cannot be only a feeling, because 2:168 connects inward recognition with a discernible choice. Nor can it be only an outward display, because the choice in 2:168 loses its Qur'anic meaning when it is made for reputation rather than for Allah. The passage holds intention and action together in 2:168.

The relation between humanity and earth also protects the verse from two opposite misreadings. Short Qur'anic statements such as 2:168 often function as hinges: they close one movement, open another, and give the next command its moral setting. Those questions keep 2:168 specific while allowing its guidance to reach a new circumstance.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:172

> **O believers! Eat from the good things We have provided for you. And give thanks to Allah if you ˹truly˺ worship Him ˹alone˺.**

### Expanded Commentary

**From Mankind to the Believers**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings belief and thanks into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. Its first term in 2:172 sets the subject, while the later term shows what that subject demands, permits, or exposes. The order of 2:172 gives the reader a path through the verse: begin with what Allah names, follow the consequence, and resist the temptation to turn a living address into a slogan.

**Food as Primary Worship**

The good things (Ṭayyibāt) are those things that Allah has not forbidden or singled out as being sinful (al-Ṭabarī). See also 2:57c. In a ḥadīth the Prophet said, Allah is good (ṭayyib), and only accepts that which is good. Offered to other than Allah means food that is sacrificed to an idol, thus excluding the meat eaten by the idolaters (but not that of the People of the Book according to many jurists). In Islamic practice, an animal is slaughtered with the words, In the Name of Allah. It can occur that one is compelled by necessity, meaning by hunger, to eat under certain circumstances things that are forbidden in order to survive and protect ones life, but this should be done neither coveting nor transgressing, meaning not with the intention of bypassing Allahs Commandments in order to enjoy something that is forbidden (al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī). In such cases of necessity one is therefore permitted to eat what in normal circumstances would be forbidden.

**The If-Clause That Tests Every Mouthful**

Coveting renders bāghin, which has the sense of rebellion. For some the idea of transgressing (ʿādin) also refers to the practice of highway robbery, going against the authorities, or setting out to disobey Allah, presumably meaning that it is not permissible to pursue food in these ways even in cases of need (al-Ṭabarī). Regarding the legal and ritual issues of carrion, blood, and the flesh of swine, see 5:3c.

The verse's reference to belief widens the scene beyond the immediate reward or pain. Warning and mercy belong together in 2:172: accountability is serious because the human being is not abandoned to meaninglessness.

A useful way to test the verse is to ask what would change if belief were taken seriously when no audience was present. The answer cannot be only a feeling, because 2:172 connects inward recognition with a discernible choice. Nor can it be only an outward display, because the choice in 2:172 loses its Qur'anic meaning when it is made for reputation rather than for Allah. The passage holds intention and action together in 2:172.

The relation between belief and thanks also protects the verse from two opposite misreadings. ## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:174

> **Indeed, those who hide Allah’s revelations, trading them for a fleeting gain consume nothing but fire into their bellies. Allah will neither speak to them on the Day of Judgment, nor will He purify them. And they will suffer a painful punishment.**

### Expanded Commentary

**Concealing-and-Selling: The Double Verb**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings indeed and revelations into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. Its first term in 2:174 sets the subject, while the later term shows what that subject demands, permits, or exposes. The order of 2:174 gives the reader a path through the verse: begin with what Allah names, follow the consequence, and resist the temptation to turn a living address into a slogan.

Regarding sell it for a paltry price, see 2:79c. On fire in their bellies, also see 4:10c. Both phrases make the point that instead of consuming the wealth they sought in earthly life, in the Hereafter such people will consume only fire. On Allahs speaking to human beings in the Hereafter, also see 3:77, which, like this verse, states, Allah will not speak to them, nor will He look at them on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He purify them. And theirs shall be a painful punishment.

**Silent Allah, Ungreeting Allah**

However, elsewhere in the Qur'an Allah speaks to human beings on the Day of Resurrection: So by thy Lord, We shall question them all concerning that which they used to do (15:92–93); Then We shall surely question those unto whom Our message was sent, and We shall surely question the messengers (7:6); and He will say, Be gone therein, and speak not to Me (23:108, spoken by Allah in response to those asking to be removed from the Fire). According to al-Rāzī, the plain sense of v. 174 and 3:77 is that He will not speak to them at all, but in light of these other Qur'anic verses it is to be understood, rather, as a description of a punishment, meaning that He will not speak words of peace and welcome.

**The Verse in Islamic Ethics of the 'Ulamāʾ**

Al-Rāzī notes that this resembles intimacy with a king, who shows his displeasure through imposing exile and cutting off contact, and suggests that it will be the angels who speak to people on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Ṭabarī offers a similar interpretation, taking it to mean that Allah will not say things agreeable to them. Al-Qurṭubī points out that one says, He did not speak to him, to describe someone who is angry.

Nor will He purify them means He will not praise them for their goodness or call them purified (al-Ṭabarī), that He will not set right their evil deeds (al-Qurṭubī), or that He will not accept their deeds as He accepts those of the purified. The verb zakkā can mean both to purify and to deem purified, as in 53:32: So do not deem yourselves purified. Al-Rāzī points out that the punishment of indignity and humiliation is worse than that of physical punishment, which is a way of implying that the spiritual punishment of distance and separation from Allah constitutes the worst suffering in Hell.

The passage holds intention and action together in 2:174.

That is because indicates that the punishment applies because of their treatment of Allahs Book, going back to v. 174 (al-Ṭabarī). For schism (shiqāq; see also 22:53; 38:2; 41:52), see 2:137c. It is also possible that Book could refer to the Torah and the Gospel, which attest to the truth of the Prophet according to Islamic belief, and that differ pertains to questions of interpretation and distortion (see 2:75c), or it could refer to the Bible as well as the Qur'an together as being collectively Allahs Book .

**Schism Pronounced on Dissension**

The wording around because assumes that revelation is meant to be heard with intelligence and humility together. Understanding is not an invitation to place the reader above the text; neither is obedience a reason to stop thinking. The classical tradition preserved both tasks: clarify the language, then ask what kind of person the clarified command is meant to form.

A useful way to test the verse is to ask what would change if because were taken seriously when no audience was present. The answer cannot be only a feeling, because 2:176 connects inward recognition with a discernible choice. Nor can it be only an outward display, because the choice in 2:176 loses its Qur'anic meaning when it is made for reputation rather than for Allah. The passage holds intention and action together in 2:176.

**The Rule of the Single Truth-Book**

The relation between because and differ also protects the verse from two opposite misreadings. It should not be expanded into a claim the wording of 2:176 does not make, but neither should its brevity be used to make it weightless. Short Qur'anic statements such as 2:176 often function as hinges: they close one movement, open another, and give the next command its moral setting. The careful reader of 2:176 therefore asks what has just been established, what response is now being required, and what kind of character could respond without evasion. Those questions keep 2:176 specific while allowing its guidance to reach a new circumstance.

The commentators sometimes preserve more than one report about the setting of 2:176. Such reports should be weighed rather than treated as interchangeable decoration. An occasion can explain why a question arose, but the wording of 2:176 determines how far the guidance travels. The verse speaks first to the situation that occasioned it and then to every reader who meets the same relation between because and differ.

**The Book as an address**

In 2:176, the distinction between public appearance and inward truth is especially relevant. A person may use the language of because while arranging the act around another purpose. Allah's judgment in 2:176 is not limited to the visible outline, yet the inner intention is not an excuse for ignoring the rights and forms that the revelation establishes. Sincerity completes obedience; it does not cancel it.

One can see the social wisdom of 2:176 in a small everyday case. When people share responsibility for because, uncertainty about the duty tends to fall on the person with less power or less information. A clear moral rule changes that balance. In 2:176, it tells the stronger party what must not be taken, and gives the weaker party language with which to name the wrong.

**The word that carries the argument**

In 2:176, the verse also sits within the Qur'an's larger refusal to separate worship from truthfulness. Prayer, remembrance, generosity, patience, and justice are different acts in 2:176, but they are trained by the same capacity to stand before Allah without constructing a false account. The statement in 2:176 strengthens that capacity by making one particular choice visible.

A reader who finds the command in 2:176 difficult should distinguish difficulty from impossibility. For 2:176, difficulty may be the place where desire, habit, or social pressure is being corrected; impossibility is a separate legal and moral question. The passage does not praise needless hardship, but it does not permit comfort to redefine because until the demand disappears.

**Knowledge joined to obedience**

The final emphasis of 2:176 returns to responsibility. No explanation of because is complete if it leaves the reader with information about earlier communities but no question about present conduct. The verse 2:176 asks what can be repaired now: a promise kept, a right restored, a motive purified, or a harmful practice abandoned. That is where knowledge becomes guidance.

The choice of the word because in 2:176 also matters. It leaves room for the full context of 2:176 instead of allowing one translation gloss to carry every shade of meaning. Classical Arabic often places a broad word inside a narrow scene; in 2:176, the surrounding clauses determine whether the emphasis falls on an act, an intention, a condition, or a consequence. Here the reader should let the sentence do that work.

**The reader’s responsibility**

The exegetical tradition approaches because from more than one angle, but its differences are more useful when their shared question is made visible. The commentators ask what the wording of 2:176 includes, what it excludes, and how it fits with the other passages of the Qur'an. A responsible reading can preserve those alternatives in 2:176 without pretending that every possibility has equal strength.

There is also a distinction between understanding because and using it as a label for other people. The first task belongs to learning; the second requires evidence, fairness, and awareness of one's own motives in 2:176. The verse 2:176 addresses the reader before it supplies material for judging a neighbour. Its warning becomes safer and more productive when self-examination comes first.

**Why the wording is exact**

The theology and practical instruction of 2:176 therefore support one another. If Allah knows or commands differ, that knowledge or command changes how a person handles time, power, money, speech, and private desire. A doctrine that never reaches those choices has not yet been read at the level demanded by 2:176.

An ordinary example makes the moral structure of 2:176 visible without replacing the revelation. Two people may perform an outwardly similar act involving because; one may be protecting a right, while the other is seeking praise, escaping a duty, or taking advantage of confusion. The act's surface does not settle its value. Intention, circumstance, and the rights of others complete the judgment.

**A question answered by the surrounding verses**

The surrounding verses keep the reader from isolating because from the rest of life. In 2:176, revelation corrects the mind but also trains habits: how a person speaks when challenged, gives when unseen, waits when angry, and returns after error. Those habits are where this verse becomes more than information about because. They are the place in which assent to 2:176 is either confirmed or quietly withdrawn.

The most balanced response to 2:176 is neither to make the passage vague nor to claim more than it says. Its boundaries are part of its guidance. Within them, the verse can illuminate a new situation because its underlying moral relation remains stable: because is joined to differ, and the person is responsible for how that relation is honoured.

The wording of 2:176 gives the reader a useful order of questions about because. What does the term because mean in ordinary Arabic, what does the surrounding sentence restrict it to, and what consequence follows when the command is obeyed or refused in 2:176? These questions prevent a commentary on 2:176 from becoming a list of slogans. They make the act of interpretation answerable to grammar, context, and the moral end of this passage at 2:176.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:177

> **Righteousness is not in turning your faces towards the east or the west. Rather, the righteous are those who believe in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Books, and the prophets; who give charity out of their cherished wealth to relatives, orphans, the poor, ˹needy˺ travellers, beggars, and for freeing captives; who establish prayer, pay alms-tax, and keep the pledges they make; and who are patient in times of suffering, adversity, and in ˹the heat of˺ battle. It is they who are true ˹in faith˺, and it is they who are mindful ˹of Allah˺.**

### Expanded Commentary

**Opening the Verse of Birr**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between righteousness and towards. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:177. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:177. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:177.

Piety (birr) is understood as the obedience to Allah that is well established in the heart (al-Ṭabarī) or as the sum of acts of obedience and devotion that lead us closer to Allah; it is also used this way in relation to parents, as when one speaks of filial piety (al-Rāzī). It is reported that this verse was revealed when, after coming to Madinah, the Muslims observed the Jews praying westward and the Christians eastward (see 2:145c).

**The Five Creed-Articles Folded In**

Faith in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Book (in other passages, Books), and the prophets are the five principal articles of faith upon which all Islamic creedal statements are based. They are also listed as such in the famous ḥadīth of Gabriel, where the Prophet is asked by the archangel to describe what Islam is. See 4:136, where this list of five also appears, and commentary.

To give wealth despite loving it (ʿalā ḥubbihi) means that one parts with it even when one fears poverty or yearns for the benefits of wealth (al-Ṭabarī); this phrase also appears in 76:8. It is interpreted by some to mean, because of love for Him, where the pronoun refers to Allah rather than to wealth and the preposition ʿalā is read as because of instead of despite. Many argue that this wealth must be other than what is given in alms (zakāh), since alms is listed later in the verse as one of the things to which one contributes that wealth (al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī).

The recipients of charity listed here (e.g., orphans, the indigent, and travelers) are also mentioned in v. 215; virtuous behavior is enjoined in relation to them in 4:36; part of the spoils of war go to them (8:41; 59:7); and each of these classes of needy people is mentioned singly in many passages throughout the Qur'an. See also the essay Qur'anic Ethics, Human Rights, and Society. According to some, misfortune (baʾsāʾ) refers to challenges such as poverty, while hardship (ḍarrāʾ) refers to matters such as sickness (al-Ṭabarī). Moments of peril (ḥīn al-baʾs) is understood to mean during battle or war or when meeting the enemy (al-Ṭabarī).

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:178

> **O believers! ˹The law of˺ retaliation is set for you in cases of murder— a free man for a free man, a slave for a slave, and a female for a female. But if the offender is pardoned by the victim’s guardian, then bloodmoney should be decided fairly and payment should be made courteously. This is a concession and a mercy from your Lord. But whoever transgresses after that will suffer a painful punishment.**

### Expanded Commentary

**Retaliation Anchored and Bounded**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings belief and murder into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. Its first term in 2:178 sets the subject, while the later term shows what that subject demands, permits, or exposes. The order of 2:178 gives the reader a path through the verse: begin with what Allah names, follow the consequence, and resist the temptation to turn a living address into a slogan.

Here retribution renders qiṣāṣ, which means retaliation for physical injury, most important for murder; in the context of Islamic Law it also means punishment. It falls under the general legal category of ḥudūd, or corporal punishments for crimes considered especially grievous (see the essay “The Qur'an as Source of Islamic Law”). The broad legal, social, and cultural context of this verse is the system of tribal feuds and vendettas in the Arabia of the time, which, as the commentators describe, would often escalate to proportions way beyond the original crime.

**Pardoner's Handheld Restitution**

Thus one tribe might retaliate for the killing of a man by killing not only his murderer, but many other members of his tribe, which served the purpose of not only exacting revenge for past crimes, but also sustaining the status and esteem of one’s own tribe. Often a tribe bent on maintaining or exalting its position would target a person of higher social standing than the one who was originally killed: killing a free person for the death of a slave, a man for the death of a woman, a notable for the death of a person of low station (al-Qurṭubī).

Like vendettas in other cultures throughout history, often the original crime was irrelevant to the ongoing status of the conflict, which was fueled simply by the most recent act of retaliation.

**But After Pardon, No Transgression**

The commentators explain this verse as a limitation on such disproportionate use of revenge and as an injunction to carry out remedies strictly in proportion to the crime. This verse was not interpreted as saying that a woman should necessarily be killed if a woman is murdered, for example, or that anyone but the perpetrator was responsible for the act. Rather, it restricts retaliation to just compensation, leading to the prevention of escalating vendettas and a predictable set of consequences for ensuing crimes. Against the prevailing practice, the verse is understood to maintain that responsibility, for a crime is dictated precisely by the nature of the crime. Hence the wording of the verse implies that the retribution for a crime against a woman could neither fall short of nor exceed the retribution appropriate to that crime, which could vary, as will be discussed below.

**The horizon beyond the immediate scene**

Although a complex part of Islamic Law, the question of retribution for murder does have some basic features. Any punishment must be carried out only by the authorities; this verse is interpreted as disallowing vigilantism. The crime of homicide places the destiny of the perpetrator largely in the hands of the victims next of kin, who can (1) request that the authorities carry out retaliation (qiṣāṣ); (2) accept a wergild, or monetary sum (diyah); or (3) forgive the crime. Some legal scholars did not accept retaliation and wergild as equal alternatives in the case of clear and intentional homicide, in which case capital punishment would necessarily be carried out.

**A divine name that governs the meaning**

Most left the choice to the victims next of kin. Each option (punishment or wergild), once carried out, cancels the other two. Thus, once a wergild is accepted, the next of kin can no longer seek execution, and vice versa. Some jurists maintain that a killer can refuse the wergild option and submit himself for the punishment against the will of the next of kin (Ibn Kathīr). The understanding of qiṣāṣ in Islamic Law resembles lex talionis in Roman Law as well as other systems of compensation/retaliation in the ancient and premodern worlds, including the Anglo-Saxon and other European legal traditions.

It also clearly resembles certain laws in the Torah, such as Deuteronomy 19:21 (life for life, eye for eye . . .) and Exodus 21:23, which were also interpreted by Jews in terms of compensation, often with a version of diyah, or wergild. The hallmark of such systems, like the Islamic one, is not revenge, but making the punishment proportional to the crime. The Torahs rules are mentioned in 5:45.

**Mercy and warning held together**

Generally the amount of diyah, or wergild, for a woman was half that of a man, reflecting the economic and social position of men and women and the difference in expected financial loss to the family of the victim. As in contemporary wrongful-death civil suits, which calculate compensation based upon expected income that is now lost, the diyah, or wergild, reflects the economic realities of the time. Similar positions regarding the different financial worth and responsibility of men and women underlie the inheritance laws in 4:11–12, where, as a general rule, the inheritance of a woman is half that of a man, in light of the financial responsibilities placed on the shoulders of men in the Muslim family.

**The deed before its final account**

The majority of jurists make two points of equality a condition of qiṣāṣ, or retribution: both the murder victim and the perpetrator must be free and be Muslims. They say that a Muslim would not be executed for killing a kāfir (a disbeliever), nor a free man for killing a slave, though there would be some punishment in these cases if there was intentional murder. The Ḥanafī school, however, makes no distinction, since for it the operative part of the law is that a life is a life (a life for a life, 5:45) and that it is the fact that a person has been slain, and nothing else, that is operative legally, as in the present verse.

**Why the promise or threat is just**

Followers of this school also note that the Prophet said, The blood of all Muslims is equal. For other possible scenarios all jurists are agreed on the matter of qiṣāṣ, which is to say that there is no distinction made in capital punishment between victims who are male or female, adult or child, sane or insane, or notables or commoners, with the possible exception that some jurists disallow the possibility of forgiveness for someone who murders a woman (Ibn Kathīr). Qiṣāṣ is not applied in the case of the killing of someone who has the legal status of a belligerent enemy, which is to say that, although qiṣāṣ would apply for the killing of a dhimmī, or non-Muslim treaty holder (see 9:29), it would not apply during a state of war for the killing of a person from a non-Muslim state with which there was no established treaty.

**The Hereafter in the argument**

Beyond these general guidelines regarding qiṣāṣ, legal authorities have differed over other considerations, such as whether the death was direct (e.g., by knife) or indirect (e.g., by falling into a pit); how the execution should be carried out; standards of evidence; what constitutes fair wergild (diyah); how it should be paid out, by whom, and to whom; and the role of the state in such matters. These questions gave rise to a variety of opinions regarding qiṣāṣ and the diyah among the various schools of Islamic Law.

The second part of the verse enjoins that wergild, if chosen, be collected with propriety and that the payment likewise be paid out honorably (al-Qurṭubī). The alleviation refers to the very fact that a wergild can be accepted for homicide. Some interpret this Qur'anic injunction as being lighter in comparison with the laws of the Children of Israel, although the laws were in many ways similar. The Torah says, Show no pity (Deuteronomy 19:21), whereas the Qur'anic text discourages harshness by saying, But whosoever forgoes it out of charity, it shall be an expiation for him (5:45). The rabbinical tradition, however, did incorporate the possibility of wergild into the law of punishment.

The last sentence in this verse is understood to address those who might seek retaliation after the settling of the wergild, which, as mentioned above, cancels any further claim on the part of the next of kin. Should a person accept a wergild, then go on to kill the perpetrator, execution of that person becomes mandatory and no wergild can be accepted from him.

The verse's reference to belief widens the scene beyond the immediate reward or pain. A deed in 2:178 may appear small when measured by public attention, yet its meaning changes when it is known by Allah and carried into the final account. Warning and mercy belong together in 2:178: accountability is serious because the human being is not abandoned to meaninglessness.

A useful way to test the verse is to ask what would change if belief were taken seriously when no audience was present. The answer cannot be only a feeling, because 2:178 connects inward recognition with a discernible choice. Nor can it be only an outward display, because the choice in 2:178 loses its Qur'anic meaning when it is made for reputation rather than for Allah. The passage holds intention and action together in 2:178.

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings prescribed and leave into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. Its first term in 2:180 sets the subject, while the later term shows what that subject demands, permits, or exposes. The order of 2:180 gives the reader a path through the verse: begin with what Allah names, follow the consequence, and resist the temptation to turn a living address into a slogan.

**The Third and Its Margin: The Hadith's Frame**

Bequest (waṣiyyah) is also used in 4:12 and 5:106. Here some good (khayr) means ones property, as in, Whatever good you spend (2:272), and also, Truly he is fierce in his love for good things (100:8). According to one interpretation, the prescription here is a conditional one, being an obligation upon the reverent only if one leaves some good, which does not make such a bequest a universal obligation. This command would not change the status of those who have debts or other financial obligations, which must be paid from ones property even after death. Thus the first phrase is taken to mean, Should one desire to make a bequest. There are differences of opinion as to what amount must be involved for a bequest to be made; some jurists assign a specific amount, while others consider any sum, large or small, to be a possible bequest (al-Qurṭubī).

**The Word in Its Companions' Circle**

In general there are two main restrictions on bequests in Islamic Law: (1) that they account for no more than a third of ones property, and (2) that the bequest not be designated for a person who automatically inherits according to the Qur'anic injunctions concerning shares of inheritance. Some consider this verse to be abrogated completely; others say it is partially abrogated in the case of those legally entitled to an inheritance share as stipulated in 4:11–13, but continues to apply in the case of others (Ṭs). Some, including the Shiites (who have a substantially different interpretation of inheritance law from Sunnis when it comes to the relationship between quota and nonquota heirs), believe that this verse was not abrogated and that nothing in it contradicts any other verse of the Qur'an.

**A duty that begins with the vulnerable**

The question of abrogation arises because of the ḥadīth, Let there be no bequests for heirs. This ḥadīth, if taken as universally applicable, renders the verses concerning bequests partially incompatible with those describing inheritance shares. It means that one cannot make a bequest for those who, according to the shares specified by the Qur'an, would receive part of the deceaseds property automatically without any bequest. For some commentators and jurists, such as al-Qurṭubī, the acceptance of this ḥadīth as binding shows that the Sunnah can abrogate the Qur'an (see 2:106c for a discussion of abrogation), while for others this shows that the present verse is not abrogated for the very same reason, namely, that a ḥadīth, about which one has less certainty (yaqīn) than about the Qur'an, cannot replace a ruling of the Qur'an (Ṭs).

**The relationship named by the verse**

Al-Qurṭubī acknowledges that the only text preventing a harmonization of the Qur'anic injunctions regarding bequests and inheritance is this ḥadīth barring bequests for heirs. Some have tried to harmonize them by saying that the parents and relatives here are those who would not inherit in any case (e.g., parents who were disbelievers and thus nonquota heirs).

As a moral issue, bequests are to be made first to relatives and only secondarily to nonrelatives; early commentators severely condemned those who would leave relatives in need while giving property to nonrelatives (al-Qurṭubī). One proof text for the one-third restriction on bequests is a ḥadīth in which the Prophet said to a man who offered to make a bequest of two-thirds or one-half of his wealth, “One-third, and a third is considerable. It is better to leave your heirs free from want than to leave them destitute and begging from people.”

**Rights before sentiment**

Prior to the institution of the Qur'anic rules of bequest and inheritance, the custom of Arabia was that male relations would inherit through the male line, called agnatic inheritance. The Qur'anic shares, which included the nearest male relatives, demoted the customary agnatic heirs to a secondary status in relation to the inheritance shares; they could still inherit under Sunni law, but only from the property left after the quota shares had been distributed. In Shiism, agnatic inheritance is rejected, and a system of proximity in blood kinship is used for the residual property after the distribution of the shares, applying equally for the male and female lines.

The concern with prescribed shows that justice is measured most severely where affection, dependence, and power overlap. A person may be generous in public and still wrong a relative or a child in private. By naming the relationship, the verse makes invisible duties visible and gives moral language to the person whose claim might otherwise be dismissed.

**How neglect becomes wrongdoing**

A useful way to test the verse is to ask what would change if prescribed were taken seriously when no audience was present. The answer cannot be only a feeling, because 2:180 connects inward recognition with a discernible choice. Nor can it be only an outward display, because the choice in 2:180 loses its Qur'anic meaning when it is made for reputation rather than for Allah. The passage holds intention and action together in 2:180.

A reader who finds the command in 2:180 difficult should distinguish difficulty from impossibility. For 2:180, difficulty may be the place where desire, habit, or social pressure is being corrected; impossibility is a separate legal and moral question. The passage does not praise needless hardship, but it does not permit comfort to redefine prescribed until the demand disappears.

**The legal protection in the command**

The final emphasis of 2:180 returns to responsibility. No explanation of prescribed is complete if it leaves the reader with information about earlier communities but no question about present conduct. The verse 2:180 asks what can be repaired now: a promise kept, a right restored, a motive purified, or a harmful practice abandoned. That is where knowledge becomes guidance.

The choice of the word prescribed in 2:180 also matters. It leaves room for the full context of 2:180 instead of allowing one translation gloss to carry every shade of meaning. Classical Arabic often places a broad word inside a narrow scene; in 2:180, the surrounding clauses determine whether the emphasis falls on an act, an intention, a condition, or a consequence. Here the reader should let the sentence do that work.

**A family obligation with social reach**

The exegetical tradition approaches prescribed from more than one angle, but its differences are more useful when their shared question is made visible. The commentators ask what the wording of 2:180 includes, what it excludes, and how it fits with the other passages of the Qur'an. A responsible reading can preserve those alternatives in 2:180 without pretending that every possibility has equal strength.

There is also a distinction between understanding prescribed and using it as a label for other people. The first task belongs to learning; the second requires evidence, fairness, and awareness of one's own motives in 2:180. The verse 2:180 addresses the reader before it supplies material for judging a neighbour. Its warning becomes safer and more productive when self-examination comes first.

The theology and practical instruction of 2:180 therefore support one another. If Allah knows or commands leave, that knowledge or command changes how a person handles time, power, money, speech, and private desire. A doctrine that never reaches those choices has not yet been read at the level demanded by 2:180.

An ordinary example makes the moral structure of 2:180 visible without replacing the revelation. Two people may perform an outwardly similar act involving prescribed; one may be protecting a right, while the other is seeking praise, escaping a duty, or taking advantage of confusion. The act's surface does not settle its value. Intention, circumstance, and the rights of others complete the judgment.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:181

> **But whoever changes the will after hearing it, the blame will only be on those who made the change. Indeed, Allah is AllHearing, All-Knowing.**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Tampering Executor**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between whoever and blame. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:181. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:181. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:181.

This verse means that one cannot alter a bequest, although an inherently invalid bequest can be canceled or modified. A bequest of greater than one-third, for example, would be reduced to one-third, and a bequest to give a person a forbidden substance such as wine could be nullified (al-Qurṭubī).

**The Boundary Against the Executor's Pen**

The verse's reference to whoever widens the scene beyond the immediate reward or pain. A deed in 2:181 may appear small when measured by public attention, yet its meaning changes when it is known by Allah and carried into the final account. Warning and mercy belong together in 2:181: accountability is serious because the human being is not abandoned to meaninglessness.

The standard in 2:181 remains practical because it can be applied before a dispute reaches a court or a crisis reaches its worst point. One can notice the first small departure from whoever: an excuse, a concealed obligation, an unexamined desire, or a promise treated as optional. Returning at that point is easier than defending a settled habit. The warning is therefore also an opening for repair.

**Shield of the Dying**

The relation between whoever and blame also protects the verse from two opposite misreadings. It should not be expanded into a claim the wording of 2:181 does not make, but neither should its brevity be used to make it weightless. Short Qur'anic statements such as 2:181 often function as hinges: they close one movement, open another, and give the next command its moral setting. The careful reader of 2:181 therefore asks what has just been established, what response is now being required, and what kind of character could respond without evasion. Those questions keep 2:181 specific while allowing its guidance to reach a new circumstance.

The final emphasis of 2:181 returns to responsibility. No explanation of whoever is complete if it leaves the reader with information about earlier communities but no question about present conduct. The verse 2:181 asks what can be repaired now: a promise kept, a right restored, a motive purified, or a harmful practice abandoned. That is where knowledge becomes guidance.

Here the reader should let the sentence do that work.

A doctrine that never reaches those choices has not yet been read at the level demanded by 2:181.

**Mercy and warning held together**

An ordinary example makes the moral structure of 2:181 visible without replacing the revelation. Two people may perform an outwardly similar act involving whoever; one may be protecting a right, while the other is seeking praise, escaping a duty, or taking advantage of confusion. The act's surface does not settle its value. Intention, circumstance, and the rights of others complete the judgment.

The surrounding verses keep the reader from isolating whoever from the rest of life. In 2:181, revelation corrects the mind but also trains habits: how a person speaks when challenged, gives when unseen, waits when angry, and returns after error. Those habits are where this verse becomes more than information about whoever. They are the place in which assent to 2:181 is either confirmed or quietly withdrawn.

**The deed before its final account**

The most balanced response to 2:181 is neither to make the passage vague nor to claim more than it says. Its boundaries are part of its guidance. Within them, the verse can illuminate a new situation because its underlying moral relation remains stable: whoever is joined to blame, and the person is responsible for how that relation is honoured.

The wording of 2:181 gives the reader a useful order of questions about whoever. What does the term whoever mean in ordinary Arabic, what does the surrounding sentence restrict it to, and what consequence follows when the command is obeyed or refused in 2:181? These questions prevent a commentary on 2:181 from becoming a list of slogans. They make the act of interpretation answerable to grammar, context, and the moral end of this passage at 2:181.

**Why the promise or threat is just**

The commentators sometimes preserve more than one report about the setting of 2:181. Such reports should be weighed rather than treated as interchangeable decoration. An occasion can explain why a question arose, but the wording of 2:181 determines how far the guidance travels. The verse speaks first to the situation that occasioned it and then to every reader who meets the same relation between whoever and blame.

In 2:181, the distinction between public appearance and inward truth is especially relevant. A person may use the language of whoever while arranging the act around another purpose. Allah's judgment in 2:181 is not limited to the visible outline, yet the inner intention is not an excuse for ignoring the rights and forms that the revelation establishes. Sincerity completes obedience; it does not cancel it.

**The Hereafter in the argument**

One can see the social wisdom of 2:181 in a small everyday case. When people share responsibility for whoever, uncertainty about the duty tends to fall on the person with less power or less information. A clear moral rule changes that balance. In 2:181, it tells the stronger party what must not be taken, and gives the weaker party language with which to name the wrong.

In 2:181, the verse also sits within the Qur'an's larger refusal to separate worship from truthfulness. Prayer, remembrance, generosity, patience, and justice are different acts in 2:181, but they are trained by the same capacity to stand before Allah without constructing a false account. The statement in 2:181 strengthens that capacity by making one particular choice visible.

A reader who finds the command in 2:181 difficult should distinguish difficulty from impossibility. ## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:182

> **Whoever suspects an error or an injustice in the will and brings about a ˹fair˺ settlement among the parties will not be sinful. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Executor's Exception**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings whoever and injustice into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. Its first term in 2:182 sets the subject, while the later term shows what that subject demands, permits, or exposes. The order of 2:182 gives the reader a path through the verse: begin with what Allah names, follow the consequence, and resist the temptation to turn a living address into a slogan.

**The "Fearing" Prior to Action**

This verse addresses the possibility that a testator might act prejudicially with regard to his heirs through manipulating his bequests. For example, he might make a bequest to his daughter-in-law with the intent of enriching his son, which would violate the rule that legal heirs cannot receive bequests (al-Qurṭubī). A ḥadīth states, Injustice [janaf, the same word as in this verse] in the matter of bequests is a major sin [kabīrah]. It is the duty of the community to adjust or cancel such bequests when it becomes clear that their intent was to circumvent the Qur'anic laws of inheritance (al-Qurṭubī). Them refers to the heirs, and him to the executor of the estate, the witness of the bequest (as required by 5:106), or whoever has this responsibility (al-Rāzī), although some seem to place the responsibility on the heirs to address this question (al-Qurṭubī). There is no sin upon him in such a case because, although altering a bequest would ordinarily be a sin, in this case justice overrules the instructions of the testator (al-Rāzī).

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:183

> **O believers! Fasting is prescribed for you—as it was for those before you—so perhaps you will become mindful ˹of Allah˺.**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Fifth Pillar Announced**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between belief and perhaps. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:183. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:183.

**The Fast and the Ramadan-Binding**

Fasting (ṣiyām, also ṣawm) is the subject of vv. 183–87. These verses address some issues relating to the pre-Ramadan fasting practices of the Muslim community. As constituted in its final form, the obligatory fast of Ramadan is considered by all schools of law to be one of the five pillars of Islam. It consists of abstaining completely from food, drink, and sexual relations from dawn until sunset for all the days of the lunar month of Ramadan. In cases of hardship, including illness and travel, one can eat and drink and then make up for the lost day by fasting on another day after Ramadan or by giving alms if one is unable to make up the fast, such as in the case of diabetics.

**That You May Be Reverent — The Fast's Telos**

Women who are pregnant, nursing, or menstruating are exempted from the fast, with varying rules for replacing or expiating for those lost days. The fast of Ramadan was imposed shortly before the Battle of Badr (2/624; Th). Those before you may refer to either the Christians, all the People of the Book, or all people in general (al-Rāzī).

The verse's concern with belief shows why religious restraint is not meant to produce weakness or despair. Desire is acknowledged rather than denied, then given a disciplined place. The worshipper learns to distinguish a genuine need from an impulse, and a lawful ease from the kind of indulgence that makes obedience meaningless.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:184

> **˹Fast a˺ prescribed number of days. But whoever of you is ill or on a journey, then ˹let them fast˺ an equal number of days ˹after Ramaḍân˺. For those who can only fast with extreme difficulty, compensation can be made by feeding a needy person ˹for every day not fasted˺. But whoever volunteers to give more, it is better for them. And to fast is better for you, if only you knew.**

### Expanded Commentary

**"Days Numbered" — The Measured Term**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings fast and days into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. Its first term in 2:184 sets the subject, while the later term shows what that subject demands, permits, or exposes. The order of 2:184 gives the reader a path through the verse: begin with what Allah names, follow the consequence, and resist the temptation to turn a living address into a slogan.

**The Sick, the Traveler, and the Fed-Ransom**

The phrase days numbered is a subject of disagreement; some identify it as referring to the days of Ramadan, others the days of fasting before the fast of Ramadan was instituted. When the Prophet first came to Madinah, it is said that the community was fasting three days per month in addition to ʿĀshūrāʾ (the tenth day of Muḥarram). According to a ḥadīth, when they arrived in Madinah they found the Jews fasting on Yom Kippur (the same day as ʿĀshūrāʾ), and the Prophet ordered the Muslims to fast that day, saying that they had more right than Jews to celebrate Moses, though the commentaries are inconsistent about the nature of the Yom Kippur celebration.

**"That You Should Fast Is Better" — The Verse's Counsel**

There is disagreement about whether these three days per month were obligatory in the same way that Ramadan would come to be. Those who did not consider the pre-Ramadan fast as obligatory interpret vv. 183–84 as referring to Ramadan itself. Others say the fast of three days per month was the first to be prescribed, which was then abrogated by the fast of Ramadan, but al-Ṭabarī, among others, argues that those who say this have no firm report showing that any fast before Ramadan was made obligatory. The passage shows that fasting three days per month was and continues to be a meritorious deed that many pious Muslims perform in imitation of the Prophet.

**The discipline named by the verse**

These three days are typically the thirteenth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days, or the days of the full moon, or according to some the beginning, middle, and end of each lunar month. It is plausible that before the institution of Ramadan the Muslim community observed this practice, but not in the manner of an obligation, and that after the Ramadan fast became an obligation, it has continued on as a meritorious practice.

**Hunger, desire, and conscious worship**

One opinion holds that the fast of Ramadan was obligatory, but that in the beginning one had the option of feeding one poor person instead, per day of fasting, based upon For those who can bear it, the ransom of feeding an indigent person, but that this injunction was abrogated by Let him among you who is present fast during that [month] in v. 185. Others consider that there had been no abrogation in these verses and hold that those who can bear it refers to old people who could conceivably fast, but for whom it would be a severe hardship (al-Qurṭubī). In this latter interpretation, the verb rendered can bear it would mean something like “are burdened.” It would thus mean “they are able to bear” in the sense that “they bear it with difficulty.” This latter meaning is part of the lexical root ṭ-w-q, from which the verb originates (al-Qurṭubī).

**The room made for repentance**

Whosoever volunteers good may refer to feeding people beyond what the verse requires or to providing the person one is required to feed with more than the bare minimum of food (al-Qurṭubī). Al-Qurṭubī, among others, offers the idea that fasting is better than expiation and that choosing to fast while traveling or ill, so long as it is not too great a hardship, is better, but adds, “Allah knows best.”

The verse's concern with fast shows why religious restraint is not meant to produce weakness or despair. Desire is acknowledged rather than denied, then given a disciplined place. The worshipper learns to distinguish a genuine need from an impulse, and a lawful ease from the kind of indulgence that makes obedience meaningless.

**A private act with public consequences**

A useful way to test the verse is to ask what would change if fast were taken seriously when no audience was present. The answer cannot be only a feeling, because 2:184 connects inward recognition with a discernible choice. Nor can it be only an outward display, because the choice in 2:184 loses its Qur'anic meaning when it is made for reputation rather than for Allah. The passage holds intention and action together in 2:184.

There is also a distinction between understanding fast and using it as a label for other people. The first task belongs to learning; the second requires evidence, fairness, and awareness of one's own motives in 2:184. The verse 2:184 addresses the reader before it supplies material for judging a neighbour. Its warning becomes safer and more productive when self-examination comes first.

**The legal condition and its purpose**

The theology and practical instruction of 2:184 therefore support one another. If Allah knows or commands days, that knowledge or command changes how a person handles time, power, money, speech, and private desire. A doctrine that never reaches those choices has not yet been read at the level demanded by 2:184.

An ordinary example makes the moral structure of 2:184 visible without replacing the revelation. Two people may perform an outwardly similar act involving fast; one may be protecting a right, while the other is seeking praise, escaping a duty, or taking advantage of confusion. The act's surface does not settle its value. Intention, circumstance, and the rights of others complete the judgment.

**How restraint becomes freedom**

The surrounding verses keep the reader from isolating fast from the rest of life. In 2:184, revelation corrects the mind but also trains habits: how a person speaks when challenged, gives when unseen, waits when angry, and returns after error. Those habits are where this verse becomes more than information about fast. They are the place in which assent to 2:184 is either confirmed or quietly withdrawn.

The most balanced response to 2:184 is neither to make the passage vague nor to claim more than it says. Its boundaries are part of its guidance. Within them, the verse can illuminate a new situation because its underlying moral relation remains stable: fast is joined to days, and the person is responsible for how that relation is honoured.

The wording of 2:184 gives the reader a useful order of questions about fast. What does the term fast mean in ordinary Arabic, what does the surrounding sentence restrict it to, and what consequence follows when the command is obeyed or refused in 2:184? These questions prevent a commentary on 2:184 from becoming a list of slogans. They make the act of interpretation answerable to grammar, context, and the moral end of this passage at 2:184.

The commentators sometimes preserve more than one report about the setting of 2:184. Such reports should be weighed rather than treated as interchangeable decoration. An occasion can explain why a question arose, but the wording of 2:184 determines how far the guidance travels. The verse speaks first to the situation that occasioned it and then to every reader who meets the same relation between fast and days.

In 2:184, the distinction between public appearance and inward truth is especially relevant. A person may use the language of fast while arranging the act around another purpose. Allah's judgment in 2:184 is not limited to the visible outline, yet the inner intention is not an excuse for ignoring the rights and forms that the revelation establishes. Sincerity completes obedience; it does not cancel it.

One can see the social wisdom of 2:184 in a small everyday case. When people share responsibility for fast, uncertainty about the duty tends to fall on the person with less power or less information. A clear moral rule changes that balance. In 2:184, it tells the stronger party what must not be taken, and gives the weaker party language with which to name the wrong.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:185

> **Ramaḍân is the month in which the Quran was revealed as a guide for humanity with clear proofs of guidance and the standard ˹to distinguish between right and wrong˺. So whoever is present this month, let them fast. But whoever is ill or on a journey, then ˹let them fast˺ an equal number of days ˹after Ramaḍân˺. Allah intends ease for you, not hardship, so that you may complete the prescribed period and proclaim the greatness of Allah for guiding you, and perhaps you will be grateful.**

### Expanded Commentary

**Ramadan-Named: The Month of the Revelation**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between ramaḍân and revealed. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:185. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:185. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:185.

**Fast It — and the Exemptions of Mercy**

Some mention accounts that the Qur'an first came down to the earthly heaven (i.e., the lowest of the seven heavens) from the Preserved Tablet (85:22) and remained there and then Gabriel brought it down passage by passage to the Prophet (al-Qurṭubī); see 97:1–2c. Muslims consider Ramadan a particularly blessed month, both because it is the month of fasting and also because it is the month when the Qur'an began to be revealed. In a ḥadīth, the Prophet said, When Ramadan comes, the gates of the Garden are opened, and the gates of the Fire are locked, and the satans are fettered.

**"Allah Desires Ease for You"**

When people fall ill or are traveling, they have the option of breaking the fast and fasting on another day after Ramadan in order to make up for it. Opinions range on how sick one must be and what type of journey qualifies. These exemptions apply in another manner to the canonical prayers, which one can shorten and combine when one is on a journey. To complete the number can mean to make up all missed days of fasting by fasting on days other than those of Ramadan or simply to complete the full number of days in the lunar month itself, which is twenty-nine or thirty days.

**Completing the Count, Magnifying the Allah**

Magnify Allah is thought to refer to the practice of chanting extra formulas of takbīr (the chanting of Allāhu akbar, meaning “Allah is great!” or “Allah is greater” or “Allah is the greatest”), which takes place after the fast of Ramadan is over. This magnification takes different forms, such as chanting formulas of takbīr while on the way to the mosque for the ʿĪd prayer (the prayers in the morning after the last day of Ramadan) or repeating magnifications after each prayer during the three days of ʿĪd. Examples are “Allah is great, Allah is great, there is no god but Allah, Allah is great, Allah be praised!” and “Allah is great and grand, and praised be He often, and glorified be He day and night!” See also v. 203.

**The discipline named by the verse**

The exemptions from the rules of fasting (for the old, sick, traveling, etc.) are part of the ease that Allah bestows; the Qur'an states that Allah does not desire hardship for you, which is also mentioned in 22:78: He . . . has placed no hardship for you in the religion (Sh). In this regard, some mention the ḥadīth of the Prophet, Make things easy, not difficult. Cause people to rejoice, not to flee.

So that you may complete either is connected with the previous sentence and refers to more of what Allah desires or is a continuation of the command to fast from v. 183, so that it would mean, “Fasting is prescribed for you . . . so that you may complete” (al-Zamakhsharī).

One can notice the first small departure from ramaḍân: an excuse, a concealed obligation, an unexamined desire, or a promise treated as optional. Returning at that point is easier than defending a settled habit. The warning is therefore also an opening for repair.

The relation between ramaḍân and revealed also protects the verse from two opposite misreadings. It should not be expanded into a claim the wording of 2:185 does not make, but neither should its brevity be used to make it weightless. Short Qur'anic statements such as 2:185 often function as hinges: they close one movement, open another, and give the next command its moral setting. The careful reader of 2:185 therefore asks what has just been established, what response is now being required, and what kind of character could respond without evasion. Those questions keep 2:185 specific while allowing its guidance to reach a new circumstance.

The theology and practical instruction of 2:185 therefore support one another.
