## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:186

> **When My servants ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about Me: I am truly near. I respond to one’s prayer when they call upon Me. So let them respond ˹with obedience˺ to Me and believe in Me, perhaps they will be guided ˹to the Right Way˺.**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Verse at the Center of the Sūrah**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings servants and near into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. Its first term in 2:186 sets the subject, while the later term shows what that subject demands, permits, or exposes. The order of 2:186 gives the reader a path through the verse: begin with what Allah names, follow the consequence, and resist the temptation to turn a living address into a slogan.

It is reported that this verse came as a response to some Companions who asked the Prophet, Where is our Lord? or At what hour should we call upon Allah? after the revelation of 40:60: Call upon Me, and I shall respond to you. Others mention that it was a response to questions such as, How shall we make our call, O Prophet of Allah? (al-Ṭabarī). Others say it was revealed after a Bedouin came and asked the Prophet, Is our Lord near, such that I shall whisper to Him, or far, such that I shall shout to Him? (al-Rāzī).

**Asked and Answered in One Breath**

In a related vein, the Prophet, while on a journey, reportedly reprimanded some Companions who were shouting their prayers, saying, You are calling One who is neither deaf nor absent, but are calling One who is Hearing, Near (al-Rāzī); al-Qarīb (the Near) is a Divine Name. Some interpret the verb rendered let them respond to Me (yastajībū) to mean let them ask of Me, which would echo the first phrase of this verse (al-Rāzī). This verse is one of the most central and often quoted verses of the Qur'an concerning Allahs nearness to us and the reality of reciprocity between the human call to Allah and His response.

**Duʿāʾ as Worship**

The Prophet said, Calling [upon Allah] is a form of worship. Call renders duʿāʾ, which can also mean individual prayer, supplication, or summons depending on context. It can also be translated simply as prayer in the sense that one prays by calling upon Allah to receive something or to ask for a specific blessing. The sense of prayer in this verse is highlighted in M. Lings evocative translation of this verse: I answer the prayer of the pray-er when he prayeth Me, but duʿāʾ does not extend to all possible uses of the English word prayer. A similar passage can be found in 27:62, where Allah is spoken of as He Who answers the one in distress when he calls upon Him. In 7:55 believers are told, Call upon your Lord humbly and in secret; and in 42:26 it is said, He responds to those who believe and perform righteous deeds.

**"When My Servants Ask" — The Servant-Direct Address**

Several other verses mention Allahs nearness, such as 50:16: We are nearer to him than his jugular vein; and 17:57, which asks concerning Allah and other idols, Which of them is nearer? In 34:50 it is said of Allah, Truly He is Hearing, Nigh. Nearness to Allah is a part of what it means to be in Paradise, as in 38:25: Truly nearness unto Us shall be his, and a beautiful return; and at the moment of death it is said to those gathered around the dying person, We are nearer to him than you, though you see not (56:85). Other places where Allahs Nearness in mentioned include 4:135; 9:99; 34:37.

Al-Rāzī and some other commentators connect the message of this verse to the prayers of magnification commanded in the previous verse and also to the alleviation of the requirements of fasting, which came after some Companions had difficulty in fulfilling them (see v. 187).

**The act and the intention beneath it**

The subject of servants joins an act directed to Allah with a consequence visible among people. In 2:186, that union guards against two reductions: worship cannot become a private performance with no social fruit, and social generosity cannot become a substitute for worship. The verse 2:186 asks for an outward practice whose inward intention remains answerable to Allah.

A useful way to test the verse is to ask what would change if servants were taken seriously when no audience was present. The answer cannot be only a feeling, because 2:186 connects inward recognition with a discernible choice. Nor can it be only an outward display, because the choice in 2:186 loses its Qur'anic meaning when it is made for reputation rather than for Allah. The passage holds intention and action together in 2:186.

**A visible duty with an inward root**

An ordinary example makes the moral structure of 2:186 visible without replacing the revelation. Two people may perform an outwardly similar act involving servants; one may be protecting a right, while the other is seeking praise, escaping a duty, or taking advantage of confusion. The act's surface does not settle its value. Intention, circumstance, and the rights of others complete the judgment.

The surrounding verses keep the reader from isolating servants from the rest of life. In 2:186, revelation corrects the mind but also trains habits: how a person speaks when challenged, gives when unseen, waits when angry, and returns after error. Those habits are where this verse becomes more than information about servants. They are the place in which assent to 2:186 is either confirmed or quietly withdrawn.

**Why worship opens toward other people**

The most balanced response to 2:186 is neither to make the passage vague nor to claim more than it says. Its boundaries are part of its guidance. Within them, the verse can illuminate a new situation because its underlying moral relation remains stable: servants is joined to near, and the person is responsible for how that relation is honoured.

What does the term servants mean in ordinary Arabic, what does the surrounding sentence restrict it to, and what consequence follows when the command is obeyed or refused in 2:186? These questions prevent a commentary on 2:186 from becoming a list of slogans. They make the act of interpretation answerable to grammar, context, and the moral end of this passage at 2:186.

**The measure of sincere giving**

The commentators sometimes preserve more than one report about the setting of 2:186. Such reports should be weighed rather than treated as interchangeable decoration. An occasion can explain why a question arose, but the wording of 2:186 determines how far the guidance travels. The verse speaks first to the situation that occasioned it and then to every reader who meets the same relation between servants and near.

**The poor person’s dignity**

One can see the social wisdom of 2:186 in a small everyday case. When people share responsibility for servants, uncertainty about the duty tends to fall on the person with less power or less information. A clear moral rule changes that balance. In 2:186, it tells the stronger party what must not be taken, and gives the weaker party language with which to name the wrong.

In 2:186, the verse also sits within the Qur'an's larger refusal to separate worship from truthfulness. Prayer, remembrance, generosity, patience, and justice are different acts in 2:186, but they are trained by the same capacity to stand before Allah without constructing a false account. The statement in 2:186 strengthens that capacity by making one particular choice visible.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:187

> **It has been made permissible for you to be intimate with your wives during the nights preceding the fast. Your spouses are a garment for you as you are for them. Allah knows that you were deceiving yourselves. So He has accepted your repentance and pardoned you. So now you may be intimate with them and seek what Allah has prescribed for you. ˹You may˺ eat and drink until you see the light of dawn breaking the darkness of night, then complete the fast until nightfall. Do not be intimate with your spouses while you are meditating in the mosques. These are the limits set by Allah, so do not exceed them. This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to people, so they may become mindful ˹of Him˺.**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Alleviation Night**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between permissible and during. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:187. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:187. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:187.

**The Garment of Marriage**

Many commentators report that before the revelation of this verse, Muslims would fast after sleeping; after sunset, when one broke the fast, one could eat until the ʿishāʾ prayer (i.e., the end of twilight and the beginning of night), but that sleep would begin the next day’s fast. Upon waking, one would be in a state of fasting. Some maintain that the Muslim community would abstain from sexual activity for the whole of Ramadan, even during the night, though the basis of this account is unclear. This verse is considered an alleviation of those requirements.

**The White and Black Threads of Dawn**

It is reported that ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, the prominent Companion and second Caliph, confessed to having had sexual relations with his wife after she said she had fallen asleep; he was remorseful about it and sought recourse. Commentators also mention Qays ibn Ṣirmah, who came home after a harsh day of work while he was fasting. His wife did not have food for him and went out to get some, but he could not stay awake and was asleep before she returned, so he continued to fast through the next day (al-Qurṭubī).

Seek what Allah has prescribed can mean seek to have children; seek to fulfill what Qur'an commands you; seek the Night of Power, meaning a night during Ramadan when the Qur'an was first revealed (see 97:1); seek exemption and latitude when it is offered in matters of ritual; or seek to have sexual relations in a legitimate way (Ibn Kathīr).

**"Those Are the Limits of Allah"**

The white thread and the black thread refer to dawn and the night, respectively; “the white thread” is an idiom for the day (al-Qurṭubī). Various aḥādīth describe the level of light that indicates the start of daybreak and ends the night, whether the indication is seeing light in the sky itself or the illumination of the tops of mountains (Ibn Kathīr).

Retreat in the mosques refers to the practice of iʿtikāf, during which a person remains in the mosque for a number of days in a state of prayer and remembrance (dhikr). According to many reports the Prophet would spend the last ten days of Ramadan in the mosque in iʿtikāf; during his final Ramadan he spent twenty.

**A household placed under moral care**

The reference to permissible places a human being who may be dependent, exposed, or unable to defend a claim at the centre of the discussion. Responsibility here is not merely a feeling of affection. It has a form that can be recognized, a limit that can be enforced, and a purpose: to prevent the strong from making the weak carry the cost of decisions they did not control.

> **Do not consume one another’s wealth unjustly, nor deliberately bribe authorities in order to devour a portion of others’ property, knowing that it is a sin.**

What does the term consume mean in ordinary Arabic, what does the surrounding sentence restrict it to, and what consequence follows when the command is obeyed or refused in 2:188? These questions prevent a commentary on 2:188 from becoming a list of slogans. They make the act of interpretation answerable to grammar, context, and the moral end of this passage at 2:188.

The commentators sometimes preserve more than one report about the setting of 2:188. Such reports should be weighed rather than treated as interchangeable decoration. An occasion can explain why a question arose, but the wording of 2:188 determines how far the guidance travels. The verse speaks first to the situation that occasioned it and then to every reader who meets the same relation between consume and unjustly.

**Why worship opens toward other people**

In 2:188, the distinction between public appearance and inward truth is especially relevant. A person may use the language of consume while arranging the act around another purpose. Allah's judgment in 2:188 is not limited to the visible outline, yet the inner intention is not an excuse for ignoring the rights and forms that the revelation establishes. Sincerity completes obedience; it does not cancel it.

One can see the social wisdom of 2:188 in a small everyday case. When people share responsibility for consume, uncertainty about the duty tends to fall on the person with less power or less information. A clear moral rule changes that balance. In 2:188, it tells the stronger party what must not be taken, and gives the weaker party language with which to name the wrong.

**The measure of sincere giving**

In 2:188, the verse also sits within the Qur'an's larger refusal to separate worship from truthfulness. Prayer, remembrance, generosity, patience, and justice are different acts in 2:188, but they are trained by the same capacity to stand before Allah without constructing a false account. The statement in 2:188 strengthens that capacity by making one particular choice visible.

A reader who finds the command in 2:188 difficult should distinguish difficulty from impossibility. For 2:188, difficulty may be the place where desire, habit, or social pressure is being corrected; impossibility is a separate legal and moral question. The passage does not praise needless hardship, but it does not permit comfort to redefine consume until the demand disappears.

**The poor person’s dignity**

The final emphasis of 2:188 returns to responsibility. No explanation of consume is complete if it leaves the reader with information about earlier communities but no question about present conduct. The verse 2:188 asks what can be repaired now: a promise kept, a right restored, a motive purified, or a harmful practice abandoned. That is where knowledge becomes guidance.

The choice of the word consume in 2:188 also matters. It leaves room for the full context of 2:188 instead of allowing one translation gloss to carry every shade of meaning. Classical Arabic often places a broad word inside a narrow scene; in 2:188, the surrounding clauses determine whether the emphasis falls on an act, an intention, a condition, or a consequence. Here the reader should let the sentence do that work.

**A community shaped by obedience**

The exegetical tradition approaches consume from more than one angle, but its differences are more useful when their shared question is made visible. The commentators ask what the wording of 2:188 includes, what it excludes, and how it fits with the other passages of the Qur'an. A responsible reading can preserve those alternatives in 2:188 without pretending that every possibility has equal strength.

There is also a distinction between understanding consume and using it as a label for other people. The first task belongs to learning; the second requires evidence, fairness, and awareness of one's own motives in 2:188. The verse 2:188 addresses the reader before it supplies material for judging a neighbour. Its warning becomes safer and more productive when self-examination comes first.

The theology and practical instruction of 2:188 therefore support one another. If Allah knows or commands unjustly, that knowledge or command changes how a person handles time, power, money, speech, and private desire. A doctrine that never reaches those choices has not yet been read at the level demanded by 2:188.

An ordinary example makes the moral structure of 2:188 visible without replacing the revelation. Two people may perform an outwardly similar act involving consume; one may be protecting a right, while the other is seeking praise, escaping a duty, or taking advantage of confusion. The act's surface does not settle its value. Intention, circumstance, and the rights of others complete the judgment.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:189

> **They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about the phases of the moon. Say, “They are a means for people to determine time and pilgrimage.” Righteousness is not in entering your houses from the back doors. Rather, righteousness is to be mindful ˹of Allah˺. So enter your homes through their ˹proper˺ doors, and be mindful of Allah so you may be successful.**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Question of the Moons**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between prophet and means. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:189. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:189. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:189.

**Houses from the Rear: The Old and the New**

Here new moons (ahillah, sing. hilāl) does not refer to the new moon considered purely astronomically, which refers to when the moon is still invisible (dark moon), but to the first visible crescent of the lunar cycle. During the dark moon, the moon is between the earth and the sun, so that the dark side of the moon faces the earth; this is referred to as lunar conjunction. A lunar conjunction does not usually cause a solar eclipse, because the lunar orbit is tilted several degrees in relation to the earth’s orbit around the sun, and hence the three bodies are only in an approximately straight line. (That is also why the full moon is visible from the earth when the earth is approximately in between the moon and the sun.) The new moon or crescent (hilāl) appears when the moon moves far enough out of conjunction for a thin strip of the illuminated side of the moon to become visible.

**"Piety Is the Reverent"**

During the dark moon phase, the sun and moon set together over the western horizon, but at the start of a new lunar month, the sun sets first, leaving the moon just above the horizon for a short time. If the moon is far enough out of line between the earth and the sun, the crescent will become visible before the moon follows the sun below the horizon and disappears. The sighting of this new crescent begins the new lunar month in the Islamic calendar. (In the last part of the lunar month leading up to the dark moon, the moon “sets” before the sun and is below the horizon until it rises later in the night.)

**A journey ordered toward Allah**

On the question of entering houses from their rear or by their doors, it was reported that the Helpers, or Anṣār (the natives of Madinah who had become Muslims), would not enter their houses by their doors when returning from a journey, but would go over a wall instead in order to enter the house (Ibn Kathīr). Others relate that the Anṣār and the rest of the Arabs (other than the religious confederation called the Ḥums, which included the Quraysh; see v. 199) would not enter through their doors in a state of iḥrām (a state of ritual purity in preparation for pilgrimage). Others say that when the people of Yathrib would return from a festival, they would enter their houses from the back, considering this to be a pious act. This verse brought the emphasis back to reverence (taqwā) over a superstitious practice (Ibn Kathīr).

**The sacred limit in the command**

This verse is interpreted spiritually in many Islamic sources to mean that everything should be approached properly and in conformity with its essential nature. Ibn ʿAjībah, for example, notes in his commentary on this verse that spiritual wayfarers on their journey to Allah have three houses whose gates they must pass through: the Law (sharīʿah), the Spiritual Path (ṭarīqah), and the Truth (ḥaqīqah), each of which has three gates. The three gates of the Law are repentance, obedience, and reverence; those of the Path are sincerity, the purification from faults, and the realization of virtue; and the three gates of the Truth (also translated as the Reality) are concentration, contemplation, and gnosis (spiritual knowledge). More precisely, human beings should approach Allah through the means He accepts, the means He has given them.

**Ritual detail and spiritual purpose**

The treatment of prophet joins movement through a place or ritual with movement of the heart. Sacred practice has boundaries precisely because it is not ordinary travel or ordinary habit. The limits teach the pilgrim to receive meaning rather than manufacture it, while the concessions show that obedience is addressed to human beings with real capacities and pressures.

The standard in 2:189 remains practical because it can be applied before a dispute reaches a court or a crisis reaches its worst point. One can notice the first small departure from prophet: an excuse, a concealed obligation, an unexamined desire, or a promise treated as optional. Returning at that point is easier than defending a settled habit. The warning is therefore also an opening for repair.

The verse speaks first to the situation that occasioned it and then to every reader who meets the same relation between prophet and means.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:190

> **Fight in the cause of Allah ˹only˺ against those who wage war against you, but do not exceed the limits. Surely Allah does not like transgressors.**

### Expanded Commentary

**The First Verse of Qitāl**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings fight and exceed into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. Its first term in 2:190 sets the subject, while the later term shows what that subject demands, permits, or exposes. The order of 2:190 gives the reader a path through the verse: begin with what Allah names, follow the consequence, and resist the temptation to turn a living address into a slogan.

**In the Way of Allah — Fī Sabīlillāh**

Many of the issues raised in this passage are addressed in the essay Conquest and Conversion, War and Peace in the Qur'an. V. 190 is considered by some to be the first verse in the chronological order of revelation to permit fighting, though others dispute this opinion and consider the first such passage to be 22:39: Permission is granted to those who are fought, because they have been wronged. Among those passages that had previously forbidden fighting (i.e., while in Makkah and initially in Madinah), some list 41:34: Repel [evil] with that which is better; then behold, the one between whom and thee there is enmity shall be as if he were a loyal protecting friend; 5:13: Thou wilt not cease to discover their treachery, from all save a few of them.

**"Do Not Transgress" — The Boundaries**

So pardon them, and forbear; 73:10: Bear patiently that which they say and take leave of them in a beautiful manner; and 88:22: Thou are not a warder over them . Some report that these verses were revealed in connection with the Treaty of Ḥudaybiyah. In 6/628 the Muslims set out from Madinah for Makkah in order to perform the ʿumrah (lesser pilgrimage), but were met on the road by the Makkans at Ḥudaybiyah. There they came to an agreement that the Muslims would turn back, but would be allowed to return to perform the ʿumrah the following year.

Then, as the time for that approached, some grew apprehensive about going to Makkah, fearing attack and being called upon to fight in the sacred precinct during the sacred months. This verse was then revealed in order to set the guidelines for engagement .

**Allah Loves Not the Transgressors**

Many commentators use this passage to discuss the usual rules of war, such as the prohibition against killing women, children, monks, hermits, the chronically ill, old men, and peasants . For example, Ibn ʿAbbās said, “Do not kill women, children, old men, or those who offer peace and restrain their hand. If you do that, you will have transgressed against them” (al-Ṭabarī). The Umayyad Caliph ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz (r. 99–101/717–20) commented on this passage in a letter, saying it meant, “Fight not those who do not fight you” (al-Ṭabarī).

**The permission is not a blank cheque**

This passage is among the most direct in describing the limits of warfare. Muslims are commanded to fight those who fight them first, to expel those who first expel them, but in doing so they are subject to limits. In transgress against him in like manner as he transgressed against you, the transgression that Muslims are ordered to commit is not seen as illegitimate, as the verb transgress (iʿtadā) would ordinarily imply. It is, rather, a legitimate response to aggression and in this sense could also be correctly translated attack him in like manner as he attacked you (al-Ṭabarī). This is similar to the message of 16:126: And if you would punish, then punish with the like of that wherewith you were punished; and also 42:40: The recompense of an evil is an evil like unto it.

**The difference between defence and aggression**

In strife is worse than slaying, strife renders fitnah, a word that can also mean trial, temptation, or sedition (see also 3:7; 3:19; 4:91). Among the acts considered worse than slaughter are disbelief, idolatry, and becoming an apostate from Islam in favor of idolatry, as these things lead to perdition in the Hereafter (al-Ṭabarī). The phrase could also mean that some fighting now is better than a state of strife that would lead to even greater fighting and death later, an important idea in later Islamic political philosophy.

**The human cost carried by the wording**

The commentators typically gloss strife as idolatry (shirk) and hence also interpret the end of fitnah to mean the end of that idolatry. Some also reason that if they desist means if they stop being idolaters and become Muslims, though others simply state that it is the fighting and hostility from which they must desist (al-Rāzī). The interpretation that the conversion of the idolaters is the final goal is problematic, not only in light of the plain sense of this verse, but also in view of other passages, such as 9:6: And if any of the idolaters seek asylum with thee, grant him asylum until he hears the Word of Allah.

**Limits that remain binding in conflict**

Then convey him to his place of safety. This passage makes a clear distinction between those who fight against Muslims and those who do not, those who expel them and those who do not, and little explanation is provided by the commentators who seem to take the position that hostilities begin with fighting and expulsion (political causes), but can end only with repentance and conversion to Islam (spiritual causes). Al-Rāzī mentions that and religion is for Allah shows that the purpose of fighting is to end disbelief and idolatry, though it is unclear why this would not be simply an extension of the goal of ending the very real danger posed by the idolaters.

For more on this issue, see commentary on 8:38–40.

**How the early community understood it**

Regarding the command do not fight with them near the Sacred Mosque until they fight with you there, it should be recalled that the precinct around the Kaʿbah, the ḥaram, was considered inviolable by the Arabs as a tradition going back to the time of Abraham; see 2:126c.

The sacred month for the sacred month refers to the fact that, although according to the terms brokered at Ḥudaybiyah (6/628) the Muslims had to turn back, they were able to return the following year (AH 7) to perform the lesser pilgrimage (ʿumrah) in the month of Dhu’l-Qaʿdah. Retribution for forbidden things refers to the rites of pilgrimage, which were restored by the return in that second year, meaning they were a compensation from Allah for the rites that they were unable to perform the previous year (al-Ṭabarī). The multiple “sacred things” are thought to refer to the sacred or inviolable month, the sacred land of Makkah, and iḥrām (the ritual state of pilgrims before performing the pilgrimage rites; R, Ṭ).

Others state that when the Makkans heard that Muslims had been forbidden to fight during the sacred months, they thought they could take advantage of their quiescence. This verse was revealed indicating that if any shed the blood of a Muslim during the sacred month, their blood is liable to be shed in the sacred month as well, meaning that Muslims should observe the inviolability of forbidden things (e.g., spilling blood in the sacred precincts of Makkah), but not to the point of self-destruction (al-Rāzī).

The mention of fight must be read with the restraints carried by the same revelation. Permission to resist wrongdoing does not erase the prohibition of wrongdoing. The verse therefore asks the community to hold two truths together: injustice may have to be confronted, and the means used in confronting it remain subject to Allah's judgment.

A useful way to test the verse is to ask what would change if fight were taken seriously when no audience was present. The answer cannot be only a feeling, because 2:190 connects inward recognition with a discernible choice. Nor can it be only an outward display, because the choice in 2:190 loses its Qur'anic meaning when it is made for reputation rather than for Allah. The passage holds intention and action together in 2:190.

The commentators typically gloss strife as idolatry (shirk) and hence also interpret the end of fitnah to mean the end of that idolatry. Some also reason that if they desist means if they stop being idolaters and become Muslims, though others simply state that it is the fighting and hostility from which they must desist (al-Rāzī). The interpretation that the conversion of the idolaters is the final goal is problematic, not only in light of the plain sense of this verse, but also in view of other passages, such as 9:6: And if any of the idolaters seek asylum with thee, grant him asylum until he hears the Word of Allah.

**Why the promise or threat is just**

Then convey him to his place of safety. This passage makes a clear distinction between those who fight against Muslims and those who do not, those who expel them and those who do not, and little explanation is provided by the commentators who seem to take the position that hostilities begin with fighting and expulsion (political causes), but can end only with repentance and conversion to Islam (spiritual causes). Al-Rāzī mentions that and religion is for Allah shows that the purpose of fighting is to end disbelief and idolatry, though it is unclear why this would not be simply an extension of the goal of ending the very real danger posed by the idolaters.

For more on this issue, see commentary on 8:38–40.

**The Hereafter in the argument**

Regarding the command do not fight with them near the Sacred Mosque until they fight with you there, it should be recalled that the precinct around the Kaʿbah, the ḥaram, was considered inviolable by the Arabs as a tradition going back to the time of Abraham; see 2:126c.

The sacred month for the sacred month refers to the fact that, although according to the terms brokered at Ḥudaybiyah (6/628) the Muslims had to turn back, they were able to return the following year (AH 7) to perform the lesser pilgrimage (ʿumrah) in the month of Dhu’l-Qaʿdah. Retribution for forbidden things refers to the rites of pilgrimage, which were restored by the return in that second year, meaning they were a compensation from Allah for the rites that they were unable to perform the previous year (al-Ṭabarī). The multiple “sacred things” are thought to refer to the sacred or inviolable month, the sacred land of Makkah, and iḥrām (the ritual state of pilgrims before performing the pilgrimage rites; R, Ṭ).

Others state that when the Makkans heard that Muslims had been forbidden to fight during the sacred months, they thought they could take advantage of their quiescence. This verse was revealed indicating that if any shed the blood of a Muslim during the sacred month, their blood is liable to be shed in the sacred month as well, meaning that Muslims should observe the inviolability of forbidden things (e.g., spilling blood in the sacred precincts of Makkah), but not to the point of self-destruction (al-Rāzī).

The verse's reference to cease widens the scene beyond the immediate reward or pain. A deed in 2:192 may appear small when measured by public attention, yet its meaning changes when it is known by Allah and carried into the final account. Warning and mercy belong together in 2:192: accountability is serious because the human being is not abandoned to meaninglessness.

A useful way to test the verse is to ask what would change if cease were taken seriously when no audience was present. The answer cannot be only a feeling, because 2:192 connects inward recognition with a discernible choice. Nor can it be only an outward display, because the choice in 2:192 loses its Qur'anic meaning when it is made for reputation rather than for Allah. The passage holds intention and action together in 2:192.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:193

> **Fight against them ˹if they persecute you˺ until there is no more persecution, and ˹your˺ devotion will be to Allah ˹alone˺. If they stop ˹persecuting you˺, let there be no hostility except against the aggressors.**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Terminus of Fighting**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between fight and more. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:193. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:193. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:193.

**No Enmity Save Against the Wrongdoers**

Many of the issues raised in this passage are addressed in the essay Conquest and Conversion, War and Peace in the Qur'an. V. 190 is considered by some to be the first verse in the chronological order of revelation to permit fighting, though others dispute this opinion and consider the first such passage to be 22:39: Permission is granted to those who are fought, because they have been wronged. Among those passages that had previously forbidden fighting (i.e., while in Makkah and initially in Madinah), some list 41:34: Repel [evil] with that which is better; then behold, the one between whom and thee there is enmity shall be as if he were a loyal protecting friend; 5:13: Thou wilt not cease to discover their treachery, from all save a few of them.

**The Begun Will of Peace**

So pardon them, and forbear; 73:10: Bear patiently that which they say and take leave of them in a beautiful manner; and 88:22: Thou are not a warder over them. Some report that these verses were revealed in connection with the Treaty of Ḥudaybiyah. In 6/628 the Muslims set out from Madinah for Makkah in order to perform the ʿumrah (lesser pilgrimage), but were met on the road by the Makkans at Ḥudaybiyah. There they came to an agreement that the Muslims would turn back, but would be allowed to return to perform the ʿumrah the following year.

Then, as the time for that approached, some grew apprehensive about going to Makkah, fearing attack and being called upon to fight in the sacred precinct during the sacred months. This verse was then revealed in order to set the guidelines for engagement.

**The permission is not a blank cheque**

Many commentators use this passage to discuss the usual rules of war, such as the prohibition against killing women, children, monks, hermits, the chronically ill, old men, and peasants. For example, Ibn ʿAbbās said, “Do not kill women, children, old men, or those who offer peace and restrain their hand. If you do that, you will have transgressed against them” (al-Ṭabarī). The Umayyad Caliph ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz (r. 99–101/717–20) commented on this passage in a letter, saying it meant, “Fight not those who do not fight you” (al-Ṭabarī).

**The difference between defence and aggression**

This passage is among the most direct in describing the limits of warfare. Muslims are commanded to fight those who fight them first, to expel those who first expel them, but in doing so they are subject to limits. In transgress against him in like manner as he transgressed against you, the transgression that Muslims are ordered to commit is not seen as illegitimate, as the verb transgress (iʿtadā) would ordinarily imply. It is, rather, a legitimate response to aggression and in this sense could also be correctly translated attack him in like manner as he attacked you (al-Ṭabarī). This is similar to the message of 16:126: And if you would punish, then punish with the like of that wherewith you were punished; and also 42:40: The recompense of an evil is an evil like unto it.

**The human cost carried by the wording**

In strife is worse than slaying, strife renders fitnah, a word that can also mean trial, temptation, or sedition (see also 3:7; 3:19; 4:91). Among the acts considered worse than slaughter are disbelief, idolatry, and becoming an apostate from Islam in favor of idolatry, as these things lead to perdition in the Hereafter (al-Ṭabarī). The phrase could also mean that some fighting now is better than a state of strife that would lead to even greater fighting and death later, an important idea in later Islamic political philosophy.

**Limits that remain binding in conflict**

The commentators typically gloss strife as idolatry (shirk) and hence also interpret the end of fitnah to mean the end of that idolatry. Some also reason that if they desist means if they stop being idolaters and become Muslims, though others simply state that it is the fighting and hostility from which they must desist (al-Rāzī). The interpretation that the conversion of the idolaters is the final goal is problematic, not only in light of the plain sense of this verse, but also in view of other passages, such as 9:6: And if any of the idolaters seek asylum with thee, grant him asylum until he hears the Word of Allah.

**How the early community understood it**

Then convey him to his place of safety. This passage makes a clear distinction between those who fight against Muslims and those who do not, those who expel them and those who do not, and little explanation is provided by the commentators who seem to take the position that hostilities begin with fighting and expulsion (political causes), but can end only with repentance and conversion to Islam (spiritual causes). Al-Rāzī mentions that and religion is for Allah shows that the purpose of fighting is to end disbelief and idolatry, though it is unclear why this would not be simply an extension of the goal of ending the very real danger posed by the idolaters.

For more on this issue, see commentary on 8:38–40.

**Power restrained by accountability**

Regarding the command do not fight with them near the Sacred Mosque until they fight with you there, it should be recalled that the precinct around the Kaʿbah, the ḥaram, was considered inviolable by the Arabs as a tradition going back to the time of Abraham; see 2:126c.

The sacred month for the sacred month refers to the fact that, although according to the terms brokered at Ḥudaybiyah (6/628) the Muslims had to turn back, they were able to return the following year (AH 7) to perform the lesser pilgrimage (ʿumrah) in the month of Dhu’l-Qaʿdah. Retribution for forbidden things refers to the rites of pilgrimage, which were restored by the return in that second year, meaning they were a compensation from Allah for the rites that they were unable to perform the previous year (al-Ṭabarī). The multiple “sacred things” are thought to refer to the sacred or inviolable month, the sacred land of Makkah, and iḥrām (the ritual state of pilgrims before performing the pilgrimage rites; R, Ṭ).

Others state that when the Makkans heard that Muslims had been forbidden to fight during the sacred months, they thought they could take advantage of their quiescence. This verse was revealed indicating that if any shed the blood of a Muslim during the sacred month, their blood is liable to be shed in the sacred month as well, meaning that Muslims should observe the inviolability of forbidden things (e.g., spilling blood in the sacred precincts of Makkah), but not to the point of self-destruction (al-Rāzī).

The mention of fight must be read with the restraints carried by the same revelation. Permission to resist wrongdoing does not erase the prohibition of wrongdoing. The verse therefore asks the community to hold two truths together: injustice may have to be confronted, and the means used in confronting it remain subject to Allah's judgment.

The standard in 2:193 remains practical because it can be applied before a dispute reaches a court or a crisis reaches its worst point. One can notice the first small departure from fight: an excuse, a concealed obligation, an unexamined desire, or a promise treated as optional. Returning at that point is easier than defending a settled habit. The warning is therefore also an opening for repair.

> **˹There will be retaliation in˺ a sacred month for ˹an offence in˺ a sacred month, and all violations will bring about retaliation. So, if anyone attacks you, retaliate in the same manner. ˹But˺ be mindful of Allah, and know that Allah is with those mindful ˹of Him˺.**

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:195

> **Spend in the cause of Allah and do not let your own hands throw you into destruction ˹by withholding˺. And do good, for Allah certainly loves the good-doers.**

### Expanded Commentary

**Spend — Then the Second Command**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between spend and throw. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:195. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:195. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:195.

**"Do Not Cast Yourselves Into Ruin"**

One casts oneself into ruin by being miserly and ungenerous with regard to giving charity and spending in the way of Allah or, according to some, by being satisfied with family and wealth and abandoning struggle in the way of Allah . This verse is also sometimes invoked to condemn recklessness. For example, during a battle with the Byzantines, the Companion Abū Ayyūb al-Anṣārī heard some people reference do not . . . cast yourselves into ruin when a man charged the Byzantine lines and was killed. He corrected them and said that the verse was revealed in connection with some Companions who had secretly begun talking about their desire to live with their wealth and replenish what they had lost rather than continuing to strive in the way of Allah (al-Ṭabarī).

**"And Be Virtuous — Allah Loves the Virtuous"**

Another interpretation sees this verse as addressed to people who, having committed a sin for which they think they cannot be forgiven, continue sinning because they feel doomed in any case (Ibn Kathīr). Instead of turning in repentance, they surrender to moral despair (al-Ṭabarī). Others interpret it according to its plain sense, understanding it as a warning to avoid anything that would lead to self-destruction, including courting Divine Punishment by doing what Allah has forbidden (al-Ṭabarī).

The subject of spend joins an act directed to Allah with a consequence visible among people. In 2:195, that union guards against two reductions: worship cannot become a private performance with no social fruit, and social generosity cannot become a substitute for worship. The verse 2:195 asks for an outward practice whose inward intention remains answerable to Allah.

**The act and the intention beneath it**

The standard in 2:195 remains practical because it can be applied before a dispute reaches a court or a crisis reaches its worst point. One can notice the first small departure from spend: an excuse, a concealed obligation, an unexamined desire, or a promise treated as optional. Returning at that point is easier than defending a settled habit. The warning is therefore also an opening for repair.

The relation between spend and throw also protects the verse from two opposite misreadings. It should not be expanded into a claim the wording of 2:195 does not make, but neither should its brevity be used to make it weightless. Short Qur'anic statements such as 2:195 often function as hinges: they close one movement, open another, and give the next command its moral setting. The careful reader of 2:195 therefore asks what has just been established, what response is now being required, and what kind of character could respond without evasion. Those questions keep 2:195 specific while allowing its guidance to reach a new circumstance.

**A visible duty with an inward root**

The final emphasis of 2:195 returns to responsibility. No explanation of spend is complete if it leaves the reader with information about earlier communities but no question about present conduct. The verse 2:195 asks what can be repaired now: a promise kept, a right restored, a motive purified, or a harmful practice abandoned. That is where knowledge becomes guidance.

The choice of the word spend in 2:195 also matters. It leaves room for the full context of 2:195 instead of allowing one translation gloss to carry every shade of meaning. Classical Arabic often places a broad word inside a narrow scene; in 2:195, the surrounding clauses determine whether the emphasis falls on an act, an intention, a condition, or a consequence. Here the reader should let the sentence do that work.

**Why worship opens toward other people**

The exegetical tradition approaches spend from more than one angle, but its differences are more useful when their shared question is made visible. The commentators ask what the wording of 2:195 includes, what it excludes, and how it fits with the other passages of the Qur'an. A responsible reading can preserve those alternatives in 2:195 without pretending that every possibility has equal strength.

There is also a distinction between understanding spend and using it as a label for other people. The first task belongs to learning; the second requires evidence, fairness, and awareness of one's own motives in 2:195. The verse 2:195 addresses the reader before it supplies material for judging a neighbour. Its warning becomes safer and more productive when self-examination comes first.

**The measure of sincere giving**

The theology and practical instruction of 2:195 therefore support one another. If Allah knows or commands throw, that knowledge or command changes how a person handles time, power, money, speech, and private desire. A doctrine that never reaches those choices has not yet been read at the level demanded by 2:195.

An ordinary example makes the moral structure of 2:195 visible without replacing the revelation. Two people may perform an outwardly similar act involving spend; one may be protecting a right, while the other is seeking praise, escaping a duty, or taking advantage of confusion. The act's surface does not settle its value. Intention, circumstance, and the rights of others complete the judgment.

**The poor person’s dignity**

The surrounding verses keep the reader from isolating spend from the rest of life. In 2:195, revelation corrects the mind but also trains habits: how a person speaks when challenged, gives when unseen, waits when angry, and returns after error. Those habits are where this verse becomes more than information about spend. They are the place in which assent to 2:195 is either confirmed or quietly withdrawn.

The most balanced response to 2:195 is neither to make the passage vague nor to claim more than it says. Its boundaries are part of its guidance. Within them, the verse can illuminate a new situation because its underlying moral relation remains stable: spend is joined to throw, and the person is responsible for how that relation is honoured.

**A community shaped by obedience**

The wording of 2:195 gives the reader a useful order of questions about spend. What does the term spend mean in ordinary Arabic, what does the surrounding sentence restrict it to, and what consequence follows when the command is obeyed or refused in 2:195? These questions prevent a commentary on 2:195 from becoming a list of slogans. They make the act of interpretation answerable to grammar, context, and the moral end of this passage at 2:195.

The commentators sometimes preserve more than one report about the setting of 2:195. Such reports should be weighed rather than treated as interchangeable decoration. An occasion can explain why a question arose, but the wording of 2:195 determines how far the guidance travels. The verse speaks first to the situation that occasioned it and then to every reader who meets the same relation between spend and throw.

In 2:195, the distinction between public appearance and inward truth is especially relevant. A person may use the language of spend while arranging the act around another purpose. Allah's judgment in 2:195 is not limited to the visible outline, yet the inner intention is not an excuse for ignoring the rights and forms that the revelation establishes. Sincerity completes obedience; it does not cancel it.

One can see the social wisdom of 2:195 in a small everyday case. When people share responsibility for spend, uncertainty about the duty tends to fall on the person with less power or less information. A clear moral rule changes that balance. In 2:195, it tells the stronger party what must not be taken, and gives the weaker party language with which to name the wrong.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:196

> **Complete the pilgrimage and minor pilgrimage for Allah. But if prevented ˹from proceeding˺, then ˹offer˺ whatever sacrificial animals you can afford. And do not shave your heads until the sacrificial animal reaches its destination. But if any of you is ill or has a scalp ailment ˹requiring shaving˺, then compensate either by fasting, charity, or a sacrificial offering. In times of peace, you may combine the pilgrimage and minor pilgrimage then make the sacrificial offering you can afford. Whoever cannot afford that ˹offering˺, let them fast three days during pilgrimage and seven after returning ˹home˺—completing ten. These offerings are for those who do not live near the Sacred House. And be mindful of Allah, and know that Allah is severe in punishment.**

### Expanded Commentary

**Complete for Allah**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings complete and prevented into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. Its first term in 2:196 sets the subject, while the later term shows what that subject demands, permits, or exposes. The order of 2:196 gives the reader a path through the verse: begin with what Allah names, follow the consequence, and resist the temptation to turn a living address into a slogan.

The command to complete . . . the ʿumrah raises the question of whether and/or how the ʿumrah is considered obligatory. The ḥajj, or “pilgrimage,” is one of the five pillars of Islam and is universally considered an obligation upon all able-bodied Muslims who can afford it. The ʿumrah, or “visit,” however, is generally considered to be a voluntary pilgrimage according to Islamic Law, although some scholars consider it to be a requirement like the ḥajj. As will be seen below, the ḥajj and ʿumrah were often performed during the same trip. The ḥajj and ʿumrah are sometimes rendered as the greater pilgrimage and the lesser pilgrimage, respectively, and sometimes ʿumrah is referred to as ḥajj al-ʿumrah.

**The Hinderer's Offering — and its Scalp-Ransom**

Others take the word complete to mean that once one sets out to perform the ḥajj or ʿumrah, one should complete it without interruption; this is not unlike the obligation to complete a fast outside of Ramadan once it is begun, which is to say one is obligated to finish a supererogatory fast once it has been started, and if one does break it, one must make up that day. Thus one could be commanded to complete the ʿumrah without the ʿumrah being obligatory a priori. This interpretation of the command to complete would also apply to anyone performing the ḥajj for a second time, since the ḥajj is only obligatory once. To complete these rites for Allah means that one should not perform them for the purposes of trade, meeting people, or other worldly benefits, but only to worship Allah (al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī). This intention is concretely manifested by entering into the state of iḥrām, when many ordinarily permissible things are forbidden (al-Ṭabarī).

**Tamattuʿ — The Ten Days**

Thus a few commentators say that complete does not mean that either rite is obligatory, but rather means institute them according to their rules (al-Ṭabarī). The obligation of the ḥajj is, however, established through other verses, such as 3:97, Pilgrimage to the House is a duty upon mankind before Allah for those who can find a way, as well as in many aḥādīth. But al-Ṭabarī also mentions opinions that consider the ʿumrah to be a requirement associated with the ḥajj in the same way that alms and prayer are two requirements often associated with each other and mentioned together. The schools of law differ on this question, although, as will be seen below, the question tends to become moot since the ʿumrah is often performed in conjunction with the ḥajj. Some read the declension after ʿumrah in a way that would allow the verse to mean, Complete the ḥajj, and the ʿumrah is for Allah, though this is a minority opinion (al-Ṭabarī).

**The discipline named by the verse**

Being hindered can describe anything that obstructs believers in their performance of the ḥajj, such as being ill or injured or in danger of encountering a hostile party on the way. A person in those circumstances may send such offering as is easy instead (al-Ṭabarī). The offering is almost unanimously specified to be a sacrifice of, at a minimum, a sheep, but other sacrificed animals, such as cows or camels, are also mentioned (al-Ṭabarī). At Ḥudaybiyah (on the road from Madinah to Makkah), when the Prophet and his Companions were hindered from making the ʿumrah, they shaved their heads and sacrificed their animals there, not in Makkah as they ordinarily would have done.

Because of this fact, some maintain that for the offering to reach its place means for it to reach the place where it will be eaten (al-Ṭabarī), since most of the animals sacrificed ritually during the ḥajj or ʿumrah are consumed after slaughter. Others argue that depending on circumstances the sacrifice should actually reach Makkah before one shaves one’s head or cuts one’s hair, which is the final act of the ʿumrah (although not obligatory).

**Hunger, desire, and conscious worship**

Since one who is sick is exempted from the ḥajj and ʿumrah in any case, it would seem that being hindered, which can include illness, refers to hindrances that arise after one has already set out in a state of iḥrām (al-Ṭabarī). The Ḥanafī school of law, for example, says that if any are on the road and get lost, stung, bitten, or sick, they should send the offering or its monetary equivalent ahead, and then their ʿumrah will be considered complete (al-Qurṭubī). In general there is a range of positions regarding what constitutes a hindrance to the pilgrimage, where the offering should go, and whether one needs to make up a missed attempt at the ʿumrah or ḥajj.

**The room made for repentance**

At the end of both ḥajj and ʿumrah, one usually shaves one’s head or cuts one’s hair, and in the case of one who has a head or scalp ailment preventing this act, a ransom by fasting, charity, or rite is required. Rite (nusuk) here refers specifically to sacrifice, though the word literally means “ritual” or “act of worship.” The ransom of fasting is to fast for ten days; the ransom of feeding the poor is to feed ten poor people; and the ransom of sacrifice is at least a sheep (al-Qurṭubī).

Let those who enjoy the ʿumrah ahead of the ḥajj refers to one of three combinations of ʿumrah and ḥajj carried out by those coming from outside of Makkah to perform them. In the first case, one enters into the state of iḥrām, performs the ḥajj, and then leaves iḥrām; one then reenters iḥrām and performs the ʿumrah. This is called ifrād, or “isolating.” In the second case, which this verse addresses, one enters into the state of iḥrām, performs the ʿumrah, leaves that iḥrām, then enters into a new state of iḥrām to perform the ḥajj.

**A private act with public consequences**

This practice, sometimes also called tamattuʿ, or “enjoyment,” is when one performs the ʿumrah before the ḥajj, but does not remain in one’s iḥrām between the ʿumrah and ḥajj. In this case one can then “enjoy” being out of iḥrām and free of the restrictions it entails before reentering iḥrām for the ḥajj. In the third case, one performs the ʿumrah, but remains in one’s state of iḥrām and performs the ḥajj, which is called qirān, or “joining.” The schools of law differ over which of these methods is most meritorious.

It is reported that the Arabs had severely frowned upon performing the ʿumrah during the time of the ḥajj and were reluctant to do so until the Prophet himself performed the ʿumrah during Dhu’l-Ḥijjah, the month of the ḥajj (al-Qurṭubī). Thus, according to one view, since the month of the ḥajj is for the ḥajj and not for the ʿumrah (which can be done anytime during the year), the offering or fasting was instituted if one carried out the “enjoyment” of leaving iḥrām between performing the ʿumrah and ḥajj, since even the performance of the ʿumrah itself during the month of ḥajj is a mercy from Allah (al-Qurṭubī).

**The legal condition and its purpose**

As for the three days of fasting enjoined for those who are unable to make an offering, opinions differ. Some allow it to be the three days preceding the stay in ʿArafah, others the three days after, when the pilgrims stay in Mina (al-Qurṭubī). The seven days are considered by some to be best performed when one returns to one’s homeland, while for others when you return simply refers to the state of leaving one’s iḥrām (al-Qurṭubī). Those who were local to Makkah were not subject to these same guidelines regarding the practice of the ʿumrah and ḥajj.

One opinion is that those who dwell near the Sacred Mosque are those who would not shorten their prayers if they traveled there, while others place the limits at the border points (mawāqīt) in the environs of Makkah where one enters into a state of iḥrām when intending to perform a pilgrimage.

**How restraint becomes freedom**

The verse's concern with complete shows why religious restraint is not meant to produce weakness or despair. Desire is acknowledged rather than denied, then given a disciplined place. The worshipper learns to distinguish a genuine need from an impulse, and a lawful ease from the kind of indulgence that makes obedience meaningless.

A useful way to test the verse is to ask what would change if complete were taken seriously when no audience was present. The answer cannot be only a feeling, because 2:196 connects inward recognition with a discernible choice. Nor can it be only an outward display, because the choice in 2:196 loses its Qur'anic meaning when it is made for reputation rather than for Allah. The passage holds intention and action together in 2:196.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:197

> **˹Commitment to˺ pilgrimage is made in appointed months. Whoever commits to ˹performing˺ pilgrimage, let them stay away from intimate relations, foul language, and arguments during pilgrimage. Whatever good you do, Allah ˹fully˺ knows of it. Take ˹necessary˺ provisions ˹for the journey˺—surely the best provision is righteousness. And be mindful of Me, O people of reason!**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Known Months**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between commitment and months. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:197. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:197. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:197.

**No Lewdness, Iniquity, Quarreling**

The months well known are considered to be Shawwāl, Dhul-Qaʿdah, and Dhul-Ḥijjah, although some say only the first ten days of Dhul-Ḥijjah, since the rules regarding sacrifice change after the Day of Sacrifice. According to many authorities it is discouraged (makrūh) to enter iḥrām for the ḥajj in months other than these; that is, one should not enter iḥrām and stay in it until the ḥajj is performed in Dhul-Ḥijjah. Lewdness refers to sexual intercourse, which, if it occurs before the Day of ʿArafah, invalidates the ḥajj and requires a person to make a sacrificial offering and perform the ḥajj again.

**The Best Provision**

Others point out that lewdness refers to talking with or about women to whom one is not closely related (in the case of men). A ḥadīth states, By Him in Whose Hand is my soul, there is no deed between Heaven and earth better than struggle in the way of Allah, and a ḥajj performed faithfully in which there is no lewdness, iniquity, or argument. The quarreling does not refer to intellectual disagreements, but to interchanges resulting in anger and insults. Al-Qurṭubī notes that there used to be arguments about the Station of Abraham (see 2:125c), as the Quraysh would observe a spot different from that of the other Arabs.

He prefers to think that the prohibition here is about the place and time of the ḥajj, but it could also refer to the practice of boasting that sometimes accompanied the pilgrimage, where some would claim that their ḥajj was better than that of others, that their forefathers were better, and so forth (al-Qurṭubī).

**"Reverence Me, O Possessors of Intellect"**

To make provision means to come materially prepared for the ḥajj and not to rely upon the locals and other pilgrims for food and shelter. The ḥajj is not in any case incumbent upon those without the necessary financial means. At a spiritual level, one can speak of reverence (taqwā) as a provision for the Hereafter, likened to the provision one makes for the pilgrimage in this world (al-Qurṭubī).

The treatment of commitment joins movement through a place or ritual with movement of the heart. Sacred practice has boundaries precisely because it is not ordinary travel or ordinary habit. The limits teach the pilgrim to receive meaning rather than manufacture it, while the concessions show that obedience is addressed to human beings with real capacities and pressures.

**A journey ordered toward Allah**

The standard in 2:197 remains practical because it can be applied before a dispute reaches a court or a crisis reaches its worst point. One can notice the first small departure from commitment: an excuse, a concealed obligation, an unexamined desire, or a promise treated as optional. Returning at that point is easier than defending a settled habit. The warning is therefore also an opening for repair.

The relation between commitment and months also protects the verse from two opposite misreadings. It should not be expanded into a claim the wording of 2:197 does not make, but neither should its brevity be used to make it weightless. Short Qur'anic statements such as 2:197 often function as hinges: they close one movement, open another, and give the next command its moral setting. The careful reader of 2:197 therefore asks what has just been established, what response is now being required, and what kind of character could respond without evasion. Those questions keep 2:197 specific while allowing its guidance to reach a new circumstance.

**The sacred limit in the command**

The exegetical tradition approaches commitment from more than one angle, but its differences are more useful when their shared question is made visible. The commentators ask what the wording of 2:197 includes, what it excludes, and how it fits with the other passages of the Qur'an. A responsible reading can preserve those alternatives in 2:197 without pretending that every possibility has equal strength.

There is also a distinction between understanding commitment and using it as a label for other people. The first task belongs to learning; the second requires evidence, fairness, and awareness of one's own motives in 2:197. The verse 2:197 addresses the reader before it supplies material for judging a neighbour. Its warning becomes safer and more productive when self-examination comes first.

**Ritual detail and spiritual purpose**

The theology and practical instruction of 2:197 therefore support one another. If Allah knows or commands months, that knowledge or command changes how a person handles time, power, money, speech, and private desire. A doctrine that never reaches those choices has not yet been read at the level demanded by 2:197.

An ordinary example makes the moral structure of 2:197 visible without replacing the revelation. Two people may perform an outwardly similar act involving commitment; one may be protecting a right, while the other is seeking praise, escaping a duty, or taking advantage of confusion. The act's surface does not settle its value. Intention, circumstance, and the rights of others complete the judgment.

**What pilgrims must leave behind**

The surrounding verses keep the reader from isolating commitment from the rest of life. In 2:197, revelation corrects the mind but also trains habits: how a person speaks when challenged, gives when unseen, waits when angry, and returns after error. Those habits are where this verse becomes more than information about commitment. They are the place in which assent to 2:197 is either confirmed or quietly withdrawn.

The most balanced response to 2:197 is neither to make the passage vague nor to claim more than it says. Its boundaries are part of its guidance. Within them, the verse can illuminate a new situation because its underlying moral relation remains stable: commitment is joined to months, and the person is responsible for how that relation is honoured.

**The community gathered by one sign**

The wording of 2:197 gives the reader a useful order of questions about commitment. What does the term commitment mean in ordinary Arabic, what does the surrounding sentence restrict it to, and what consequence follows when the command is obeyed or refused in 2:197? These questions prevent a commentary on 2:197 from becoming a list of slogans. They make the act of interpretation answerable to grammar, context, and the moral end of this passage at 2:197.

The commentators sometimes preserve more than one report about the setting of 2:197. Such reports should be weighed rather than treated as interchangeable decoration. An occasion can explain why a question arose, but the wording of 2:197 determines how far the guidance travels. The verse speaks first to the situation that occasioned it and then to every reader who meets the same relation between commitment and months.

In 2:197, the distinction between public appearance and inward truth is especially relevant. A person may use the language of commitment while arranging the act around another purpose. Allah's judgment in 2:197 is not limited to the visible outline, yet the inner intention is not an excuse for ignoring the rights and forms that the revelation establishes. Sincerity completes obedience; it does not cancel it.

One can see the social wisdom of 2:197 in a small everyday case. When people share responsibility for commitment, uncertainty about the duty tends to fall on the person with less power or less information. A clear moral rule changes that balance. In 2:197, it tells the stronger party what must not be taken, and gives the weaker party language with which to name the wrong.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:199

> **Then go forth with the rest of the pilgrims. And seek Allah’s forgiveness. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.**

This verse refers to the movement of pilgrims from ʿArafah to Muzdalifah. It is said to be addressed to the Ḥums, a confederation of the Quraysh and other tribes linked by a professed devotion to the Kaʿbah and the ḥaram, the immediate environs around the Kaʿbah. ## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:200

> **When you have fulfilled your sacred rites, praise Allah as you used to praise your forefathers ˹before Islam˺, or even more passionately. There are some who say, “Our Lord! Grant us ˹Your bounties˺ in this world,” but they will have no share in the Hereafter.**

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:203

> **And remember Allah during ˹these˺ appointed days. Whoever departs swiftly on the second day is not sinful, neither are those who stay behind ˹till the third—seeking additional reward˺, so long as they are mindful ˹of their Lord˺. And be mindful of Allah, and know that to Him you will ˹all˺ be gathered.**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Days of Tashrīq Named**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between during and whoever. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:203. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:203. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:203.

**Two Days or Three: The Counting Flex of Allah**

Days numbered refers to the eleventh through the thirteenth of Dhu’l-Ḥijjah, which pilgrims spend at Mina, often called the days of tashrīq, a word of uncertain derivation and hence difficult to translate. These are the three days after the Day of Sacrifice, not including that day, and during those days one rite that the pilgrims perform is to cast stones at the columns representing Satan (al-Rāzī and al-Qurṭubī). Hastens on after two days means that one stays in Mina for only two days (until the twelfth of the month) rather than remaining three days (until the thirteenth). One then makes a farewell circumambulation around the Kaʿbah, and the ḥajj is complete.

**"Unto Him Shall You Be Gathered"**

The command to remember Allah is thought to refer to the magnification of Allah, or takbīr (Allāhu akbar, “Allah is great!”), recited while throwing pebbles at the columns and also at the times of the prayers during those days. The takbīr during the prayers is recited not only by the pilgrims, but by all Muslims during this period, from the day of the Feast of Sacrifice (the tenth of Dhu’l-Ḥijjah) until the last days of tashrīq (see above; Q). The litanies of takbīr are very similar to those recited at the end of Ramadan, the foundation of which is a variation of Allāhu akbar, Allāhu akbar, lā ilāha illa’Llāh, wa’Llāhu akbar wa li’lLāhi’l-ḥamd (“Allah is Great! Allah is Great! There is no god but Allah! Allah is Great, and praise be to Allah!”); other litanies are also sometimes added.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:205

> **And when they leave ˹you˺, they strive throughout the land to spread mischief in it and destroy crops and cattle. Allah does not like mischief.**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Turning Away and the Rushing**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between leave and land. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:205. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:205. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:205.

**The Destruction of Tillage and Offspring**

Turns away can refer to becoming angry or more generally to leaving the presence of those one is deceiving (al-Ṭabarī). According to some this verse describes a particular hypocrite who burned some people’s fields and hamstrung their donkey. The tillage refers to crops and agriculture, while the offspring refers to livestock, though some commentators say it can mean any offspring, including human ones . Corruption (fasād), literally “rot,” is used here, as in most instances in the Qur'an, to mean corruption in the broadest sense, including decadence and immorality. Such verses about the corruption of the earth are interpreted by some Muslims to also be referring to injustice in society and also to the destruction of the natural environment, as in vv. 11, 30.

**"Allah Loves Not Corruption" — The Seal of All the Corrupt**

The verse's reference to leave widens the scene beyond the immediate reward or pain. A deed in 2:205 may appear small when measured by public attention, yet its meaning changes when it is known by Allah and carried into the final account. Warning and mercy belong together in 2:205: accountability is serious because the human being is not abandoned to meaninglessness.

The standard in 2:205 remains practical because it can be applied before a dispute reaches a court or a crisis reaches its worst point. One can notice the first small departure from leave: an excuse, a concealed obligation, an unexamined desire, or a promise treated as optional. Returning at that point is easier than defending a settled habit. The warning is therefore also an opening for repair.

**The horizon beyond the immediate scene**

The relation between leave and land also protects the verse from two opposite misreadings. It should not be expanded into a claim the wording of 2:205 does not make, but neither should its brevity be used to make it weightless. Short Qur'anic statements such as 2:205 often function as hinges: they close one movement, open another, and give the next command its moral setting. The careful reader of 2:205 therefore asks what has just been established, what response is now being required, and what kind of character could respond without evasion. Those questions keep 2:205 specific while allowing its guidance to reach a new circumstance.

**A divine name that governs the meaning**

In 2:205, the distinction between public appearance and inward truth is especially relevant. A person may use the language of leave while arranging the act around another purpose. In this sense sells his soul can also mean sells his life, since nafs can also mean life in addition to soul or self. Others suggest that this verse may refer to those Companions of the Prophet who spent money on the emigration from Makkah to Madinah or who lost it by being forced to leave their wealth behind in Makkah when they migrated . Some mention that this verse was connected with ʿAlīs act of sleeping in the Prophets bed while he migrated from Makkah for Madinah during the hijrah in order to buy time for the Prophet, who was a target of the Makkans hostility .

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:208

> **O believers! Enter into Islam wholeheartedly and do not follow Satan’s footsteps. Surely he is your sworn enemy.**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Summons of the Silm — Completely**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings belief and wholeheartedly into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. Its first term in 2:208 sets the subject, while the later term shows what that subject demands, permits, or exposes. The order of 2:208 gives the reader a path through the verse: begin with what Allah names, follow the consequence, and resist the temptation to turn a living address into a slogan.

**The Possible Background and the Universal Command**

Many interpret peace (silm) here to mean submission (islām; R, Ṭ), but acknowledge that this is not the words literal meaning. Others interpret it to mean enter into obedience (Ibn Kathīr). All together renders kāffatan, an adverb that can also be read as altogether (al-Rāzī), in which case the command would mean enter into all of it, not all of you enter it. Some report that this verse was revealed in connection with a group of Jewish converts who still desired to observe the Sabbath and other specifically Jewish rituals that did not explicitly contradict Islamic teachings (e.g., by continuing to abstain from certain foods that Muslims are permitted to eat).

**"Follow Not the Footsteps of Satan" — The Second Panel**

One possible interpretation is that, if it does mean islām and is addressed to Muslims, it means that Muslims should immerse themselves more deeply and completely in islām and not omit any of its rites and commands (al-Rāzī). Others think that it is addressed to Jews and Christians (i.e., believers in Moses and Jesus), urging them to convert en masse to Islam or to embrace the totality of Islam (al-Qurṭubī). The verse can also suggest that when people enter into peace, they should do so together and not be factionalized.

Follow not the footsteps of Satan also appears in v. 168; 6:142; 24:21.

The mention of belief must be read with the restraints carried by the same revelation. Permission to resist wrongdoing does not erase the prohibition of wrongdoing. ## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:210

> **Are they waiting for Allah ˹Himself˺ to come to them in the shade of clouds, along with the angels? ˹If He did˺, then the matter would be settled ˹at once˺. And to Allah ˹all˺ matters will be returned ˹for judgment˺.**

Some say this means that [the Judgment/Command of] Allah should come, indicating that what Allah has promised or threatened will come in the clouds. For some this verse refers to the angels who come at the moment of death (see 32:11 and commentary), while others interpret it as a description of events on the Day of Resurrection (al-Rāzī), as in 25:25: And the day when the heavens are split open with clouds and the angels are sent down in a descent.
