## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:212

> **The life of this world has been made appealing to the disbelievers, and they mock the believers. Those who are mindful ˹of Allah˺ will rank above them on the Day of Judgment. And Allah provides for whoever He wills without limit.**

### Expanded Commentary

**Beautified to the Unbelieving Eye**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings life and mock into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. Its first term in 2:212 sets the subject, while the later term shows what that subject demands, permits, or exposes. The order of 2:212 gives the reader a path through the verse: begin with what Allah names, follow the consequence, and resist the temptation to turn a living address into a slogan.

**"Above Them on the Day of Resurrection"**

This verse is said to have been revealed about the Makkan idolaters, or the Madinan hypocrites, or the Jewish leaders in Madinah who belittled the Muslim community for being made up of the poor and the weak . There are various aḥādīth that describe how the believers who were belittled and mocked will receive great fame on the Day of Resurrection, while their abusers will be humiliated and punished (al-Qurṭubī). The Companion Abū Dharr related the following exchange between him and the Prophet: “‘Abū Dharr, look around and find the most exalted man you can see in the mosque.’ I looked, and there was a man sitting wearing fine clothes, and I said, ‘That one.’ Then he said, ‘Look around and find the lowliest man you can see in the mosque.’ So I looked, and there was a weak man wearing tattered clothes, and I said, ‘That one.’ Then the Prophet said, ‘By Him in Whose Hand is my soul, that latter is better in the Sight of Allah than a world full of that former’s kind.’”

**"Allah Provides for Whom He Wills, Without Reckoning"**

Allah provides for whomsoever He will without reckoning (cf. 3:37; 24:38) can mean either that Allah does not give a reckoning to anyone concerning what He does or that because of His Infinitude, He does not need to reckon or keep an account of what He gives fearing that it will dwindle . Furthermore, this giving can be both in this world and in the Hereafter (al-Rāzī). For some it could refer to the absence of a reckoning on the Day of Judgment for a select few who will enter Paradise directly, hence without reckoning (al-Rāzī). It can also allude to the incommensurability of Allahs Blessings and Punishments, as in 6:160, Whosoever brings a good deed shall have ten times the like thereof (see also 2:245, 261; 4:40; 64:17). It can moreover be seen to point to Allahs infinite Mercy and the imponderable nature of Divine Mercy and Forgiveness.

The verse describes life not as a private opinion but as a direction that changes perception and conduct. In 2:212, guidance is recognized by what it makes a person do with knowledge, power, and desire. ## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:213

> **Humanity had once been one community ˹of believers before they lost faith˺. Then Allah raised prophets as deliverers of good news and as warners, and revealed to them the Scriptures in truth to judge among people regarding their disputes. And no one disputed the Scriptures except the very people who received them after clear proofs had come to them—out of jealousy. Then Allah, by His grace, has guided the believers to the truth regarding those disputes. And Allah guides whoever He wills to the Straight Path.**

### Expanded Commentary

**The One Community — Before the rift**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between humanity and belief. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:213. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:213. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:213.

**Prophets and the Judging Book**

That mankind was one community refers, for some, to the period between Adam and Noah; al-Ṭabarī states that the exact dates are not significant to the meaning of the verse. Some believe that people were unified in disbelief and degradation, which was then corrected by Noah and later Abraham; others describe a state of unity in submission (islām) to Allah when all human beings followed one religion . Another interpretation attributes this oneness to the person of Adam, meaning that humanity began as one individual, but then became many. Such a usage of community (ummah) referring to a single person is found in 16:120: Truly Abraham was a community. Others understand one community as an allusion to the pretemporal covenant all human beings made with Allah, described in 7:172 . See also 10:19, which mentions the one community of the past; other verses (5:48; 11:118; 16:93; 42:8) mention that had Allah willed, humanity would be one community.

**Envy After Evidences**

Many understand an implied phrase in this first sentence, so that it would read Mankind was one community (and then they differed); then Allah sent the prophets (al-Rāzī). This reading would explain why Allah would then send the prophets to judge concerning that wherein they differed. Most commentators reason that the purpose of sending prophets is to correct error and sin, and they would be superfluous if human beings were united in one true religion (al-Rāzī).

**"And Allah Guides Whom He Wills Unto a Straight Path"**

Another interpretation is that the initial history of humanity was one without the need for the commands and prohibitions of religion, and the sending of prophets mentioned in this verse refers to a later time when prophecy became necessary . Al-Rāzī disapprovingly relates an opinion he attributes to Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ (d. 544 /1149), a prominent Mālikī jurist and theologian, that the first period was one in which human beings acted according to the intellect (both theoretical and practical); that is, they knew that there was a Creator, that one should be good to others, that lying and oppression are bad, that one should be just, and so forth. Pride, envy, and other vices eventually crept in and led to division, which then necessitated the sending of prophets.

**The first movement of a guided life**

But such a view would have to take into account that Adam was the first prophet according to Islamic belief, and the clear proofs would have begun with him and continued throughout history. It is useful to recall here that in discussing 3:19 (Those who were given the Book differed not until after knowledge had come to them), many commentators point out that after several generations the Jews and Christians came to differ each within their own group, and an analogy can be made with Adam and the initial one community, whose members began as one, but then came to differ among themselves over the truth.

**Belief made visible in conduct**

The Israelite prophets, for example, were sent to one people with one religion, who nevertheless differed among themselves. See 3:19c (and also 98:4c), where the apparent paradox of differences arising after the coming of revelation is discussed further. Here, as in 3:19 and 98:4, the passage suggests that it is upon receiving truth and guidance that people enter into differences over questions of belief and practice, and that there is something almost inevitable about this occurrence given the tendencies of human nature.

Here the Book is taken as the general name for all the revealed books (Sh), or it is simply a specific book, namely, the Torah, if this verse is read in connection with only the Jews and Christians (al-Ṭabarī). Clear proofs (bayyināt) refers not only to revealed books, but also to any reality that demonstrates the Truth of Allah. Some commentators variously identify that wherein they differed to be the Truth as such, the revealed Book (including their own), or Islam and/or the Prophet (Sh).

**The choice hidden inside the command**

The verse describes humanity not as a private opinion but as a direction that changes perception and conduct. In 2:213, guidance is recognized by what it makes a person do with knowledge, power, and desire. For 2:213, inward assent is linked to an observable response: the heart's claim is tested by the path it chooses when the claim becomes costly.

The standard in 2:213 remains practical because it can be applied before a dispute reaches a court or a crisis reaches its worst point. One can notice the first small departure from humanity: an excuse, a concealed obligation, an unexamined desire, or a promise treated as optional. Returning at that point is easier than defending a settled habit. The warning is therefore also an opening for repair.

**How guidance becomes discernment**

The theology and practical instruction of 2:213 therefore support one another. If Allah knows or commands belief, that knowledge or command changes how a person handles time, power, money, speech, and private desire. A doctrine that never reaches those choices has not yet been read at the level demanded by 2:213.

An ordinary example makes the moral structure of 2:213 visible without replacing the revelation. Two people may perform an outwardly similar act involving humanity; one may be protecting a right, while the other is seeking praise, escaping a duty, or taking advantage of confusion. The act's surface does not settle its value. Intention, circumstance, and the rights of others complete the judgment.

**The contrast drawn by the verse**

The surrounding verses keep the reader from isolating humanity from the rest of life. In 2:213, revelation corrects the mind but also trains habits: how a person speaks when challenged, gives when unseen, waits when angry, and returns after error. Those habits are where this verse becomes more than information about humanity. They are the place in which assent to 2:213 is either confirmed or quietly withdrawn.

The most balanced response to 2:213 is neither to make the passage vague nor to claim more than it says. Its boundaries are part of its guidance. Within them, the verse can illuminate a new situation because its underlying moral relation remains stable: humanity is joined to belief, and the person is responsible for how that relation is honoured.

The wording of 2:213 gives the reader a useful order of questions about humanity. What does the term humanity mean in ordinary Arabic, what does the surrounding sentence restrict it to, and what consequence follows when the command is obeyed or refused in 2:213? These questions prevent a commentary on 2:213 from becoming a list of slogans. They make the act of interpretation answerable to grammar, context, and the moral end of this passage at 2:213.

The commentators sometimes preserve more than one report about the setting of 2:213. Such reports should be weighed rather than treated as interchangeable decoration. An occasion can explain why a question arose, but the wording of 2:213 determines how far the guidance travels. The verse speaks first to the situation that occasioned it and then to every reader who meets the same relation between humanity and belief.

In 2:213, the distinction between public appearance and inward truth is especially relevant. A person may use the language of humanity while arranging the act around another purpose. Allah's judgment in 2:213 is not limited to the visible outline, yet the inner intention is not an excuse for ignoring the rights and forms that the revelation establishes. Sincerity completes obedience; it does not cancel it.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:214

> **Do you think you will be admitted into Paradise without being tested like those before you? They were afflicted with suffering and adversity and were so ˹violently˺ shaken that ˹even˺ the Messenger and the believers with him cried out, “When will Allah’s help come?” Indeed, Allah’s help is ˹always˺ near.**

### Expanded Commentary

**"Did You Suppose?" — The Wrong Assumption**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings think and without into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. Its first term in 2:214 sets the subject, while the later term shows what that subject demands, permits, or exposes. The order of 2:214 gives the reader a path through the verse: begin with what Allah names, follow the consequence, and resist the temptation to turn a living address into a slogan.

**Shaken Until the Prophet Himself Cried**

Similar verses mentioning the testing of faith include 3:142 and 29:2–3. According to some this verse was revealed in connection with the Battle of the Trench (al-Khandaq, 5/627), also called the Battle of the Parties (al-Aḥzāb), which is discussed in 33:9–20; others connect it to the Battle of Uḥud (3/625; Th). It is related that the burden of being exiled and living without their property was a hardship for those who had left it behind in Makkah to migrate to Madinah, and they suffered the taunts and insults of the locals and hypocrites who asked them how long they would sacrifice themselves and their property for a seemingly losing cause .

**This World Is a Test-Garland**

The Messenger is not identified, but some interpret it to mean Muhammad; others say that, because all prophets encounter severe trials, it could be a general description of all of them . Perhaps to protect the idea of the perfect faith of the prophets, some interpret the question When will Allahs Help come? to mean that, although the Messenger knew the help was coming, he was seeking to hasten it (al-Qurṭubī). Examples of prophets being troubled include 12:110: The messengers despaired and thought that they were deemed liars; 15:97: We know that thy breast is straitened; and 26:3: Perhaps thou dost torment thyself that they are not believers. Indeed, the station of prophethood in the Qur'an does not preclude the prophets human vulnerability to fear, sadness, and discouragement. See 21:83, which mentions the story of Job.

**The horizon beyond the immediate scene**

The verse's reference to think widens the scene beyond the immediate reward or pain. A deed in 2:214 may appear small when measured by public attention, yet its meaning changes when it is known by Allah and carried into the final account. Warning and mercy belong together in 2:214: accountability is serious because the human being is not abandoned to meaninglessness.

A useful way to test the verse is to ask what would change if think were taken seriously when no audience was present. The answer cannot be only a feeling, because 2:214 connects inward recognition with a discernible choice. Nor can it be only an outward display, because the choice in 2:214 loses its Qur'anic meaning when it is made for reputation rather than for Allah. The passage holds intention and action together in 2:214.

**A divine name that governs the meaning**

The relation between think and without also protects the verse from two opposite misreadings. It should not be expanded into a claim the wording of 2:214 does not make, but neither should its brevity be used to make it weightless. Short Qur'anic statements such as 2:214 often function as hinges: they close one movement, open another, and give the next command its moral setting. The careful reader of 2:214 therefore asks what has just been established, what response is now being required, and what kind of character could respond without evasion. Those questions keep 2:214 specific while allowing its guidance to reach a new circumstance.

An ordinary example makes the moral structure of 2:214 visible without replacing the revelation. Two people may perform an outwardly similar act involving think; one may be protecting a right, while the other is seeking praise, escaping a duty, or taking advantage of confusion. The act's surface does not settle its value. Intention, circumstance, and the rights of others complete the judgment.

Those habits are where this verse becomes more than information about think. They are the place in which assent to 2:214 is either confirmed or quietly withdrawn.

Within them, the verse can illuminate a new situation because its underlying moral relation remains stable: think is joined to without, and the person is responsible for how that relation is honoured.

The wording of 2:214 gives the reader a useful order of questions about think. What does the term think mean in ordinary Arabic, what does the surrounding sentence restrict it to, and what consequence follows when the command is obeyed or refused in 2:214? These questions prevent a commentary on 2:214 from becoming a list of slogans. They make the act of interpretation answerable to grammar, context, and the moral end of this passage at 2:214.

The commentators sometimes preserve more than one report about the setting of 2:214. Such reports should be weighed rather than treated as interchangeable decoration. An occasion can explain why a question arose, but the wording of 2:214 determines how far the guidance travels. The verse speaks first to the situation that occasioned it and then to every reader who meets the same relation between think and without.

**Why the promise or threat is just**

In 2:214, the distinction between public appearance and inward truth is especially relevant. A person may use the language of think while arranging the act around another purpose. Allah's judgment in 2:214 is not limited to the visible outline, yet the inner intention is not an excuse for ignoring the rights and forms that the revelation establishes. Sincerity completes obedience; it does not cancel it.

One can see the social wisdom of 2:214 in a small everyday case. When people share responsibility for think, uncertainty about the duty tends to fall on the person with less power or less information. A clear moral rule changes that balance. In 2:214, it tells the stronger party what must not be taken, and gives the weaker party language with which to name the wrong.

**The Hereafter in the argument**

In 2:214, the verse also sits within the Qur'an's larger refusal to separate worship from truthfulness. Prayer, remembrance, generosity, patience, and justice are different acts in 2:214, but they are trained by the same capacity to stand before Allah without constructing a false account. The statement in 2:214 strengthens that capacity by making one particular choice visible.

A reader who finds the command in 2:214 difficult should distinguish difficulty from impossibility. For 2:214, difficulty may be the place where desire, habit, or social pressure is being corrected; impossibility is a separate legal and moral question. The passage does not praise needless hardship, but it does not permit comfort to redefine think until the demand disappears.

The final emphasis of 2:214 returns to responsibility. No explanation of think is complete if it leaves the reader with information about earlier communities but no question about present conduct. The verse 2:214 asks what can be repaired now: a promise kept, a right restored, a motive purified, or a harmful practice abandoned. That is where knowledge becomes guidance.

The choice of the word think in 2:214 also matters. It leaves room for the full context of 2:214 instead of allowing one translation gloss to carry every shade of meaning. Classical Arabic often places a broad word inside a narrow scene; in 2:214, the surrounding clauses determine whether the emphasis falls on an act, an intention, a condition, or a consequence. Here the reader should let the sentence do that work.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:216

> **Fighting has been made obligatory upon you ˹believers˺, though you dislike it. Perhaps you dislike something which is good for you and like something which is bad for you. Allah knows and you do not know.**

### Expanded Commentary

**Kutiba — Written Over You**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings fighting and belief into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. Its first term in 2:216 sets the subject, while the later term shows what that subject demands, permits, or exposes. The order of 2:216 gives the reader a path through the verse: begin with what Allah names, follow the consequence, and resist the temptation to turn a living address into a slogan.

**The Asymmetry of Hate and Good**

On the general topic of warfare, see the essay “Conquest and Conversion, War and Peace in the Qur'an.” Some early commentators argued that fighting has been prescribed for you referred only to the Companions of the Prophet and that fighting alongside him was an individual responsibility for each of them, but later became a communal responsibility; that is, after Islam’s precarious beginnings in Makkah, where warfare was forbidden, and its initial phase in Madinah, to which Muslims had migrated to survive and where they continued to fight to ensure their survival as a religious community, Islam itself was no longer in danger of being eradicated, and the universal prescription was lifted .

**Of Battle-Fields and All Fields**

Some scholars of the early generations, such as Saʿīd ibn al-Muṣayyab (d. 94/713), deemed fighting in the way of Allah to be an everlasting obligation upon Muslims, while others, such as Sufyān al-Thawrī (d. 161/778), said it was a voluntary action (al-Qurṭubī). When challenged as to why he would not participate in fighting during the First Civil War, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar (d. 74/693), the son of the second Caliph, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, told his interlocutors, “We did that during the time of the Prophet, when Islam was small, when a man would be tried in his religion, and they would either kill him or torture him.

But then Islam became great, and there was no trial (fitnah).” Al-Rāzī notes that the “unanimous consensus,” or ijmāʿ, is that when fighting is called for, it is a communal responsibility, except if Muslim lands are invaded, in which case it becomes an individual responsibility.

**The Men of Knowledge on Their Feet**

The mention of fighting must be read with the restraints carried by the same revelation. Permission to resist wrongdoing does not erase the prohibition of wrongdoing. The verse therefore asks the community to hold two truths together: injustice may have to be confronted, and the means used in confronting it remain subject to Allah's judgment.

The answer cannot be only a feeling, because 2:216 connects inward recognition with a discernible choice. Nor can it be only an outward display, because the choice in 2:216 loses its Qur'anic meaning when it is made for reputation rather than for Allah. The passage holds intention and action together in 2:216.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:217

> **They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about fighting in the sacred months. Say, “Fighting during these months is a great sin. But hindering ˹others˺ from the Path of Allah, rejecting Him, and expelling the worshippers from the Sacred Mosque is ˹a˺ greater ˹sin˺ in the sight of Allah. For persecution is far worse than killing. And they will not stop fighting you until they turn you away from your faith—if they can. And whoever among you renounces their own faith and dies a disbeliever, their deeds will become void in this life and in the Hereafter. It is they who will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever.”**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Question at Madinah's Gate**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between prophet and months. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:217. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:217. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:217.

**Grave — but Graver**

It is said that this verse was revealed in connection with a Companion, ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Jaḥsh, who led a scouting mission against the Quraysh a year and a half after the migration from Makkah to Madinah, but before the Battle of Badr in 2/624. At an oasis between Ṭāʾif and Makkah, they killed a certain ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥaḍramī, took two prisoners, and returned with the spoils. These Companions claimed to have thought it was the last day of Jumādāl-Ākhirah, not knowing that it was actually the first of Rajab, one of the sacred months in Arabia, since the calendar was dependent upon sighting the crescent moon (see 2:189c).

**"They Will Not Cease"**

When they returned to Madinah, the Prophet refused the portion of the spoils they had brought him and told them, I did not command you to fight during the sacred months. The Quraysh condemned the breach and accused the Prophet of transgressing the accepted norm of observing the sacred months and spilling blood when it was forbidden. Eventually the matter was settled through a prisoner exchange and the payment of wergild for ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥaḍramī. The verse reminds all concerned that the current state of affairs was a result of Qurayshī transgressions, and that their enmity was unremitting and included not only expelling the Muslims, but preventing them from making pilgrimage and torturing them in order to make them renounce their religion.

**The Apostatized Deeds Voided**

Any who renounce their religion can reenter Islam, although in such a case some jurists believe that certain obligations, notably the ḥajj, must be performed again. The verb for renounce (irtaddā) is often translated apostasy, but this can be a misleading translation in some cases. On the matter of choosing religion the Qur'an says elsewhere, And say, It is the truth from your Lord! So whosoever will, let him believe, and whosoever will, let him disbelieve (18:29); There is no coercion in religion. Sound judgment has become clear from error (2:256). It also commands the Prophet to say to the disbelievers, Unto you your religion, and unto me my religion (109:6); and Allah tells the Prophet and his followers, So leave Me with those who deny this discourse (68:44).

**A journey ordered toward Allah**

Many classical and contemporary scholars, although not a majority, have declared that the mere changing of one’s religion is no cause for punishment by the community, especially in light of the Qur'anic passages quoted above. Rather, such a move must amount to a seditious or destabilizing act in a political sense. This was, in their view, why the first Caliph, Abū Bakr, took up arms against the tribes who left the Muslim community in the so-called riddah wars, and why the Prophet left many people alone who left the religion.

**The sacred limit in the command**

It would explain, for example, why some early religious authorities, such as Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, as well as Abū Ḥanīfah and Sufyān al-Thawrī, did not allow the execution of women who renounced Islam (al-Qurṭubī). This would seem to reflect a political and social cause rather than an intrinsically theological one, a cause that would be contingent upon external circumstances. During certain periods of the Prophet’s life, changing religion amounted to changing sides in the political sense and thus to high treason, and hypocrites were among the deadliest of enemies of the early community, often collaborating with the Qurayshī idolaters and those tribes who were allied with them.

The treatment of prophet joins movement through a place or ritual with movement of the heart. Sacred practice has boundaries precisely because it is not ordinary travel or ordinary habit. The limits teach the pilgrim to receive meaning rather than manufacture it, while the concessions show that obedience is addressed to human beings with real capacities and pressures.

**Ritual detail and spiritual purpose**

The standard in 2:217 remains practical because it can be applied before a dispute reaches a court or a crisis reaches its worst point. One can notice the first small departure from prophet: an excuse, a concealed obligation, an unexamined desire, or a promise treated as optional. Returning at that point is easier than defending a settled habit. The warning is therefore also an opening for repair.

The wording of 2:217 gives the reader a useful order of questions about prophet. What does the term prophet mean in ordinary Arabic, what does the surrounding sentence restrict it to, and what consequence follows when the command is obeyed or refused in 2:217? ## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:218

> **Surely those who have believed, emigrated, and struggled in the Way of Allah—they can hope for Allah’s mercy. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Comfort Clause After the Trial Clause**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings believed and hope into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. Its first term in 2:218 sets the subject, while the later term shows what that subject demands, permits, or exposes. The order of 2:218 gives the reader a path through the verse: begin with what Allah names, follow the consequence, and resist the temptation to turn a living address into a slogan.

When v. 217 was revealed, it is said that ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Jaḥsh and those with him despaired and doubted that they would receive merit for their actions, even though they were absolved of having committed a crime, and this verse was a comfort and promise to them (al-Rāzī).

**"It Is They Who Hope" — The Theology of Hope**

The notion of hope reflects the idea that no reward is certain, that everything is in Allahs Hands, and that one might still die a disbeliever, but it may also be understood as a descriptive statement, indicating that believers should approach Allah with an attitude of hope and fear (al-Rāzī). This idea of hope is also connected by some with 2:46 (Who reckon that they shall meet their Lord and that they shall return unto Him) in that the hoping and reckoning are descriptions of both what believers do and what they are called to do.

The verse's reference to believed widens the scene beyond the immediate reward or pain. A deed in 2:218 may appear small when measured by public attention, yet its meaning changes when it is known by Allah and carried into the final account. Warning and mercy belong together in 2:218: accountability is serious because the human being is not abandoned to meaninglessness.

**Believer, Emigrant, Warrior**

A useful way to test the verse is to ask what would change if believed were taken seriously when no audience was present. The answer cannot be only a feeling, because 2:218 connects inward recognition with a discernible choice. Nor can it be only an outward display, because the choice in 2:218 loses its Qur'anic meaning when it is made for reputation rather than for Allah. The passage holds intention and action together in 2:218.

**The horizon beyond the immediate scene**

The relation between believed and hope also protects the verse from two opposite misreadings. It should not be expanded into a claim the wording of 2:218 does not make, but neither should its brevity be used to make it weightless. Short Qur'anic statements such as 2:218 often function as hinges: they close one movement, open another, and give the next command its moral setting. The careful reader of 2:218 therefore asks what has just been established, what response is now being required, and what kind of character could respond without evasion. Those questions keep 2:218 specific while allowing its guidance to reach a new circumstance.

One can see the social wisdom of 2:218 in a small everyday case. In 2:218, it tells the stronger party what must not be taken, and gives the weaker party language with which to name the wrong.

Prayer, remembrance, generosity, patience, and justice are different acts in 2:218, but they are trained by the same capacity to stand before Allah without constructing a false account. The statement in 2:218 strengthens that capacity by making one particular choice visible.

**The deed before its final account**

A reader who finds the command in 2:218 difficult should distinguish difficulty from impossibility. For 2:218, difficulty may be the place where desire, habit, or social pressure is being corrected; impossibility is a separate legal and moral question. The passage does not praise needless hardship, but it does not permit comfort to redefine believed until the demand disappears.

The final emphasis of 2:218 returns to responsibility. No explanation of believed is complete if it leaves the reader with information about earlier communities but no question about present conduct. The verse 2:218 asks what can be repaired now: a promise kept, a right restored, a motive purified, or a harmful practice abandoned. That is where knowledge becomes guidance.

**Why the promise or threat is just**

The choice of the word believed in 2:218 also matters. It leaves room for the full context of 2:218 instead of allowing one translation gloss to carry every shade of meaning. Classical Arabic often places a broad word inside a narrow scene; in 2:218, the surrounding clauses determine whether the emphasis falls on an act, an intention, a condition, or a consequence. Here the reader should let the sentence do that work.

The exegetical tradition approaches believed from more than one angle, but its differences are more useful when their shared question is made visible. The commentators ask what the wording of 2:218 includes, what it excludes, and how it fits with the other passages of the Qur'an. A responsible reading can preserve those alternatives in 2:218 without pretending that every possibility has equal strength.

There is also a distinction between understanding believed and using it as a label for other people. The first task belongs to learning; the second requires evidence, fairness, and awareness of one's own motives in 2:218. The verse 2:218 addresses the reader before it supplies material for judging a neighbour. Its warning becomes safer and more productive when self-examination comes first.

The theology and practical instruction of 2:218 therefore support one another. If Allah knows or commands hope, that knowledge or command changes how a person handles time, power, money, speech, and private desire. A doctrine that never reaches those choices has not yet been read at the level demanded by 2:218.

Two people may perform an outwardly similar act involving believed; one may be protecting a right, while the other is seeking praise, escaping a duty, or taking advantage of confusion. The surrounding verses keep the reader from isolating believed from the rest of life. In 2:218, revelation corrects the mind but also trains habits: how a person speaks when challenged, gives when unseen, waits when angry, and returns after error. Those habits are where this verse becomes more than information about believed. They are the place in which assent to 2:218 is either confirmed or quietly withdrawn.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:219

> **They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about intoxicants and gambling. Say, “There is great evil in both, as well as some benefit for people—but the evil outweighs the benefit.” They ˹also˺ ask you what they should donate. Say, “Whatever you can spare.” This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to you ˹believers˺, so perhaps you may reflect**

### Expanded Commentary

**Wine and Gambling — the First Verdict**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between prophet and great. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:219. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:219. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:219.

**Benefit and Sin Presently Weighed**

For a discussion of the proscription of drinking wine, see 4:43c. Gambling renders maysir, which literally denotes one type of gambling; gambling more generally is known as qimār. In maysir people draw arrows over meat, akin to drawing straws; the loser has to pay for the meat without getting any and is chided and ribbed, while the winners give their portions to the poor as a demonstration of generosity (al-Zamakhsharī). In this connection many of the commentators discuss various kinds of play (laʿb) and debate their legitimacy. In Islamic Law generally gambling in the form of wagering is forbidden, while playing games, such as chess and backgammon, as an idle pastime is frowned upon by many as a spiritual distraction, usually without being forbidden outright. Both games in fact came to the West from the Islamic world, and not being forbidden in the technical legal sense, both are popular among Muslims, even many devout ones.

**"Spend What Can Be Spared"**

Regarding the benefits for mankind in wine, al-Qurṭubī mentions that it helps with digestion, makes a miserly person magnanimous, gives boldness to the timid, gives color to the face, helps one to have sex, and makes one feel good for a short time. (Although this verse mentions specifically wine, Islamic Law understands this ruling to apply to all alcoholic drinks.) As for the benefits of gambling, he mentions that one can acquire wealth without effort and that the poor can benefit, since it was customary for the winners to distribute the meat of the maysir.

**The horizon beyond the immediate scene**

As for their harm, intoxication leads to loss of one’s rational faculties, quarreling, violence, promiscuity, impaired judgment, and forgetting the remembrance of Allah. In later judicial philosophy, the ruling on intoxication played a major part in identifying “protection of the intelligence” as one of the essential objectives of the Law (maqāsid al-Sharīʿah). Similarly, gambling creates enmity and despair (al-Rāzī), produces ill-gotten gains, and is thus a diversion from the healthy and wholesome pursuit of profit and gain. The risk associated with gambling factors into Islamic financial theory, in that certain kinds of transactions are invalid because they entail excessive risk, and this risk is related to the prohibition against ribā (usually but imperfectly translated “usury”), which is discussed by some Islamic financial theorists as carrying a severe form of risk.

**A divine name that governs the meaning**

Ribā is discussed in vv. 275–80.

On the question of spending in charity, what can be spared renders al-ʿafw, which means what is easy or what is done without difficulty (al-Rāzī) and in other contexts means pardon or forgiveness. There is disagreement over whether this refers to voluntary giving or to a required duty. Among those who uphold the former view are those who believe that this directive was abrogated by the institution of the alms (zakāh); others point out that there is no contradiction between the existence of the institution of the zakāh and a command to give charity (al-Qurṭubī).

**Mercy and warning held together**

The commentators note here that this means that one should be neither miserly nor improvident in matters of charity and that one should never impoverish oneself as a result of charitable giving. This verse is seen as expanding upon the question of giving in v. 215, which describes the recipients of charity, by further describing how much one should give (al-Qurṭubī). The extent of proper charitable giving is also discussed in 17:29: And let not thine hand be shackled to thy neck; nor let it be entirely open.

Warning and mercy belong together in 2:219: accountability is serious because the human being is not abandoned to meaninglessness.

**The deed before its final account**

One can notice the first small departure from prophet: an excuse, a concealed obligation, an unexamined desire, or a promise treated as optional. Returning at that point is easier than defending a settled habit. The warning is therefore also an opening for repair.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:220

> **upon this world and the Hereafter. And they ask you concerning orphans. Say, “Improving their condition is best. And if you partner with them, they are bonded with you ˹in faith˺. And Allah knows who intends harm and who intends good. Had Allah willed, He could have made it difficult for you. Surely Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.”**

### Expanded Commentary

**This World and the Hereafter — the Two Balances**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings upon and concerning into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. Its first term in 2:220 sets the subject, while the later term shows what that subject demands, permits, or exposes. The order of 2:220 gives the reader a path through the verse: begin with what Allah names, follow the consequence, and resist the temptation to turn a living address into a slogan.

The Qur'anic theme of the Hereafter’s superiority over this world is connected here with wine and gambling; one should reflect upon the transitory goods and lasting evils engendered by them and judge them in relation to the fleeting world and the abiding Hereafter . It is possible to read the end of the previous verse and the start of this one as “Thus does Allah make clear, in this world and the Hereafter, the signs.”

**"They Ask You About Orphans" — The Scrupulous Custodians**

Other verses that mention taking care of orphans property include 4:10 and 6:152. It is related that Muslims were scrupulous in keeping the property of orphans separate and would eat and drink from completely separate sources so as not to consume what belonged to the orphans; when this became difficult for the custodians, they would therefore sometimes stay aloof from the orphans in their care, so that at times the property of the orphans would spoil or become ruined (al-Ṭabarī). It is useful to remember that an orphans inheritance would have often been in the form of fruit trees and livestock, and it is precisely through using them (e.g., by picking the fruit and riding and breeding the livestock) that their value and usefulness would have been maintained until the orphan could grow up and take possession of them.

**"Had Allah Willed, He Would Have Put You to Hardship"**

Another opinion sees this verse as addressing not a prior Muslim practice but a prevailing Arab custom of staying separate from orphans, not eating together with them or riding on the mounts used by them, as it was considered inauspicious or an ill omen to be guilty of stealing from an orphan even in pre-Islamic Arabia (al-Qurṭubī).

In the Qur'an the opposite of corruption (ifsād or fasād) is often an act of setting matters aright, or iṣlāḥ, related by root to ṣulḥ, meaning peacemaking or reconciliation, and ṣāliḥ or righteous. Intermingling means drinking the same drink, eating the same food, riding the same mounts, being served by the same servants, and so on (al-Ṭabarī). The message in this verse is to deal equitably with the orphans property, which is legally inviolable, but whose inviolability is not meant to harm the orphan. Hence reasonable latitude is given for the just use of an orphans property, avoiding a pedantic and counterproductive separation between the custodians property and that of the orphan .

**The first movement of a guided life**

They are your brothers is not conditional upon the preceding phrase, if you intermingle with them; rather, it is a clarification that intermingling with their property in a just fashion carries no blame . That Allah could have put you to hardship highlights the inherent difficulties associated with maintaining the property of orphans, and that to balance the responsibility of disposing of that property with observing its intrinsic inviolability is often a matter of judgment. This judgment is itself overseen by Allah, who knows the one who works corruption from one who sets aright.

For a longer treatment on other aspects of the law pertaining to orphans, see commentary on 4:2–10.

**Belief made visible in conduct**

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:221

> **Do not marry polytheistic women until they believe; for a believing slave-woman is better than a free polytheist, even though she may look pleasant to you. And do not marry your women to polytheistic men until they believe, for a believing slave-man is better than a free polytheist, even though he may look pleasant to you. They invite ˹you˺ to the Fire while Allah invites ˹you˺ to Paradise and forgiveness by His grace. He makes His revelations clear to the people so perhaps they will be mindful.**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Matrimonial Borderline**

Some commentators believe that 5:5 partially abrogated the ruling in this present verse so as to allow marriage between Muslim men and women from among the People of the Book (al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī), but the question arises only if the People of the Book were to be taken as a class of idolaters.

In either case, the final legal ruling allows marriage with Jews and Christians, though some jurists have also included in this category marriage with Zoroastrians and, in India, with Hindus. A minority opinion held that in fact this verse abrogates 5:5 and hence no marriage with a non-Muslim is allowed. And marry none to the idolaters is most often, but not always, understood as a command to not give any Muslim woman in marriage to a non-Muslim man.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:222

> **They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about menstruation. Say, “Beware of its harm! So keep away, and do not have intercourse with your wives during their monthly cycles until they are purified. When they purify themselves, then you may approach them in the manner specified by Allah. Surely Allah loves those who always turn to Him in repentance and those who purify themselves.”**

### Expanded Commentary

**"They Ask You About the Monthly Course"**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings prophet and harm into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. Its first term in 2:222 sets the subject, while the later term shows what that subject demands, permits, or exposes. The order of 2:222 gives the reader a path through the verse: begin with what Allah names, follow the consequence, and resist the temptation to turn a living address into a slogan.

This verse is understood to prohibit vaginal intercourse during menstruation without prohibiting other contact. The commentators mention that before Islam menstruating women would not sleep in the same bed or eat from the same plate as others, Arab customs that may have been influenced by Jewish (Leviticus 15:19–33) or Zoroastrian (Avesta, Vendidad 16) prescriptions and proscriptions, which mandated a relatively high level of separation for menstruating women and the ritual purification of objects that they had touched (al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī).

**Purified — and Allah's Own Command**

For some the hurt (adha) refers to the discomfort it causes women (al-Qurṭubī); many others understand it to mean “uncleanness” specifically relating to the menstrual blood (al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī); still others simply gloss the hurt as a reference to the blood without attaching the notion of uncleanness to it.

Some interpret until they are purified to mean the cessation of the flow of menstrual blood. Most schools of law understand this verse to mean that a woman, at the end of her period, should perform the major ablution, or ghusl, which entails a washing of the entire body ritually with water, before having intercourse. Under certain circumstances the Ḥanafī school allows intercourse after the cessation of blood, but before the major ablution, or ghusl. There is no formal expiation or punishment for having intercourse during menstruation, although some monetary payment to the poor such as a dīnār or half a dīnār is sometimes mentioned in this connection (al-Qurṭubī). It is not considered a major act of disobedience, although pious Muslims refrain from it.

**Loves the Repenters, Loves the Purified**

Other actions generally prohibited for menstruating women include the canonical prayer (ṣalāh), fasting, circumambulation of the Kaʿbah during the ḥajj or ʿumrah, reciting the Qur'an aloud, and physically touching the Qur'an. Also restricted are remaining inside the mosque (rather than passing through) and retreat in the mosque (iʿtikāf), although these seem to have more to do with blood staining the mosque than any other concern. In this vein, the Prophet asked his wife to bring him a mat from the mosque. She said, “I am menstruating.” And he said, “Your menses are not in your hands.”

**The horizon beyond the immediate scene**

Go in unto them in the way Allah has commanded you refers to resuming vaginal intercourse, which is forbidden during menses. Jurists are unanimous in forbidding intercourse during menstruation as well as anal sex at any time, but in general have allowed other types of physical affection and fondling during menstruation. In many aḥādīth it is reported that the Prophet would not stay aloof from his wives during their periods, but would show them physical affection such as kissing and fondling, short of engaging in intercourse. Other than ensuring that an item be cleaned if menstrual blood comes in contact with it, Islamic teaching does not deem the touch of a menstruating woman to be unclean or to render anything unclean, although she should not touch the Qur'an.

**A divine name that governs the meaning**

The verse's reference to prophet widens the scene beyond the immediate reward or pain. A deed in 2:222 may appear small when measured by public attention, yet its meaning changes when it is known by Allah and carried into the final account. Warning and mercy belong together in 2:222: accountability is serious because the human being is not abandoned to meaninglessness.

A useful way to test the verse is to ask what would change if prophet were taken seriously when no audience was present. The answer cannot be only a feeling, because 2:222 connects inward recognition with a discernible choice. Nor can it be only an outward display, because the choice in 2:222 loses its Qur'anic meaning when it is made for reputation rather than for Allah. The passage holds intention and action together in 2:222.

**Mercy and warning held together**

The relation between prophet and harm also protects the verse from two opposite misreadings. It should not be expanded into a claim the wording of 2:222 does not make, but neither should its brevity be used to make it weightless. Short Qur'anic statements such as 2:222 often function as hinges: they close one movement, open another, and give the next command its moral setting. The careful reader of 2:222 therefore asks what has just been established, what response is now being required, and what kind of character could respond without evasion. Those questions keep 2:222 specific while allowing its guidance to reach a new circumstance.

A reader who finds the command in 2:222 difficult should distinguish difficulty from impossibility. For 2:222, difficulty may be the place where desire, habit, or social pressure is being corrected; impossibility is a separate legal and moral question. The passage does not praise needless hardship, but it does not permit comfort to redefine prophet until the demand disappears.

**The deed before its final account**

The final emphasis of 2:222 returns to responsibility. No explanation of prophet is complete if it leaves the reader with information about earlier communities but no question about present conduct. The verse 2:222 asks what can be repaired now: a promise kept, a right restored, a motive purified, or a harmful practice abandoned. That is where knowledge becomes guidance.

The choice of the word prophet in 2:222 also matters. It leaves room for the full context of 2:222 instead of allowing one translation gloss to carry every shade of meaning. Classical Arabic often places a broad word inside a narrow scene; in 2:222, the surrounding clauses determine whether the emphasis falls on an act, an intention, a condition, or a consequence. Here the reader should let the sentence do that work.

**Why the promise or threat is just**

The exegetical tradition approaches prophet from more than one angle, but its differences are more useful when their shared question is made visible. The commentators ask what the wording of 2:222 includes, what it excludes, and how it fits with the other passages of the Qur'an. A responsible reading can preserve those alternatives in 2:222 without pretending that every possibility has equal strength.

There is also a distinction between understanding prophet and using it as a label for other people. The first task belongs to learning; the second requires evidence, fairness, and awareness of one's own motives in 2:222. The verse 2:222 addresses the reader before it supplies material for judging a neighbour. Its warning becomes safer and more productive when self-examination comes first.

**The Hereafter in the argument**

The theology and practical instruction of 2:222 therefore support one another. If Allah knows or commands harm, that knowledge or command changes how a person handles time, power, money, speech, and private desire. A doctrine that never reaches those choices has not yet been read at the level demanded by 2:222.

An ordinary example makes the moral structure of 2:222 visible without replacing the revelation. Two people may perform an outwardly similar act involving prophet; one may be protecting a right, while the other is seeking praise, escaping a duty, or taking advantage of confusion. The act's surface does not settle its value. Intention, circumstance, and the rights of others complete the judgment.

The surrounding verses keep the reader from isolating prophet from the rest of life. In 2:222, revelation corrects the mind but also trains habits: how a person speaks when challenged, gives when unseen, waits when angry, and returns after error. Those habits are where this verse becomes more than information about prophet. They are the place in which assent to 2:222 is either confirmed or quietly withdrawn.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:223

> **Your wives are like farmland for you, so approach them ˹consensually˺ as you please. And send forth something good for yourselves. Be mindful of Allah, and know that you will meet Him. And give good news to the believers.**

### Expanded Commentary

**A Tilth of Allah**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between wives and approach. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:223. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:223. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:223.

This verse is seen by some as giving permission for any kind of vaginal intercourse, the symbolism of tilth referring to procreation . In a clash of prevailing customs, some Companions abhorred intercourse in positions where the man was behind the woman, while others practiced intercourse in all positions. In some cases, Emigrants from Makkah married Helpers, who were natives of Madinah, and the latter refused certain positions for intercourse. In some accounts, certain Companions came to the Prophet to inquire about these matters, which served as the occasion for the revelation of this verse.

**As You Will — the Freedom of the Law**

In some narrations, the Prophet said of this verse, A single orifice (al-Ṭabarī), referring to vaginal intercourse. Most commentators note that the grammar of the verse in Arabic denotes direction and place and devote their primary attention in commenting on this verse to in what part of the body one has intercourse and coming from what direction; they are generally emphatic that this verse does not refer to when or how or at whose behest intercourse takes place (R, Ṭ, Ṭs). Send forth means to perform good deeds that will benefit one in the Hereafter; see 5:80–81c; 82:5c; 75:13c.

The verse describes wives not as a private opinion but as a direction that changes perception and conduct. In 2:223, guidance is recognized by what it makes a person do with knowledge, power, and desire. ## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:226

> **Those who swear not to have intercourse with their wives must wait for four months. If they change their mind, then Allah is certainly AllForgiving, Most Merciful.**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Oath That Imprisons a Woman**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings swear and wait into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. Its first term in 2:226 sets the subject, while the later term shows what that subject demands, permits, or exposes. The order of 2:226 gives the reader a path through the verse: begin with what Allah names, follow the consequence, and resist the temptation to turn a living address into a slogan.

**The Clock's Expiry Forces a Choice**

These verses address the practice of a man staying away from his wife but not divorcing her, leaving her without the sexual benefits of marriage and without the freedom to marry another, which in pre-Islamic times could last years . In this context to forswear means to make an oath that one would not have sexual relations with one’s wife. To forswear in this sense is not the same as divorce, and the period of four months sets an upper limit on this abstention within marriage. Specifically, it is understood to draw a line beyond which the abstention is taken as an intent to cause harm to the wife (al-Rāzī).

**A Mercy for the One Wielded Against**

If they return means that they resume intercourse; the return is still valid if one intends to return to one’s wife, but is hindered for some reason, as the intent to cause harm no longer exists, while for some it simply means that one bear witness that he has returned (al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī). Many understand Allah is Forgiving, Merciful in this context to indicate that no expiation is necessary if they return (al-Ṭabarī), though others believe some form of expiation, such as feeding the poor, is necessary, as returning to one’s wife would then constitute going back on the oath of staying away from her (al-Ṭabarī).

**The horizon beyond the immediate scene**

Some say that these stipulations only apply when the oath is made in anger with the intent to cause harm, and that when someone swears not to have sexual relations for some other reason, for example, with the intention of protecting the well-being of a nursing child, the ruling of this verse does not apply . Others say that the forswearing mentioned here can refer to any oath that keeps one from having sexual relations with one’s wife, while others say that the forswearing need not even pertain to sexual relations, but may pertain to any matter where the intent is to cause harm to the wife, such as not speaking to her or touching her (al-Ṭabarī). Perhaps the most serious point of disagreement is whether, upon the completion of the four months, divorce is effected automatically in the eyes of the Law or whether other steps must be taken. Some maintain that after the period of four months, divorce could be imposed by a judge at the request of the wife (al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī).

**A divine name that governs the meaning**

The verse's reference to swear widens the scene beyond the immediate reward or pain. A deed in 2:226 may appear small when measured by public attention, yet its meaning changes when it is known by Allah and carried into the final account. Warning and mercy belong together in 2:226: accountability is serious because the human being is not abandoned to meaninglessness.

A useful way to test the verse is to ask what would change if swear were taken seriously when no audience was present. The answer cannot be only a feeling, because 2:226 connects inward recognition with a discernible choice. Nor can it be only an outward display, because the choice in 2:226 loses its Qur'anic meaning when it is made for reputation rather than for Allah. The passage holds intention and action together in 2:226.

**Mercy and warning held together**

The relation between swear and wait also protects the verse from two opposite misreadings. It should not be expanded into a claim the wording of 2:226 does not make, but neither should its brevity be used to make it weightless. Short Qur'anic statements such as 2:226 often function as hinges: they close one movement, open another, and give the next command its moral setting. The careful reader of 2:226 therefore asks what has just been established, what response is now being required, and what kind of character could respond without evasion. Those questions keep 2:226 specific while allowing its guidance to reach a new circumstance.

There is also a distinction between understanding swear and using it as a label for other people. The first task belongs to learning; the second requires evidence, fairness, and awareness of one's own motives in 2:226. The verse 2:226 addresses the reader before it supplies material for judging a neighbour. Its warning becomes safer and more productive when self-examination comes first.

**The deed before its final account**

The theology and practical instruction of 2:226 therefore support one another. If Allah knows or commands wait, that knowledge or command changes how a person handles time, power, money, speech, and private desire. A doctrine that never reaches those choices has not yet been read at the level demanded by 2:226.

An ordinary example makes the moral structure of 2:226 visible without replacing the revelation. Two people may perform an outwardly similar act involving swear; one may be protecting a right, while the other is seeking praise, escaping a duty, or taking advantage of confusion. The act's surface does not settle its value. Intention, circumstance, and the rights of others complete the judgment.

**Why the promise or threat is just**

The surrounding verses keep the reader from isolating swear from the rest of life. In 2:226, revelation corrects the mind but also trains habits: how a person speaks when challenged, gives when unseen, waits when angry, and returns after error. Those habits are where this verse becomes more than information about swear. They are the place in which assent to 2:226 is either confirmed or quietly withdrawn.

The most balanced response to 2:226 is neither to make the passage vague nor to claim more than it says. Its boundaries are part of its guidance. Within them, the verse can illuminate a new situation because its underlying moral relation remains stable: swear is joined to wait, and the person is responsible for how that relation is honoured.

**The Hereafter in the argument**

The wording of 2:226 gives the reader a useful order of questions about swear. What does the term swear mean in ordinary Arabic, what does the surrounding sentence restrict it to, and what consequence follows when the command is obeyed or refused in 2:226? These questions prevent a commentary on 2:226 from becoming a list of slogans. They make the act of interpretation answerable to grammar, context, and the moral end of this passage at 2:226.

The commentators sometimes preserve more than one report about the setting of 2:226. Such reports should be weighed rather than treated as interchangeable decoration. An occasion can explain why a question arose, but the wording of 2:226 determines how far the guidance travels. The verse speaks first to the situation that occasioned it and then to every reader who meets the same relation between swear and wait.

In 2:226, the distinction between public appearance and inward truth is especially relevant. A person may use the language of swear while arranging the act around another purpose. Allah's judgment in 2:226 is not limited to the visible outline, yet the inner intention is not an excuse for ignoring the rights and forms that the revelation establishes. Sincerity completes obedience; it does not cancel it.

One can see the social wisdom of 2:226 in a small everyday case. When people share responsibility for swear, uncertainty about the duty tends to fall on the person with less power or less information. A clear moral rule changes that balance. In 2:226, it tells the stronger party what must not be taken, and gives the weaker party language with which to name the wrong.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:228

> **Divorced women must wait three monthly cycles ˹before they can remarry˺. It is not lawful for them to conceal what Allah has created in their wombs, if they ˹truly˺ believe in Allah and the Last Day. And their husbands reserve the right to take them back within that period if they desire reconciliation. Women have rights similar to those of men equitably, although men have a degree ˹of responsibility˺ above them. And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Waiting Period — ʿIddah**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings divorced and three into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. Its first term in 2:228 sets the subject, while the later term shows what that subject demands, permits, or exposes. The order of 2:228 gives the reader a path through the verse: begin with what Allah names, follow the consequence, and resist the temptation to turn a living address into a slogan.

**No Conceiving by Concealment**

In the type of divorce discussed here, called ṭalāq, the husband declares divorce from his wife, after which she observes a period of waiting (ʿiddah) amounting to three courses, during which the couple do not have sexual relations, before the divorce is final. These three courses are three menstrual periods, but some disagreement exists over whether the courses (qurūʾ) are marked by the actual menstrual flow, the flows cessation, or by the ritual washing (ghusl) that allows the wife to then perform the canonical prayer. Until the waiting period is over, the husband can still withdraw his intention to divorce and the couple can resume normal marital relations.

**"Husbands Have Better Right to Restore"**

It is not lawful for them to conceal means that they should not conceal any possible pregnancy from the husbands who have just divorced them. That the husbands have better right to restore them during that time means that husbands, being the party who initiated the divorce, retain the right to resume the marriage before the waiting period is over. In Islamic Law the wifes options for divorce do not operate under the rubric of ṭalāq divorce, but under khulʿ divorce, discussed in v. 229 and 4:20. The women appears in brackets in place of the feminine plural pronoun.

**"The Like of What They Owe — and a Degree Over Them"**

According to some, [The women] are owed obligations the like of those they owe means that each side owes something to the other—that is, wives should obey their husbands and husbands should treat their wives well and with respect; for others, it means that women have a right to sexual relations similar to that of men (al-Ṭabarī). It is reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said, I beautify myself for my wife, just as she beautifies herself for me (al-Qurṭubī). For others, it is a question of mutual protection from harm, where the man does not harm the wife through an endless cycle of divorce and reconciliation, and the wife does not harm the husband by hiding what she might be carrying in her womb (al-Ṭabarī).

**A household placed under moral care**

Others mention that the point of marriage is closeness, love, and peace, which should be shared between husband and wife, and al-Rāzī says, One might even say that [in this] the share of the woman is more abundant.

In And men have a degree over them, many commentators understand a kind of noblesse oblige. Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have said, “This degree is a reference to men’s encouraging good relations and their generosity toward women in wealth and virtuous behavior, which means that the one possessing the upper hand must be biased against himself” (al-Qurṭubī). Others state that this degree over them consists of men’s economic advantages and also obligations and their ability to fight in the way of Allah (although some female Companions of the Prophet did participate in fighting) or refers to qualities such as strength and intelligence (al-Qurṭubī).

**The rights concealed in the wording**

Interpreted spiritually, this verse can mean that the soul (nafs) has rights owed to it and rights that it owes, which in the context of Islamic spiritual psychology means that, although the spirit (rūḥ) dominates over the powers of the soul, it is precisely through the soul that spiritual progress takes place. Thus, one must be gentle with the soul, letting it rest when it needs it, to ensure healthy spiritual progress (Aj). The wedding of the soul to the spirit is a common motif in Islamic spiritual literature.

The reference to divorced places a human being who may be dependent, exposed, or unable to defend a claim at the centre of the discussion. Responsibility here is not merely a feeling of affection. It has a form that can be recognized, a limit that can be enforced, and a purpose: to prevent the strong from making the weak carry the cost of decisions they did not control.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:229

> **Divorce may be retracted twice, then the husband must retain ˹his wife˺ with honour or separate ˹from her˺ with grace. It is not lawful for husbands to take back anything of the dowry given to their wives, unless the couple fears not being able to keep within the limits of Allah. So if you fear they will not be able to keep within the limits of Allah, there is no blame if the wife compensates the husband to obtain divorce. These are the limits set by Allah, so do not transgress them. And whoever transgresses the limits of Allah, they are the ˹true˺ wrongdoers.**

### Expanded Commentary

**Twice — and No More**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between divorce and husband. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:229. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:229. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:229.

**"Not Lawful to Take Back Aught"**

A couple can reconcile after a declarative divorce (ṭalāq) only twice. After the third divorce declaration, the divorce is final. The third divorce declaration is referred to either by the phrase release [her] virtuously or, in v. 230, Should he then divorce her (al-Qurṭubī). In the other main type of divorce, called a khulʿ divorce (see also 4:20), the wife initiates the divorce and can give a ransom as part of obtaining the divorce. More precisely, a wifes property becomes material to the khulʿ divorce procedure, while the man may divorce without any transfer of wealth, which is the inverse of the procedure of marriage, where a wife collects a bridewealth from her husband as a part of the marriage contract, but has no financial responsibility within the marriage. Put another way, a man negotiates his way into a marriage through the bridewealth, and a woman can negotiate her way out of a marriage through the khulʿ divorce process.

**Khulʿ — The Wife's Own Door**

It is not lawful for you to take aught from what you have given [your wives] refers to the bridewealth given to wives as stipulated in the marriage contract (see 4:24c); your wives appears in brackets in place of the feminine plural pronoun. The verse makes an exception in cases where a wife may, in the absence of mistreatment from her husband, negotiate a divorce from her husband by returning some or all of her bridewealth. A husband cannot initiate a ṭalāq divorce and then ask for any part of the bridewealth back, except in certain cases, such as a marriage that is not yet consummated, in which case he can expect half to be returned (see v. 237). Nor can he mistreat his wife in order to compel her to seek a khulʿ divorce and thereby regain some or all of the bridewealth.

**"These Are the Limits of Allah — So Transgress Them Not"**

In one example, described as the first instance of such a khulʿ divorce, a wife came to the Prophet and complained about her new husband’s repulsive physical appearance, and the Prophet divorced them after negotiating the return of the two orchards her husband had given her .

The limits set by Allah are those rules established by Allah governing marriage and divorce . A fear that the couple will not uphold the limits set by Allah as a condition for khulʿ divorce is generally interpreted to mean a fear that the couple would not be able to sustain a lawful marriage with its obligations of companionship and sexual relations and its prohibitions against adultery and abuse. Some have concluded that such a fear is not a necessary condition for a khulʿ divorce; others say that both spouses must have that fear.

**A household placed under moral care**

Still others assert that the wifes fear is enough, but that a mans fear alone is not sufficient (al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī); that is, if a wife wishes to remain married, but the husband does not, for whatever reason, a khulʿ divorce is not permissible, and he can take no part of her property as part of a divorce. In the ṭalāq divorce, initiated by the husband, the wife retains all her wealth. Others have interpreted so if you fear to refer to the Muslim communitys judgment of the couple. Indeed, some opinions grant arbiters, chosen by the spouses to help them reconcile their marital differences, the power to divorce them or to recommend divorce, if the arbiters think no reconciliation is possible (see 4:35c).

**The rights concealed in the wording**

For some commentators khulʿ divorce is connected with the presence of discord and animosity in the marriage (nushūz; see commentary on 4:34–35, 128) coming from both sides, as evidenced by the plain sense of the verse, which uses the dual form (that the two should fear). Others deem the discord and animosity operative in the khulʿ divorce to be what originates from the wife in the form of clearly expressed statements of hatred, physical aversion, disrespect, or contempt toward her husband (al-Qurṭubī). But these two opinions are not contradictory, as such negative feelings on the part of the wife, even in the absence of any intentional ill-treatment by her husband, can easily produce negative emotions on the part of the husband. In commentaries on this verse, there is a general message that a bad marriage could lead to other evils such as adultery and social instability and that two people who are denied companionship and intimacy may grow resentful, angry, and open to disobedience (al-Rāzī).

**Time, vulnerability, and restraint**

Opinions vary over the upper limit to be negotiated. Some say it should not exceed the amount of the bridewealth. Others say it can be any amount, since no figure is given in the verse. But even those who allow the amount to exceed the bridewealth think that it is shameful and reprehensible to accept it (al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī).

The reference to divorce places a human being who may be dependent, exposed, or unable to defend a claim at the centre of the discussion. Responsibility here is not merely a feeling of affection. It has a form that can be recognized, a limit that can be enforced, and a purpose: to prevent the strong from making the weak carry the cost of decisions they did not control.

**The difference between power and justice**

Returning at that point is easier than defending a settled habit. The warning is therefore also an opening for repair.

Those habits are where this verse becomes more than information about divorce. They are the place in which assent to 2:229 is either confirmed or quietly withdrawn.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:230

> **So if a husband divorces his wife ˹three times˺, then it is not lawful for him to remarry her until after she has married another man and then is divorced. Then it is permissible for them to reunite, as long as they feel they are able to maintain the limits of Allah. These are the limits set by Allah, which He makes clear for people of knowledge.**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Third Divorce — Finality Restored**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings husband and three into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. Its first term in 2:230 sets the subject, while the later term shows what that subject demands, permits, or exposes. The order of 2:230 gives the reader a path through the verse: begin with what Allah names, follow the consequence, and resist the temptation to turn a living address into a slogan.

The prohibition against the couple remarrying each other after the third divorce declaration unless and until the woman marries and divorces another man is an extension of the logic of limiting declarative divorce (v. 229) and the “forswearing” of marital relations (v. 226). That means that if a man were free to remarry his wife after three divorce declarations, he would then be free to conduct yet another three divorce declarations and repeat the process continuously, thus keeping the wife from the full enjoyment of marriage (through successive waiting periods) while denying her the freedom to marry another.

**The Ḥalālah Its Dreaded Guard-Rail**

Forbidding a man from remarrying a woman after making her wait three sets of three courses (one set after each divorce declaration) limits the harm he can inflict on her and discourages him from declaring divorce, since the prospect of remarrying a woman who is married to someone else is in most cases unlikely. According to most jurists the intervening marriage needs to have been consummated for the original couple to remarry . This condition applies for those who have carried out three divorces; remarriage with only a single divorce declaration is discussed in v. 232.

The reference to husband places a human being who may be dependent, exposed, or unable to defend a claim at the centre of the discussion. Responsibility here is not merely a feeling of affection. It has a form that can be recognized, a limit that can be enforced, and a purpose: to prevent the strong from making the weak carry the cost of decisions they did not control.

**Marked-Clear to People of Knowing**

A useful way to test the verse is to ask what would change if husband were taken seriously when no audience was present. The answer cannot be only a feeling, because 2:230 connects inward recognition with a discernible choice. Nor can it be only an outward display, because the choice in 2:230 loses its Qur'anic meaning when it is made for reputation rather than for Allah. The passage holds intention and action together in 2:230.

**A household placed under moral care**
