## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:233

> **˹Divorced˺ mothers will breastfeed their offspring for two whole years, for those who wish to complete the nursing ˹of their child˺. The child’s father will provide reasonable maintenance and clothing for the mother ˹during that period˺. No one will be charged with more than they can bear. No mother or father should be made to suffer for their child. The ˹father’s˺ heirs are under the same obligation. But if both sides decide—after mutual consultation and consent—to wean a child, then there is no blame on them. And if you decide to have your children nursed by a wet-nurse, it is permissible as long as you pay fairly. Be mindful of Allah, and know that Allah is All-Seeing of what you do.**

### Expanded Commentary

**Two Full Years — The Nursing Statute**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between divorced and offspring. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:233. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:233. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:233.

**The Father's Full Charge**

This verse addresses the status of women who bear children from husbands who have divorced them, since feeding and clothing ones wife is an obligation of marriage in all cases. Two full years is the maximum time period during which the father must provide material support to the nursing mother, although the parents can agree to a shorter period of nursing, as stated later in the verse, by their mutual consent and consultation. The mother can nurse for a shorter period, and the father cannot compel her to continue, but he must provide support if necessary for up to two years of nursing (al-Qurṭubī).

**No Harm's Two Sides**

That the father must provide for them and clothe them means that he must, according to his means, provide what he can. The verse acknowledges that not all fathers can provide equally, since one must do so honorably (bil-maʿrūf), meaning to an honorable or morally acceptable level, which is reinforced by the recognition that no soul is tasked beyond its capacity (cf. 2:286; 6:152; 7:42; 23:62; 65:7). See also 46:15 and 31:14, which discuss the length of pregnancy and nursing.

That neither parent be harmed on account of the child relates to either nursing or custody, or both. The mother is not to harm the father by refusing to nurse his child or by trying to keep the father away, and similarly the father is not to harm the mother by keeping her child from her and refusing to let her nurse the child when she wishes to do so (al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī).

**Weaning by Consent and Consultation**

Several opinions are offered regarding the identity of the heir who has obligations similar to those of the father, should the latter pass away. It is generally understood to refer to the heirs of the father, who inherit a portion of the wealth upon which the nursing mother and child have a claim. Upon the father’s death, during the two-year period, these heirs are responsible for the material support prescribed in this verse (al-Qurṭubī). Others say it refers to agnates (ʿaṣabah, male relatives through the male line), and others consider it to mean any relative too close in blood relation to marry (al-Qurṭubī).

**A household placed under moral care**

Another opinion states that the heir is the child himself or herself, in which case the support would come from what the child inherits from the father, but if there are no such funds, it falls upon the state to support the child, and if the state does not, it falls upon the community (al-Qurṭubī). Some interpret the heir’s obligation to include only the intent not to harm the parent by means of the child, while others say the heir’s obligation also includes the material support to the mother the father would have been obligated to provide (al-Qurṭubī).

If both parents agree, the child can have a wet nurse, who would be paid for by the father, not the mother (al-Qurṭubī).

**The rights concealed in the wording**

Most jurists agree that, so long as she does not remarry (presumably because they reason a father would not willingly allow his child to be raised by another man), the mother has greater right to custody and to raise the child than does the father. There are varying opinions on this matter, and some allow the child to choose after a certain age (al-Qurṭubī).

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:234

> **As for those of you who die and leave widows behind, let them observe a waiting period of four months and ten days. When they have reached the end of this period, then you are not accountable for what they decide for themselves in a reasonable manner. And Allah is All-Aware of what you do.**

### Expanded Commentary

**Four Months and Ten Days — the Widow's Clock**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings leave and observe into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. Its first term in 2:234 sets the subject, while the later term shows what that subject demands, permits, or exposes. The order of 2:234 gives the reader a path through the verse: begin with what Allah names, follow the consequence, and resist the temptation to turn a living address into a slogan.

Widows are to wait four months and ten days before they can remarry, unless they are pregnant, in which case they wait until they deliver, whichever period of time is longer ; this is also discussed in v. 240 and 65:4. What they do concerning themselves refers to their entering into a new marriage after the period of waiting.

**"No Blame Upon You in What They Do Themselves"**

Wait by themselves is taken by some jurists to mean that they cloister themselves in their homes, on the basis of certain aḥādīth that point to widows keeping themselves home and not putting on perfume or ornaments (al-Qurṭubī). Other prominent early jurists, such as Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, say the text simply refers to refraining from marriage.

In contrast to the waiting period outlined here, it is related that in pre-Islamic times widows were often required to wait a year, observing such practices as wearing their worst clothes, neither grooming nor bathing, and marking the end of their mourning by leaving their house; the end of the mourning period was marked by flinging a piece of animal dung and rubbing the front of their bodies with an animal, acts of unclear significance (Ibn Kathīr).

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:235

> **There is no blame on you for subtly showing interest in ˹divorced or widowed˺ women or for hiding ˹the intention˺ in your hearts. Allah knows that you are considering them ˹for marriage˺. ### Expanded Commentary

**Intimating, Not Plighting**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between blame and interest. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:235. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:235. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:235.

**"Allah Knows What Is Within Your Souls"**

Intimating a proposal means that one can express a desire for marriage, yet stop short of proposing and making an agreement. For example, a man can say, “I hope I can marry a righteous woman,” or, “I do not wish to marry any other woman,” or, “I desire to marry,” but he would not be allowed to say, “Promise me you will marry me and not another person” (Ibn Kathīr). Actually contracting a marriage during this time period is forbidden. Save that you speak in an honorable way means that one’s interaction with widows should not go beyond the limits of the intimation mentioned at the start of the verse (Ibn Kathīr). Some say that if two people actually consummate a marriage before the waiting period expires, the two are forbidden to marry each other forever, and the woman must remain unmarried for the remainder of the waiting period from her dead husband and the waiting period from her premature marriage. ## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:237

> **And if you divorce them before consummating the marriage but after deciding on a dowry, pay half of the dowry, unless the wife graciously waives it or the husband graciously pays in full. Graciousness is closer to righteousness. And do not forget kindness among yourselves. Surely Allah is All-Seeing of what you do.**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Consummation Half Measure**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between divorce and deciding. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:237. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:237. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:237.

**"To Forgo Is Nearer to Reverence"**

He whose hand holds the marriage tie is the husband himself, in which case he would forgo the half of the bridal payment that he could legitimately expect to get back . In this case “holding the marriage tie” refers to the husband’s prerogative of divorce (see v. 228), since it is he who is exercising his power to divorce his wife; this verse refers to divorce declared by the husband (ṭalāq), not khulʿ divorce (see v. 229; R). The party nearer to reverence would then be the one who forgoes one’s “half” and allows the other party to have the entirety of the bridewealth after the divorce, thus realizing the virtue of bounteousness among yourselves .

**"Forget Not Bounteousness Among Yourselves"**

Others interpret the holder of the marriage tie to be the legal guardian (wakīl) whose permission is usually necessary for a woman to marry, in which case the wife would, with the guardian’s approval, forgo the half of the bridewealth she had been entitled to keep. The difficulty with this position is that, although the guardian is necessary for marriage, he has no legal control over the bridewealth, which is the personal property of the wife (al-Qurṭubī).

There is an opinion that consummation is not necessary for a man to lose his right to half the bridewealth, and that if the husband is secluded with his wife in such a way that consummation was possible, he must pay the bridewealth in full .

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:239

> **If you are in danger, pray on foot or while riding. But when you are safe, ˹take time to˺ remember Allah for teaching you what you did not know.**

### Expanded Commentary

**Prayer Under Fire**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between danger and riding. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:239. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:239. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:239.

**"When You Are Secure, Remember Allah"**

One can be fearful when in battle or under persecution. Commentators mention that in cases of fear, such as during open warfare, one can pray while riding or walking, whether it is in the direction of the qiblah (facing the Kaʿbah) or not. One can, rather than bow and prostrate, nod and lightly move ones head in a manner corresponding to the motions of the prayer; according to some, one can shorten ones prayers down to one cycle of prayer, rather than two, three, or four (Ibn Kathīr). Prayer in conditions of fighting and fear is discussed in detail in 4:101–2.

The subject of danger joins an act directed to Allah with a consequence visible among people. In 2:239, that union guards against two reductions: worship cannot become a private performance with no social fruit, and social generosity cannot become a substitute for worship. The verse 2:239 asks for an outward practice whose inward intention remains answerable to Allah.

**The act and the intention beneath it**

The standard in 2:239 remains practical because it can be applied before a dispute reaches a court or a crisis reaches its worst point. One can notice the first small departure from danger: an excuse, a concealed obligation, an unexamined desire, or a promise treated as optional. Returning at that point is easier than defending a settled habit. The warning is therefore also an opening for repair.

The relation between danger and riding also protects the verse from two opposite misreadings. It should not be expanded into a claim the wording of 2:239 does not make, but neither should its brevity be used to make it weightless. ## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:243

> **Have you ˹O Prophet˺ not seen those who fled their homes in the thousands for fear of death? Allah said to them, “Die!” then He gave them life. Surely Allah is ever Bountiful to humanity, but most people are ungrateful.**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Thousands Who Fled Death**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between prophet and homes. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:243. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:243.

**Two Doctrines Most Pressed Upon the Madinese**

It is related that this verse refers to a group among the Children of Israel who fled either a plague or war, apparently in disobedience, in order to reach a place of safety, but were nevertheless caused to die, after which a prophet was sent to revive them (al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī). In this context some commentators mention that the Prophet Muhammad commanded people not to flee a place where there was a plague or to travel to a place where there was a plague . Some say that the historical people or time is unimportant, as a theme of the verse is that Allah has the Power of life and death over human beings, that they cannot determine their own life and death, and that the Prophet and believers should take a lesson from this fact, especially since the subsequent verse mentions a command to fight in the way of Allah (al-Qurṭubī).

**The horizon beyond the immediate scene**

Some commentators see this verse as a reference to the story described in Ezekiel 37:1–14, where Ezekiel is commanded to revive a valley filled with dry bones (al-Ṭabarī), but the Biblical account does not contain mention of why the valley was full of bones, and beyond the revival of the dead there are no similarities between the two accounts.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:245

> **Who will lend to Allah a good loan which Allah will multiply many times over? It is Allah ˹alone˺ who decreases and increases ˹wealth˺. And to Him you will ˹all˺ be returned.**

### Expanded Commentary

**"Who Shall Lend Allah?" — The Astonishing Question**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between lend and multiply. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:245. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:245. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:245.

**Withholds and Outstretches**

Some consider this verse to continue the line of thought in the previous one, in which case the goodly loan would be a metaphor for the effort expended and risk undertaken in fighting in the way of Allah. Others believe the verse begins anew and refers to the giving of ones wealth in charity or for religious causes, while still others point out there is no contradiction between these two interpretations (al-Rāzī). On lending Allah a goodly loan, see 5:12; 64:17; 73:20; 57:11c. In all such instances, commentators point out that to serve Allah and do good is always, as it were, a good bargain, and one can also engage in unprofitable transactions, such as when one sells Allahs signs for a paltry price (e.g., 2:41). Allahs multiplication of good is described in 6:160: Whosoever brings a good deed shall have ten times the like thereof, and also discussed in 57:18.

**The Verse the Whole Sūrah Rises From**

“Withholding” and “outstretching” are two very important concepts in Islamic spirituality. The verb “withholds” is related to the state of spiritual contraction (qabḍ), and the verb “outstretches” is related to the state of expansion (basṭ). Interpreted spiritually, this verse describes a threefold process of spiritual realization: inner purification (Allah withholds), the acquisition of the virtues (and outstretches), and finally spiritual realization and illumination (and unto Him shall you be returned). Some Sufis describe contraction and expansion as “two states that follow each other in the heart like the night follows the day.” Contraction and expansion are also related to the twin states of fear and hope, which must be kept in balance in order for a soul to progress spiritually. Seen in another way, when Allah withholds one is exposed to His Quality of Majesty, and when He outstretches, one experiences His Quality of Beauty (Aj).

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:247

> **Their prophet told them, “Allah has appointed Saul to be your king.” They protested, “How can he be our king when some of us are more deserving of kingship than he, and he has not been blessed with vast riches?” He replied, “Allah has chosen him over you and blessed him with knowledge and stature. Allah grants kingship to whoever He wills. And Allah is All-Bountiful, All-Knowing.”**

### Expanded Commentary

**Tālūt — Raised Out of Nowhere**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between prophet and king. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:247. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:247. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:247.

Sauls low social status, which is here the source of the Israelites disdain for his kingship, is mentioned by Saul himself when Samuel first speaks to him in 1 Samuel 9:21: Saul answered, I am only a Benjaminite, from the least of the tribes of Israel, and my family is the humblest of all the families. . . . Why then have you spoken to me in this way? And in 1 Samuel 10:27 the Israelites express their disdain: But some worthless fellows said, How can this man save us? They despised him and brought him no present.

**"He Has Not Been Given Abundance of Wealth"**

The basis for their aversion to Saul as king is similar to that for the aversion of the Quraysh and the Jews to Muhammad at his election as a prophet, namely, his lack of wealth and status among the Quraysh and his non-Jewish lineage among the Jews; see also 3:26c. In the case of Saul, the commentators understand this account to mean that Saul was from neither a kingly nor a priestly line, but hailed from the tribe of Benjamin (al-Rāzī). Sauls intelligence and physical prowess were intrinsic qualities useful for a good leader; the status and wealth expected by the people would be qualities extrinsic to any man, accidental to his nature (al-Rāzī).

Increased him amply in knowledge and body could also be rendered increased him in excellence of knowledge and body. The granting of sovereignty by Allah is also mentioned in 3:26; 4:54; 12:101.

**"Allah Gives His Sovereignty to Whom He Wills"**

The verse's reference to prophet widens the scene beyond the immediate reward or pain. A deed in 2:247 may appear small when measured by public attention, yet its meaning changes when it is known by Allah and carried into the final account. Warning and mercy belong together in 2:247: accountability is serious because the human being is not abandoned to meaninglessness.

The standard in 2:247 remains practical because it can be applied before a dispute reaches a court or a crisis reaches its worst point. ## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:248

> **Their prophet further told them, “The sign of Saul’s kingship is that the Ark will come to you—containing reassurance from your Lord and relics of the family of Moses and the family of Aaron, which will be carried by the angels. Surely in this is a sign for you, if you ˹truly˺ believe.”**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Ark as Credential**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings prophet and sauls into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. Its first term in 2:248 sets the subject, while the later term shows what that subject demands, permits, or exposes. The order of 2:248 gives the reader a path through the verse: begin with what Allah names, follow the consequence, and resist the temptation to turn a living address into a slogan.

**Sakīnah — The Tranquility Word's Winged History**

The commentators relate that the ark was returned, after being either lost or taken in battle, as a sign of Sauls right to lead, though in the case of this passage much or all of the information in the commentaries seems to be based on Biblical or Talmudic material. In the Biblical account, the ark was returned from its capture by the Philistines after they were afflicted with plagues and other torments, but it resided in a private dwelling for many years in Kiriath-jearim, northwest of Jerusalem. Biblical commentators point out that during this time the Israelites were in a state of religious decline and had grown indifferent to the ark; during this period Samuel labored to revive the religion. Indeed, in 1 Chronicles 13:3 David says, We did not turn to it [the ark] in the days of Saul. The fate of the ark during the time of Saul is not described in the Bible except with regard to its neglect.

**A Sign — If They Be Believers**

In v. 248, the ark reenters the life of the Israelites in a way that functions as a sign for Samuel’s truthful prophecy regarding Saul, but no details or chronology are given. From the Qur'anic perspective, it could mean that the chronology conventionally understood from 1 Samuel, in which the ark returns many years before Saul’s anointing, is a misreading—which is possible if one considers the history given in Samuel as that of overlapping strands rather than a linear chronology—and that the ark returned around the time Samuel designated Saul as king.

**A duty that begins with the vulnerable**

That an old but neglected sacred object should return could have had a special significance to the Israelites, leading them to rediscover a part of their own sacred history. Alternatively, it could it be that the prophet (Samuel), in pointing to the ark as a sign, was in effect saying, “The ark has returned to you while I was your judge; so believe my prophecy about Saul” (al-Ṭabarī). In one Muslim account the Israelites, except for a single family who kept the ark, were prevented from coming near the ark from the time of its return from the Philistines until the time of Saul; some understood this to mean that, even though it was not in the possession of another people, the ark and its blessings were inaccessible to the Israelites (al-Ṭabarī).

**The relationship named by the verse**

The tranquility (sakīnah) within it may refer to either an object that would arouse tranquility in the hearts of the Israelites or something, properly referred to as sakīnah, that was contained within it. Some point out that the grammar of the phrase would allow the translation that the ark come to you on account of which there will be tranquility (al-Rāzī). This tranquility (sakīnah) is also mentioned in 9:26, 40; 48:4, 18, 26. If understood as something whose presence would cause tranquility, it might refer to prophecies from books of Moses and Aaron telling of the victories to which Saul would lead them (al-Ṭabarī).

The remnant of Moses and Aaron is given several interpretations, among them the staff of Moses (v. 60), the fragments of stone tablets Moses brought from Sinai (7:150), the manna (see v. 57), and the clothing of Moses and Aaron, including Moses sandals (see 20:12; Q, Ṭ).

The concern with prophet shows that justice is measured most severely where affection, dependence, and power overlap. A person may be generous in public and still wrong a relative or a child in private. The answer cannot be only a feeling, because 2:248 connects inward recognition with a discernible choice. Nor can it be only an outward display, because the choice in 2:248 loses its Qur'anic meaning when it is made for reputation rather than for Allah. The passage holds intention and action together in 2:248.

Prayer, remembrance, generosity, patience, and justice are different acts in 2:248, but they are trained by the same capacity to stand before Allah without constructing a false account. ## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:249

> **When Saul marched forth with his army, he cautioned: “Allah will test you with a river. So whoever drinks ˹his fill˺ from it is not with me, and whoever does not taste it—except a sip from the hollow of his hands—is definitely with me.” They all drank ˹their fill˺ except for a few! When he and the ˹remaining˺ faithful with him crossed the river, they said, “Now we are no match for Goliath and his warriors.” But those ˹believers˺ who were certain they would meet Allah reasoned, “How many times has a small force vanquished a mighty army by the Will of Allah! And Allah is ˹always˺ with the steadfast.”**

### Expanded Commentary

**A River as a Sieve**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between saul and army. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:249. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:249. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:249.

**Goliath's Host and Small Companies**

Some have drawn a parallel between this verse and the account of Gideons crossing the Jordan River in Judges 7:4–7, though the similarities are typological and not historical. In the Gideon account, the test was known to Gideon alone, the army was not aware they were being divided into two categories (those who drank with their mouths and those who did so with their hands), and the purpose was to reduce the armys numbers to three hundred men, so as to show that the Will of Allah could be carried out with a small number of fighters. In the Qur'anic account, Saul openly tests the faith of his soldiers, who are commanded to take only a handful of water and no more.

**The horizon beyond the immediate scene**

From a Qur'anic point of view, Sauls test of his army could be a reenactment of sacred history (Gideon lived before Samuel and Saul), much as parting the waters is a recurring theme in the Old Testament, taking place at the hands of Moses while the Israelites were escaping from the Egyptians through the Red Sea and by the ark when the people were crossing the Jordan during the time of Joshua (Joshua 3:14–17). That this incident echoes Gideons crossing, whose purpose was to show that Allah could defeat many with few, is reinforced by the statement in this verse of those who believed that they would meet their Lord, How many a small company have overcome a large company by Allahs leave! This group deemed they would meet their Lord, meaning they were either certain of the Hereafter or prepared to die (al-Qurṭubī).

**A divine name that governs the meaning**

The verse's reference to saul widens the scene beyond the immediate reward or pain. A deed in 2:249 may appear small when measured by public attention, yet its meaning changes when it is known by Allah and carried into the final account. Warning and mercy belong together in 2:249: accountability is serious because the human being is not abandoned to meaninglessness.

The standard in 2:249 remains practical because it can be applied before a dispute reaches a court or a crisis reaches its worst point. One can notice the first small departure from saul: an excuse, a concealed obligation, an unexamined desire, or a promise treated as optional. Returning at that point is easier than defending a settled habit. The warning is therefore also an opening for repair.

**Mercy and warning held together**

The relation between saul and army also protects the verse from two opposite misreadings. It should not be expanded into a claim the wording of 2:249 does not make, but neither should its brevity be used to make it weightless. Short Qur'anic statements such as 2:249 often function as hinges: they close one movement, open another, and give the next command its moral setting. The careful reader of 2:249 therefore asks what has just been established, what response is now being required, and what kind of character could respond without evasion. Those questions keep 2:249 specific while allowing its guidance to reach a new circumstance.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:250

> **When they advanced to face Goliath and his warriors, they prayed, “Our Lord! Shower us with perseverance, make our steps firm, and give us victory over the disbelieving people.”**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Prayer of the Few**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings advanced and warriors into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. Its first term in 2:250 sets the subject, while the later term shows what that subject demands, permits, or exposes. The order of 2:250 gives the reader a path through the verse: begin with what Allah names, follow the consequence, and resist the temptation to turn a living address into a slogan.

The Qur'anic account here assumes a general knowledge of the story of Saul, David, and Goliath: though a young boy, David is appointed by Saul to face Goliath as the Israelites champion and fells the huge warrior with a stone from his sling (cf. 1 Samuel 17). He was given wisdom, meaning that, as a major prophet in the Islamic tradition, he inherited the prophethood of Samuel, and sovereignty, meaning he inherited the kingship of Saul (al-Ṭabarī). For further description of David and his prophethood and reign, see 38:17–29.

**A Duʿāʾ to Keep in Every Throat**

Were it not for Allahs repelling people, some by means of others is similar to the message of 22:40, where the destruction of houses of worship is thwarted by this repelling. Here it is the corruption of the earth as such that is averted through this repelling of some by others. Commentators state that Allah uses good people to repel the effect of evil people, but offer different interpretations as to who precisely repels whom. Some say this refers to the Substitutes (abdāl), human beings who are inwardly members of a spiritual hierarchy through which Allah dispenses grace and protection to the world; they are forty in number, and when one dies, that one is replaced by another person (al-Qurṭubī).

**The horizon beyond the immediate scene**

Others interpret it to mean that the prayerful and the pious are used to repel those who do not pray and are impious, whose sins would otherwise destroy humanity, or that the obedient repel the evil of the disobedient (al-Ṭabarī). In a ḥadīth the Prophet says, Allah repels the punishment of the one who does not pray by means of the one who prays, and of the one who does not give alms by means of the one who gives alms, and of the one who does not fast by means of the one who fasts, and of the one who does not make the ḥajj by means of the one who makes ḥajj, and of the one who does not struggle by means of the one who struggles.

The most balanced response to 2:251 is neither to make the passage vague nor to claim more than it says. Its boundaries are part of its guidance. Within them, the verse can illuminate a new situation because its underlying moral relation remains stable: defeated is joined to killed, and the person is responsible for how that relation is honoured.

The wording of 2:251 gives the reader a useful order of questions about defeated. What does the term defeated mean in ordinary Arabic, what does the surrounding sentence restrict it to, and what consequence follows when the command is obeyed or refused in 2:251? ## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:252

> **These are Allah’s revelations which We recite to you ˹O Prophet˺ in truth. And you are truly one of the messengers.**

### Expanded Commentary

**Recited Signs, Confirmed Messenger**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings allahs and prophet into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. Its first term in 2:252 sets the subject, while the later term shows what that subject demands, permits, or exposes. The order of 2:252 gives the reader a path through the verse: begin with what Allah names, follow the consequence, and resist the temptation to turn a living address into a slogan.

This verse is addressed directly to the Prophet, and some commentators see vv. 243–51 as an encouragement for the Prophet in his struggles with his own enemies, reminding him that the messengers and prophets of the past underwent similar trials (al-Ṭabarī).

**The verse in its immediate setting**

The mention of allahs gives the verse a definite centre. Its meaning in 2:252 is not a general meditation on religion but an explanation of what this word requires in the situation named here. The passage at 2:252 moves between belief, action, and consequence, so a sound reading must preserve all three rather than allowing one attractive phrase to swallow the rest.

A useful way to test the verse is to ask what would change if allahs were taken seriously when no audience was present. The answer cannot be only a feeling, because 2:252 connects inward recognition with a discernible choice. Nor can it be only an outward display, because the choice in 2:252 loses its Qur'anic meaning when it is made for reputation rather than for Allah. The passage holds intention and action together in 2:252.

**The central term and its range**

The relation between allah’s and prophet also protects the verse from two opposite misreadings. It should not be expanded into a claim the wording of 2:252 does not make, but neither should its brevity be used to make it weightless. Short Qur'anic statements such as 2:252 often function as hinges: they close one movement, open another, and give the next command its moral setting. The careful reader of 2:252 therefore asks what has just been established, what response is now being required, and what kind of character could respond without evasion. Those questions keep 2:252 specific while allowing its guidance to reach a new circumstance.

**What the early commentators preserve**

The choice of the word allahs in 2:252 also matters. It leaves room for the full context of 2:252 instead of allowing one translation gloss to carry every shade of meaning. Classical Arabic often places a broad word inside a narrow scene; in 2:252, the surrounding clauses determine whether the emphasis falls on an act, an intention, a condition, or a consequence. Here the reader should let the sentence do that work.

The exegetical tradition approaches allahs from more than one angle, but its differences are more useful when their shared question is made visible. The commentators ask what the wording of 2:252 includes, what it excludes, and how it fits with the other passages of the Qur'an. A responsible reading can preserve those alternatives in 2:252 without pretending that every possibility has equal strength.

**The reasoning within the wording**

There is also a distinction between understanding allahs and using it as a label for other people. The first task belongs to learning; the second requires evidence, fairness, and awareness of one's own motives in 2:252. The verse 2:252 addresses the reader before it supplies material for judging a neighbour. Its warning becomes safer and more productive when self-examination comes first.

The theology and practical instruction of 2:252 therefore support one another. If Allah knows or commands prophet, that knowledge or command changes how a person handles time, power, money, speech, and private desire. A doctrine that never reaches those choices has not yet been read at the level demanded by 2:252.

**The theological question beneath the sentence**

An ordinary example makes the moral structure of 2:252 visible without replacing the revelation. Two people may perform an outwardly similar act involving allahs; one may be protecting a right, while the other is seeking praise, escaping a duty, or taking advantage of confusion. The act's surface does not settle its value. Intention, circumstance, and the rights of others complete the judgment.

The surrounding verses keep the reader from isolating allahs from the rest of life. In 2:252, revelation corrects the mind but also trains habits: how a person speaks when challenged, gives when unseen, waits when angry, and returns after error. Those habits are where this verse becomes more than information about allahs. They are the place in which assent to 2:252 is either confirmed or quietly withdrawn.

**The surrounding passage as a guide**

The most balanced response to 2:252 is neither to make the passage vague nor to claim more than it says. Its boundaries are part of its guidance. Within them, the verse can illuminate a new situation because its underlying moral relation remains stable: allahs is joined to prophet, and the person is responsible for how that relation is honoured.

The wording of 2:252 gives the reader a useful order of questions about allahs. What does the term allahs mean in ordinary Arabic, what does the surrounding sentence restrict it to, and what consequence follows when the command is obeyed or refused in 2:252? These questions prevent a commentary on 2:252 from becoming a list of slogans. They make the act of interpretation answerable to grammar, context, and the moral end of this passage at 2:252.

**A distinction the verse requires**

The commentators sometimes preserve more than one report about the setting of 2:252. Such reports should be weighed rather than treated as interchangeable decoration. An occasion can explain why a question arose, but the wording of 2:252 determines how far the guidance travels. The verse speaks first to the situation that occasioned it and then to every reader who meets the same relation between allahs and prophet.

In 2:252, the distinction between public appearance and inward truth is especially relevant. A person may use the language of allahs while arranging the act around another purpose. Allah's judgment in 2:252 is not limited to the visible outline, yet the inner intention is not an excuse for ignoring the rights and forms that the revelation establishes. Sincerity completes obedience; it does not cancel it.

**From principle to practice**

One can see the social wisdom of 2:252 in a small everyday case. When people share responsibility for allahs, uncertainty about the duty tends to fall on the person with less power or less information. A clear moral rule changes that balance. In 2:252, it tells the stronger party what must not be taken, and gives the weaker party language with which to name the wrong.

In 2:252, the verse also sits within the Qur'an's larger refusal to separate worship from truthfulness. Prayer, remembrance, generosity, patience, and justice are different acts in 2:252, but they are trained by the same capacity to stand before Allah without constructing a false account. The statement in 2:252 strengthens that capacity by making one particular choice visible.

A reader who finds the command in 2:252 difficult should distinguish difficulty from impossibility. For 2:252, difficulty may be the place where desire, habit, or social pressure is being corrected; impossibility is a separate legal and moral question. The passage does not praise needless hardship, but it does not permit comfort to redefine allahs until the demand disappears.

The final emphasis of 2:252 returns to responsibility. No explanation of allahs is complete if it leaves the reader with information about earlier communities but no question about present conduct. The verse 2:252 asks what can be repaired now: a promise kept, a right restored, a motive purified, or a harmful practice abandoned. That is where knowledge becomes guidance.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:253

> **We have chosen some of those messengers above others. Allah spoke directly to some, and raised some high in rank. To Jesus, son of Mary, We gave clear proofs and supported him with the holy spirit. If Allah had willed, succeeding generations would not have fought ˹among themselves˺ after receiving the clear proofs. But they differed—some believed while others disbelieved. Yet if Allah had willed, they would not have fought one another. But Allah does what He wills.**

### Expanded Commentary

**Ranks Among the Messengers**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between chosen and others. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:253. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:253. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:253.

**Jesus and the Holy Spirit**

This verse, which states that some prophets are favored above others, and others like it (3:163, ranked in degrees) are usually understood in light of others that command believers to say, We make no distinction between any of His messengers (v. 285; see also 2:136; 3:84). In Islamic belief this ranking in degrees is understood to pertain to the prophets missions, not their individual spiritual perfections. Thus, all prophets are considered equally to be protected from sin (maʿṣūm), but are given varying levels of earthly power (Solomon had a great earthly kingdom, Jesus did not), different kinds of miraculous signs (Moses staff, Solomons commanding the wind), and are sent to different segments of humanity (in Islamic belief the Prophet Muhammad was sent to all people, while other prophets were sent only to their own). To whom Allah spoke is usually considered to mean Moses specifically (see 7:143).

Jesus strengthening with the Holy Spirit is also mentioned in v. 87 and 5:110; and in 16:102 the Holy Spirit is mentioned in connection with Muhammad. See 2:87c, where this Spirit is variously identified as the Spirit Allah breathed into human beings (15:29), the Archangel Gabriel, or the Gospel itself, all of which share the quality of being life-giving, whether it is bodily quickening or the nourishment of the heart and intelligence (al-Rāzī). The word holy, or sacred (qudus), can also mean pure.

Fighting after the clear proofs had come refers to the conflict between communities who have received Divine revelation; on this question see also 2:213c as well as 3:19; 42:14; 45:17; 98:1.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:255

> **Allah! There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him, the EverLiving, All-Sustaining. Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Who could possibly intercede with Him without His permission? He ˹fully˺ knows what is ahead of them and what is behind them, but no one can grasp any of His knowledge—except what He wills ˹to reveal˺. His Seat encompasses the heavens and the earth, and the preservation of both does not tire Him. For He is the Most High, the Greatest.**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Greatest Verse**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between worthy and everliving. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:255. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:255. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:255.

This verse is known as Āyat al-Kursī, the Pedestal Verse, sometimes rendered Throne Verse, and is perhaps the most well known single verse of the Qur'an, taking its name from the Pedestal (kursī) mentioned in it. It is often recited by Muslims setting out on a journey or seeking either spiritual or physical protection; and like the short sūrahs toward the end of the Qur'an, it is often one of the first passages Muslims memorize. The Prophet told his Companions to recite it before going to sleep, identified it as the greatest verse (āyah) of the Qur'an, and said that it was a fourth of the Qur'an.

**Al-Ḥayy, Al-Qayyūm — The Two Mother-Names**

This is one among many other aḥādīth that speak of its special place (Ibn Kathīr). It is one of the most common passages of the Qur'an to adorn mosques and private homes and is often carried on ones person in the form of pendant, amulet, or similar object. There is no god but He also appears in v. 163; 3:2 (where the Living, the Self-Subsisting also appears); 3:6; 4:87; 6:102; 7:158; and in many other places. Within the text of the Qur'an, the shahādah, or testimony of faith, takes the form Allah, there is no god but He much more often than There is no god but Allah.

**No Slumber, No Sleep**

The Living (al-Ḥayy) is, doctrinally speaking, one of the most important Divine Names in Islam, considered to be among the mothers of the Names (ummahāt al-asmāʾ), and occupies a place in Islamic theology conceptually equivalent to Being. Theologically, a living being is that which is able to fully actualize all its perfections (al-Rāzī). Thus, in describing Allahs fundamental perfections, Muslims often say that Allahs Power is directed by His Will, which is determined by His Knowledge, all of which depend on His Life. The Self-Subsisting translates al-Qayyūm, an intensive form of a root meaning to stand, to sustain, or to establish, which means that Allah subsists through Himself, but also that all things subsist through Him .

**"Unto Him Belongs Whatsoever Is"**

Slumber (sinah) and sleep (nawm) are usually understood to mean a kind of dozing and deep sleep, respectively, and Allahs eternal wakefulness is connected by commentators with protecting [the heavens and the earth] tires Him not. It also means that He is always aware of His creation, and there is no interruption in this awareness. The question of intercession (shafāʿah) is also discussed in v. 48, where the plain sense of the verse would seem to deny the possibility of anyone interceding on behalf of anyone else before Allah. Here, the possibility of intercession is affirmed conditionally, by posing a question regarding who could intercede with Allah save by His leave.

In Islamic belief, the most significant kind of intercession is carried out by the Prophet on the Day of Judgment for the sake of his community, but also for all of the world, a status that Muslims understand to be conferred upon him by virtue of his praiseworthy station (maqām maḥmūd), mentioned in 17:79.

**The Pedestal and the Unwearied Sustainer**

However, many Muslims, for example, the theologian al-Ghazzālī, have said that intercession is also granted to the saints and even ordinary believers in keeping with their spiritual rank. In Shiite doctrine, intercession is also available through the Imams, who play a central role in intercession for the faithful. In one respect, and as discussed in 2:48c, without the reality of intercession there would be no meaning to the prayers of forgiveness the angels make on behalf of human beings (e.g., 40:7) or to those prayers human beings make on behalf of other human beings (e.g., 12:97–98; 24:62, which commands the Prophet, Seek forgiveness for them from Allah).

**The horizon beyond the immediate scene**

Indeed, anytime one prays for someone else, one is affirming a belief in intercession, because one believes that Allah responds to that prayer. In this sense, intercession is a special kind of supplicatory prayer. Many other verses convey a message similar to There is no intercessor, save by His leave (10:3; 19:87; 20:109; 21:28; 39:44; 43:86; 53:26), meaning that intercession itself can be performed only if the Divine Will permits it. Other verses that deny intercession do so for those who do wrong or disbelieve (40:18; 74:48), and still others say that Allah is the only intercessor (6:51, 70; 32:4; 39:44), which means ultimately it is only He who intercedes.

**A divine name that governs the meaning**

That which is before them refers to the Hereafter, and that which is behind them refers to the life of the world, or the two phrases can mean what is to come after people die and what happened before they were created. They may also refer to good and evil deeds, those they have committed and those they have yet to carry out (al-Rāzī). The pronoun them refers to all those who would intercede and all those for whom intercession is offered (al-Rāzī).

Knowledge here is used in the sense of what is known (al-Rāzī). A similar passage speaks of Allah as Knower of the Unseen; He does not disclose His Unseen to anyone, save to the one whom He approves as a messenger (72:26–27). In 2:32 the angels say to Allah, We have no knowledge save what Thou hast taught us.

**Mercy and warning held together**

Some interpret the Pedestal (kursī) to be the “place of the feet,” where one places one’s feet while sitting on a throne, hence the common translation of kursī as “Footstool,” but this translation is problematic, especially since commentators often see kursī as another name for the Throne (ʿarsh; Ṭ, R). Since a pedestal can mean a throne as well as that upon which a throne rests (and hence where one places one’s feet), the rendering of “pedestal” for kursī is preferable. Indeed, in many Islamic cosmologies the Pedestal is above the cosmos, and the Throne is above the Pedestal, a symbolism that would collapse with the use of “footstool” to translate kursī, since a footstool sits in front of a throne, not underneath it.

**The deed before its final account**

There are various aḥādīth that state that the Pedestal encompasses the heavens and the earth, and the Throne encompasses the Pedestal (Ibn Kathīr). According to Ibn ʿAbbās the heavens and the earth in comparison to the Pedestal are like a ring cast into the wilderness (Ibn Kathīr). Others interpret Pedestal to mean knowledge, sovereignty, or authority, used metonymously here the way one uses “the crown” to refer to a monarch (al-Rāzī). Muslims attempt to avoid the two extremes of interpreting such passages as only metaphor or allegory, which allows human beings to read their own desires into the meaning of the Qur'an, and literalistic anthropomorphism, which assigns to Allah location in space and feet comparable to our own.

In esoteric commentaries on the Qur'an, both kursī and ʿarsh possessed specific symbolic meanings, and the verse is seen to contain in its inner meaning a whole cosmology.

Protecting them, referring to the aforementioned heavens and earth, means that Allah sustains their very being encompassing the whole created order. Tires Him not can also mean “is not difficult for Him” (al-Rāzī) or it does not cause Him to stop.

The verse's reference to worthy widens the scene beyond the immediate reward or pain. A deed in 2:255 may appear small when measured by public attention, yet its meaning changes when it is known by Allah and carried into the final account. ## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:256

> **Let there be no compulsion in religion, for the truth stands out clearly from falsehood. So whoever renounces false gods and believes in Allah has certainly grasped the firmest, unfailing hand-hold. And Allah is AllHearing, All-Knowing.**

### Expanded Commentary

**"No Coercion in Religion" — The Charter Flourish**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings compulsion and stands into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. Its first term in 2:256 sets the subject, while the later term shows what that subject demands, permits, or exposes. The order of 2:256 gives the reader a path through the verse: begin with what Allah names, follow the consequence, and resist the temptation to turn a living address into a slogan.

**Truth Clear from Error — Enough**

Similar statements regarding faith are also found in 10:99–100: And had thy Lord willed, all those who are on the earth would have believed all together. Wouldst thou compel men till they become believers? It is not for a soul to believe, save by Allahs Leave; and 18:29: And say, It is the truth from your Lord! So whosoever will, let him believe, and whosoever will, let him disbelieve (see also 76:3; 2:217c). Some report that this verse was revealed in connection with some Muslims who had children among the Banū Naḍīr, a Jewish tribe that was exiled by the Muslim community from Madinah after they were found plotting against the Prophet.

**The Handhold Unbreakable — al-ʿUrwah al-Wuthqā**

Before the coming of Islam, some women of Yathrib (later Madinah) whose children died in infancy made a vow that, if they had children who survived, they would have them raised Jewish, which is how these children came to be among the Banū Naḍīr. These Muslim parents questioned whether they should force their children to join the Muslim community (al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī). Another account describes a Muslim man whose two sons became Christians and left for Syria with the merchants who had converted them (al-Ṭabarī). And a third account mentions that some Muslims were wet-nursed by Jews, and when the Jewish clans to which they belonged were exiled, they wanted to leave with them and become Jews, but their families forced them to remain Muslims (al-Ṭabarī).

**No Compulsion — Because the Handhold Takes Care of Itself**

According to some sources this verse refers specifically to the People of the Book or to anyone from whom one can take the jizyah (see 9:29c; IK, R). Indeed, many argue that the import of this verse is not absolute, since the Prophet, in his campaign and ultimate victory against the idolatrous Arabs, did not give them the option of remaining idolaters or paying the jizyah . The Arabs were in fact forced to abandon idol worship, although some disagree over whether they could become Jews and Christians and fall under the protected status of There is no coercion in religion (al-Rāzī).

**The horizon beyond the immediate scene**

This position would entail, in effect, that among a certain group of religions recognized by Islam (including Judaism, Christianity, and Zoroastrianism), there is no coercion in religion. Others argue that this verse was abrogated by those verses that command Muslims to fight (e.g., 9:5), but this interpretation is not chronologically consistent with the three possible occasions of revelation for this verse, which all involve conditions resulting from conflict with the Jews, who were banished by force. This shows, as do many other verses in the Qur'an, that the fighting Muslims carried out was motivated by political circumstances and not the desire to convert.

**A divine name that governs the meaning**

More important, coercion in religion negates the idea of responsibility before Allah (taklīf), in which one is taken to account for ones actions in both this life and the Hereafter (al-Rāzī). As an ethical or moral pronouncement, this verse is not subject to abrogation at all (see 2:106c). The Makkan idolaters were a special case, because they had been for years the primary threat to the very existence of Islam as a religion. Although forced conversions were not completely unknown in later Islamic history (including from Sunnism to Shiism and vice versa), they can be counted as rare exceptions to the historical rule.

For a more detailed treatment of these questions, see the essay Conquest and Conversion, War and Peace in the Qur'an.

**Mercy and warning held together**

Sound judgment translates rushd, which also means maturity and being rightly guided; error translates ghayy, which also carries the sense of transgression and temptation. False deities renders ṭāghūt, a word that seems to be related to the verb meaning to rebel and that is interpreted variously to refer to Satan, magicians, soothsayers, idols, or any being who rebels and trespasses against Allah (al-Rāzī); for a longer discussion, see 4:51–52c. The unfailing handhold (cf. 31:22) refers to either faith or the shahādah, There is no god but Allah (lā ilāha illaLlāh). The word for breaks refers to fractures that do not show or cause separation, meaning that the handhold does not give way even slightly or imperceptibly.

**The deed before its final account**

The verse's reference to compulsion widens the scene beyond the immediate reward or pain. A deed in 2:256 may appear small when measured by public attention, yet its meaning changes when it is known by Allah and carried into the final account. Warning and mercy belong together in 2:256: accountability is serious because the human being is not abandoned to meaninglessness.

A useful way to test the verse is to ask what would change if compulsion were taken seriously when no audience was present. The answer cannot be only a feeling, because 2:256 connects inward recognition with a discernible choice. Nor can it be only an outward display, because the choice in 2:256 loses its Qur'anic meaning when it is made for reputation rather than for Allah. The passage holds intention and action together in 2:256.

**Why the promise or threat is just**

An ordinary example makes the moral structure of 2:256 visible without replacing the revelation. Two people may perform an outwardly similar act involving compulsion; one may be protecting a right, while the other is seeking praise, escaping a duty, or taking advantage of confusion. The act's surface does not settle its value. Intention, circumstance, and the rights of others complete the judgment.

The surrounding verses keep the reader from isolating compulsion from the rest of life. In 2:256, revelation corrects the mind but also trains habits: how a person speaks when challenged, gives when unseen, waits when angry, and returns after error. Those habits are where this verse becomes more than information about compulsion. They are the place in which assent to 2:256 is either confirmed or quietly withdrawn.

The most balanced response to 2:256 is neither to make the passage vague nor to claim more than it says. Its boundaries are part of its guidance. Within them, the verse can illuminate a new situation because its underlying moral relation remains stable: compulsion is joined to stands, and the person is responsible for how that relation is honoured.

The wording of 2:256 gives the reader a useful order of questions about compulsion. What does the term compulsion mean in ordinary Arabic, what does the surrounding sentence restrict it to, and what consequence follows when the command is obeyed or refused in 2:256? These questions prevent a commentary on 2:256 from becoming a list of slogans. They make the act of interpretation answerable to grammar, context, and the moral end of this passage at 2:256.

The commentators sometimes preserve more than one report about the setting of 2:256. Such reports should be weighed rather than treated as interchangeable decoration. An occasion can explain why a question arose, but the wording of 2:256 determines how far the guidance travels. The verse speaks first to the situation that occasioned it and then to every reader who meets the same relation between compulsion and stands.

In 2:256, the distinction between public appearance and inward truth is especially relevant. A person may use the language of compulsion while arranging the act around another purpose. Allah's judgment in 2:256 is not limited to the visible outline, yet the inner intention is not an excuse for ignoring the rights and forms that the revelation establishes. Sincerity completes obedience; it does not cancel it.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:257

> **Allah is the Guardian of the believers—He brings them out of darkness and into light. As for the disbelievers, their guardians are false gods who lead them out of light and into darkness. It is they who will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever.**

### Expanded Commentary

**Walī — The Allies in High**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between guardian and darkness. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:257. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:257. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:257.

On the concept of Protector (walī), which can also mean ally and friend, see 3:28c; 4:88–90c. The symbolism of light and darkness, which appears throughout the Qur'an, is presented here with an explicit symmetry describing the ascent into light and the plunge into darkness; also see 5:16c; 24:35c. For the majority of commentators, light and darkness refer to belief or faith (īmān) and disbelief or denial (kufr), or guidance and error (al-Ṭabarī). Going from darkness into the light is also mentioned in 5:16; 14:1, 5; 33:43; 57:9; 65:11.

**The deed before its final account**

One can see the social wisdom of 2:257 in a small everyday case. When people share responsibility for guardian, uncertainty about the duty tends to fall on the person with less power or less information. A clear moral rule changes that balance. In 2:257, it tells the stronger party what must not be taken, and gives the weaker party language with which to name the wrong.

Here the reader should let the sentence do that work.

The commentators ask what the wording of 2:257 includes, what it excludes, and how it fits with the other passages of the Qur'an. ## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:259

> **Or ˹are you not aware of˺ the one who passed by a city which was in ruins. He wondered, “How could Allah bring this back to life after its destruction?” So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years then brought him back to life. Allah asked, “How long have you remained ˹in this state˺?” He replied, “Perhaps a day or part of a day.” Allah said, “No! You have remained here for a hundred years! Just look at your food and drink— they have not spoiled. ˹But now˺ look at ˹the remains of˺ your donkey! And ˹so˺ We have made you into a sign for humanity. And look at the bones ˹of the donkey˺, how We bring them together then clothe them with flesh!” When this was made clear to him, he declared, “˹Now˺ I know that Allah is Most Capable of everything.”**

### Expanded Commentary

**The Town Upon Its Roofs**

The force of this verse lies in the connection between aware and ruins. A reader can miss that force by isolating one phrase and treating it as a general maxim in 2:259. The verse itself is more exact. It speaks to a particular condition in the sūrah and directs attention to the kind of response that condition requires in 2:259. Reading the terms together keeps both the theology and the practical instruction in view at 2:259.

Commentators typically identify the man in this verse as Ezra, but others mention Ezekiel and even Khiḍr (see Sūrah 18), which is why the thou is used in the translation. Others say that this verse refers not to a saint or prophet, but to a disbeliever who is shown the reality of Resurrection (al-Rāzī). Fallen upon its roofs means that the roofs had collapsed and the walls fell onto them; the word for fallen (khāwiyah) also evokes the sense of “empty.”

The question How long hast thou tarried? is also asked of the sleepers in the cave in 18:19 and the resurrected soul on the Day of Judgment (23:112). Some say that the bones of the donkey were made to come back to life and be clothed with flesh, though others believe this phrase refers to the man himself (al-Rāzī).

It is thought by some that Allahs making this person a sign means that he was made a prophet (al-Ṭabarī), but elsewhere Pharaoh was also made a sign (10:92), and he is the opposite of a prophet. If this person is understood to be a prophet, his question is not taken as one of pernicious doubt, but in the same spirit as the question posed by Abraham in v. 260: My Lord, show me how Thou givest life to the dead.

The wording around aware assumes that revelation is meant to be heard with intelligence and humility together. ## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:260

> **And ˹remember˺ when Abraham said, “My Lord! Show me how you give life to the dead.” Allah responded, “Do you not believe?” Abraham replied, “Yes I do, but just so my heart can be reassured.” Allah said, “Then bring four birds, train them to come to you, ˹then cut them into pieces,˺ and scatter them on different hilltops. Then call them back, they will fly to you in haste. And ˹so you will˺ know that Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.”**

### Expanded Commentary

**"Show Me How" — The Friend Asks His Friend**

At this point in al-Baqarah, the wording brings abraham and dead into one moral frame. The sentence should not be detached from that relationship. Its first term in 2:260 sets the subject, while the later term shows what that subject demands, permits, or exposes. The order of 2:260 gives the reader a path through the verse: begin with what Allah names, follow the consequence, and resist the temptation to turn a living address into a slogan.

**Four Birds, Every Mountain**

The verse implies no context for Abrahams question, but commentators nevertheless record several possibilities. Abraham saw a scene on a coast where creatures of the sea, land, and air were all eating other creatures and wondered how resurrection could bring all the pieces of these animals together; or it was part of his exchange with his antagonist in v. 258, where the sign would have given Abraham a stronger hand or lent support to his message to other people; or it may have been in connection with the sacrifice of his son or that Abraham wanted confirmation of his special status as prophet.

**Mighty, Wise — The Twin Seals**

Many interpret it spiritually to mean the revival of dead hearts through the Spirit (al-Rāzī). Dost thou not believe? is understood to be a kind of implicit affirmation of Abrahams faith, as if to say, You believe, so why are you asking? That my heart may be at peace evokes other Qur'anic references, such as 89:27, where the soul at peace is invited to enter Paradise, and 13:28, where souls are at peace in the remembrance of Allah. Here commentators grapple with the idea that Abraham would be out of this state of peace.

**The first movement of a guided life**

Some suggest that there are degrees of spiritual knowledge, and that Abraham is speaking of going from one depth of understanding to another, not that he is expressing doubt about Allahs existence or His Power (al-Rāzī). Since believers acknowledge no end to the Glories of Allah, Abrahams question can be seen as an expression of a desire to witness ever more of Allahs Self-Disclosure, to use the language often employed by Sufis. Regarding this verse a ḥadīth says, We have more right to doubt than did Abraham. Abrahams doubt was an entreaty for more knowledge, not a hesitation about Allahs existence.

Even the Prophet Muhammad is commanded to say, My Lord! Increase me in knowledge! (20:114), which is not meant to highlight the Prophets ignorance, but to point to Allahs Limitlessness and His infinite Reality.

**Belief made visible in conduct**

The verb in make them be drawn to thee is understood by many, perhaps even a majority, to mean “cut,” though this interpretation leaves the difficulty of the place of the prepositional phrase to thee (al-Rāzī). According to this interpretation, Abraham takes four birds (peacock, eagle, raven, and rooster), cuts them up into pieces, and then places them on four mountains, representing the four cardinal directions. He then calls them, at which point the scattered parts of the birds reassemble into their original forms and come flying back to him. According to one reading, the eagle represents lust for food; the rooster, lust for sex; the crow, excessive curiosity; and the peacock, vanity, though many different lists of birds are to be found in the commentaries (al-Rāzī).

**The choice hidden inside the command**

The other interpretation, reflected in the translation, is that there is no killing of the birds mentioned in the verse. Rather, Abraham first made each bird be drawn to him, then placed them, alive, each on a mountain, and then called them to himself. This interpretation would then represent the reunification of souls and their bodies with the ease of a man calling to a bird, which comes in haste to him (al-Rāzī).

It is related that Ibn ʿAbbās said of Abrahams question and Allahs gentle response to it, There is no more hopeful verse in the Qur'an than this one. The colleague in conversation with Ibn ʿAbbās said that for him the most hopeful verse was 39:53: O My servants who have been prodigal to the detriment of their own souls! Despair not of Allahs Mercy. Truly Allah forgives all sins (Ibn Kathīr).

**How guidance becomes discernment**

The verse describes abraham not as a private opinion but as a direction that changes perception and conduct. In 2:260, guidance is recognized by what it makes a person do with knowledge, power, and desire. For 2:260, inward assent is linked to an observable response: the heart's claim is tested by the path it chooses when the claim becomes costly.

A useful way to test the verse is to ask what would change if abraham were taken seriously when no audience was present. The answer cannot be only a feeling, because 2:260 connects inward recognition with a discernible choice. Nor can it be only an outward display, because the choice in 2:260 loses its Qur'anic meaning when it is made for reputation rather than for Allah. The passage holds intention and action together in 2:260.

**The contrast drawn by the verse**

The commentators sometimes preserve more than one report about the setting of 2:260. Such reports should be weighed rather than treated as interchangeable decoration. An occasion can explain why a question arose, but the wording of 2:260 determines how far the guidance travels. The verse speaks first to the situation that occasioned it and then to every reader who meets the same relation between abraham and dead.

In 2:260, the distinction between public appearance and inward truth is especially relevant. A person may use the language of abraham while arranging the act around another purpose. Allah's judgment in 2:260 is not limited to the visible outline, yet the inner intention is not an excuse for ignoring the rights and forms that the revelation establishes. Sincerity completes obedience; it does not cancel it.

**Certainty, doubt, and moral action**

One can see the social wisdom of 2:260 in a small everyday case. When people share responsibility for abraham, uncertainty about the duty tends to fall on the person with less power or less information. A clear moral rule changes that balance. In 2:260, it tells the stronger party what must not be taken, and gives the weaker party language with which to name the wrong.

In 2:260, the verse also sits within the Qur'an's larger refusal to separate worship from truthfulness. Prayer, remembrance, generosity, patience, and justice are different acts in 2:260, but they are trained by the same capacity to stand before Allah without constructing a false account. The statement in 2:260 strengthens that capacity by making one particular choice visible.

A reader who finds the command in 2:260 difficult should distinguish difficulty from impossibility. For 2:260, difficulty may be the place where desire, habit, or social pressure is being corrected; impossibility is a separate legal and moral question. The passage does not praise needless hardship, but it does not permit comfort to redefine abraham until the demand disappears.

The final emphasis of 2:260 returns to responsibility. No explanation of abraham is complete if it leaves the reader with information about earlier communities but no question about present conduct. The verse 2:260 asks what can be repaired now: a promise kept, a right restored, a motive purified, or a harmful practice abandoned. That is where knowledge becomes guidance.

The choice of the word abraham in 2:260 also matters. It leaves room for the full context of 2:260 instead of allowing one translation gloss to carry every shade of meaning. Classical Arabic often places a broad word inside a narrow scene; in 2:260, the surrounding clauses determine whether the emphasis falls on an act, an intention, a condition, or a consequence. Here the reader should let the sentence do that work.
